Jeff Pfeffer.blurb: Big Jeff borrowed his nickname from his older brother, who looked like heavyweight champ Jim Jeffries. A 6'2" Brooklyn workhorse, he won 25 games with a 1.91 ERA in 1916 to help the Robins to a pennant, and he was the one who pushed the club to sign lefty Sherry Smith, a teammate of his from the minors. Fittingly, both show up on your deadball rosters.

Hank Gowdy.blurb: The first active major leaguer to enlist in World War I, and he served again in World War II. Gowdy started as a first baseman until John McGraw told him to learn catching if he wanted to stick in the majors. He starred for the 1914 Braves in their famous World Series win.

Pop Corkhill.blurb: A defensive template for his time: from 1883 to 1892 Corkhill finished top-10 in fielding percentage eight times and in range factor seven times. His .254 career average kept him out of Hall of Fame talk, but deadball scholars keep rediscovering the glove. OOTP's field agrees: he's on almost every Silver roster.

Nap Lajoie.blurb: The first superstar in American League history. At 6'1" and 200 pounds, Lajoie was huge for his era yet glided around second base, leading the league in putouts five times and double plays five times over a 21-year career, while being one of the most feared hitters of the Deadball Era.

Tillie Walker.blurb: A right-handed slugger with a cannon arm, Walker tied Babe Ruth for the AL home run lead in 1918. For years he was listed as born in Denver in 1890; he was actually born in 1887 in a small Tennessee town, and legend says he built his arm throwing rocks into the Tennessee River.

Art Fletcher.blurb: The scrappy shortstop of John McGraw's hated Giants, part of one of the Deadball Era's best infields with Merkle, Doyle and Herzog. Fletcher fought opponents, umpires and fans alike, got fined and suspended often, and was as loved at the Polo Grounds as he was hated on the road.

Nick Altrock.blurb: For three years Altrock was arguably the best lefty in baseball, winning 62 games for the White Sox from 1904 to 1906 and beating Mordecai Brown in Game 1 of the 1906 World Series. Then he became one of the most popular baseball clowns ever, at one point earning a salary that rivaled Babe Ruth's.

Bill Duggleby.blurb: Duggleby's career started with a bang: in his first major-league at-bat in 1898, with the bases loaded, he hit a grand slam. Nobody did it again until Jeremy Hermida in 2005. He's been pretty good to you on the mound, too.

Bill Killefer.blurb: He weighed just 125 pounds when he turned pro in 1907, and his brother said the bats were almost as big as he was. Killefer grew into one of the best defensive catchers of all time over 1,000+ games, a pitch-caller teammates called smooth as silk with an arm that threw bullseyes.

Topsy Hartsel.blurb: Just 5'5", Hartsel used his small strike zone to become the best leadoff man of the Deadball Era. He led the American League in walks five times, and his 121 walks in 1905 stood as the AL record until Babe Ruth broke it in 1920. Connie Mack's Athletics won four pennants with him setting the table.

Ed Reulbach.blurb: Big Ed hid the ball in his windup, kicked high and threw what many called the best curveball in either league. In 1906 he allowed just 5.33 hits per nine innings, still the third-lowest ever, and in each of his 13 seasons he gave up fewer hits than innings pitched.

Mordecai Brown.blurb: Mordecai Peter Centennial Brown got his extra middle name for being born in 1876, the nation's centennial. Better known as Three Finger, he was the ace of the Cubs teams that put together the best five-year record in baseball history, and his duels with Christy Mathewson defined the Cubs-Giants rivalry.

Gene Krapp.blurb: A small right-handed spitballer best remembered for a famous sportswriter's pun: Charley Dryden snuck a line past his editor about Krapp squeezing his way out of a tight hole with the bases full. The joke has outlived most of the box scores.

Honus Wagner.blurb: Maybe the greatest player in National League history. Johannes Peter Wagner grew up in coal country near Pittsburgh, one of nine kids, and got his first pro shot when his older brother Albert, then thought the family's best player, recommended him.

Babe Ruth.blurb: Before the home runs, Ruth was one of the best left-handed pitchers in the game, winning three World Series with the Red Sox. His sale to the Yankees in December 1919 and the slugging that followed basically ended the Deadball Era. Which is why his card pitches and hits.

Jack Meyers.blurb: A Native American catcher who pushed back on the stereotypes of his day; writers found him a sharp mind with interests running from politics to Plato. On the field he was one of the top-hitting catchers of the Deadball Era, retiring with a .291/.367/.378 line.

George Gore.blurb: Piano Legs Gore was, as of 2010, Maine's only big-league batting champion. A star for a paper-mill team back home, he once hit a ball 450 feet, word got out, and he left Maine to try pro ball in 1877.

Stan Hack.blurb: Smiling Stan held down third base for the Cubs for 16 years, hit .301 with a .394 on-base percentage, and drew more than twice as many walks as strikeouts. Bill James ranks him the ninth-best third baseman ever, ahead of several Hall of Famers, yet Hack himself isn't in Cooperstown.

Bullet Campbell.blurb: William "Bullet" Campbell, also called Zip, came out of Savannah, Georgia, and pitched in the Negro leagues through the 1920s. He spent most of his career with Hilldale and was on the club in 1925, the year it won the Colored World Series.

Dave Bancroft.blurb: Beauty Bancroft followed Honus Wagner as the NL's best shortstop. A brainy switch-hitter with great range, he studied hitters closely and called batting and fielding a contest between minds. He drew walks too: second in the league in 1915.

Pythias Russ.blurb: A college All-American in football who became a Negro league star at catcher and shortstop. Russ hit .405 to win the 1928 NNL batting title for the Chicago American Giants, but his career and life were cut short by illness in 1930, at just 26.

Percy Miller.blurb: "Dimps" Miller, from Omaha, Nebraska, pitched in the Negro leagues from 1921 into the 1930s and finished his career as player-manager of the Detroit Stars in 1937.

Fritz Ostermueller.blurb: At 41, Ostermueller made the final start of a 15-year career in 1948 with Pittsburgh caught up in a pennant race. He finished exactly even: 114 wins and 114 losses for four big-league clubs.

Nelson Dean.blurb: A Negro league pitcher who could also play right field, Nelson Dean played from 1925 to 1932 for several teams.

Sam Bankhead.blurb: Judy Johnson called him one of the greatest outfielders the Negro leagues had, and a 1948 Grays teammate called him the greatest team player he ever saw. Bankhead could play every position and had a cannon: teammates said nobody tagged up and scored on him from third.

Lefty Grove.blurb: Maybe the most dominant pitcher ever: nine ERA titles and a 300-141 record, the best winning percentage among 300-game winners. He led the AL in strikeouts in each of his first seven seasons, and as a hitter he led all pitchers by striking out 593 times.

Luther Farrell.blurb: "Red" Farrell pitched and played the outfield for the Bacharach Giants, champions of the Eastern Colored League in 1926 and 1927. In Game 1 of the 1926 Colored World Series he hit a game-tying home run in the seventh, in a game later called a tie for darkness. Fittingly, his card does both jobs.

Pete Washington.blurb: Historian James A. Riley called him a very fast outfielder with exceptional range, one of the best defensive outfielders in the East in the 1920s and '30s. The glove was the reputation, but at his peak he ranked in the top half of his league in OPS+ too.

Jonas Gaines.blurb: Gaines never got his shot in the AL or NL, but his pro career ran 21 years, 1937 to 1957, around military service. In a 1951 barnstorming game in Alabama he pitched alongside Black major leaguers like Willie Mays and Roy Campanella.

Ed Rile.blurb: "Huck" Rile played first base and pitched in the Negro leagues and the Cuban League from 1918 to 1936. That two-way career is exactly why his card shows up at 1B and in your rotations.

Joe Beggs.blurb: A college grad in an era when few players were, and his school didn't even have a baseball team: he starred at the javelin. Beggs still won pennants and World Series in both leagues, plus a title with the 1937 Newark Bears, arguably the best minor-league team ever.

Count Leblanc.blurb: José "Cheo" Leblanc, the Count, was a Cuban pitcher for the Cuban Stars in the first seasons of the Negro National League. His 2.31 career ERA is among the best in the recognized Negro major leagues, yet little trace of him survives. He died during a winter game in Cuba in 1922, still in his twenties.

Frankie Frisch.blurb: Born in the Bronx, Frisch was supposed to join his father's lace-and-linen business. Instead he spent 19 years as an infielder and 16 as a manager, all in the National League, and was the player-manager of the 1934 Cardinals. Hall of Famer.

Jimmie Lyons.blurb: A Negro league outfielder and pitcher from 1910 to 1925. When the Negro National League formed in 1920, he signed with the Detroit Stars, then went back to the Chicago American Giants.

Nellie Fox.blurb: Born on Christmas Day 1927, Fox was the heart of the 1959 Go-Go White Sox. Choked up on his bottle bat with a wad of tobacco in his cheek, the 5'9" second baseman won the MVP that year, made 12 All-Star teams, and is in the Hall of Fame. He got his first pinch-hit for his hometown team at age 10.

Satchel Paige.blurb: Paige threw his first professional pitch in 1926 for the Chattanooga White Sox and his last in organized baseball in 1966, a full 40 years later. In between he pitched for more teams, in more ballparks, than anyone in history. He was born Leroy Robert Page in Mobile, Alabama, in 1906.

Luis Aparicio.blurb: Son of a Venezuelan baseball star of the same name, Aparicio became a symbol of the game's growth in Latin America and in his hometown of Maracaibo. Speed, defense and durability over 18 seasons made him a Hall of Famer.

Dick McAuliffe.blurb: From tiny Unionville, Connecticut, which columnist Jim Murray joked was better at raising chickens than ballplayers. McAuliffe learned the game under a tough high school coach who won 411 games and benched anyone who didn't hustle.

Bill Tuttle.blurb: A slick-fielding journeyman center fielder who played all 154 games for the 1955 Tigers. After oral cancer from years of chewing tobacco, Tuttle became one of baseball's most outspoken voices against smokeless tobacco.

Dave McNally.blurb: A lefty ace on one of the best staffs ever, the Orioles, and a World Series star on the mound and at the plate. He's also part of baseball history off the field: he played a key role in ending the reserve clause.

Billy Martin.blurb: Brash, bold and fearless as a player on the great 1950s Yankees and later as a manager of five clubs. Casey Stengel, who knew him from his Oakland minor-league days, called him a good manager who may think he knows more baseball than anybody.

R.T. Walker.blurb: Robert Taylor Walker pitched for the Homestead Grays from 1945 to 1949 and won the last Negro World Series game ever played, Game 5 in 1948, going nine innings before the Grays won it in the tenth.

Joe Gordon.blurb: A Hall of Fame second baseman who was with Cleveland in July 1947, when Larry Doby joined the team as the AL's first Black player and some teammates refused to shake his hand. (Read the SABR bio for Gordon's part in that story.)

Larry Jackson.blurb: Almost: he won almost 200 games, almost threw a perfect game, and almost won a Cy Young. His ERA+ beats a dozen Hall of Famers, Nolan Ryan included. Bill James said he couldn't find a single funny story about him.

Al Worthington.blurb: The seventh of ten kids in a Birmingham family, Worthington pitched 14 years for both Chicago clubs, both Sox teams, and both the New York and San Francisco Giants, then finished with six seasons in Minnesota.

Willie Mays.blurb: Leo Durocher, his first big-league manager, said that even if someone hit .450 and stole 100 bases, he'd still say Willie was better. Hit, hit for power, run, throw, field, and charisma: many still call him the best all-around player ever.

Carl Yastrzemski.blurb: Yaz had to replace Ted Williams and ended up with his own legend: three batting titles, seven Gold Gloves and 18 All-Star picks in 23 years with Boston, plus the 1967 Triple Crown that powered the Impossible Dream. He grew up on Long Island working his family's potato farm.

Ken Berry.blurb: A two-time Gold Glove center fielder, mostly with the White Sox, who made the 1967 All-Star team over a career that ran from 1962 to 1975.

Ed Bailey.blurb: A five-time All-Star catcher who threw out nearly half of base stealers and never stopped talking. A teammate joked his nickname Gar stood for garrulous (it was Edgar). After baseball he went into politics, naturally.

Gene Conley.blurb: The only athlete with championships in both MLB and the NBA: he pitched for the 1957 World Series champion Braves and won three titles with the Boston Celtics. For a stretch he played 12 pro seasons in six years with no off-season at all.

Bob Boone.blurb: A four-time All-Star catcher in a true baseball family: son of Ray Boone and father of Bret and Aaron. All four Boones made All-Star teams.

Ozzie Smith.blurb: The Wizard of Oz won 13 straight Gold Gloves and is usually called the greatest defensive shortstop ever, a 15-time All-Star. He said tumbling into the Springfield Mystery Spot on The Simpsons was one of his career highlights.

Bo Jackson.blurb: Bo Knows: the first athlete to be an All-Star in two major pro sports, baseball and the NFL. Named after a TV doctor, he got his nickname from family who called the unruly kid a boar hog. In high school in Alabama he won two state decathlon titles.

Jimmy Key.blurb: The quiet Blue Jays lefty nobody remembers next to Stieb and Morris: no blazing fastball, no flash. All he did was win The Sporting News Pitcher of the Year twice and the clinching game of two World Series.

Jose Oquendo.blurb: The Secret Weapon: a Puerto Rican utility man for the Mets and Cardinals known for playing almost anywhere, mainly second, short and right field. He later coached third base for St. Louis for 18 seasons.

Brooks Robinson.blurb: In the 1970 World Series Robinson hit .429, homered to win the opener and made diving stops that robbed Tony Perez and Johnny Bench. Baltimore fans gave him a standing ovation even after he struck out, for his dream Series.

Greg Swindell.blurb: A lefty who pitched 17 seasons for six teams and capped it as part of the 2001 Diamondbacks who beat the Yankees in the World Series.

Andy Messersmith.blurb: In 1968 a 23-year-old Angels rookie reliever was called in with the bases loaded and found himself facing his childhood idol, Mickey Mantle. Five pitches later Mantle struck out swinging. Messersmith later helped bring down the reserve clause with Dave McNally.

Milt Thompson.blurb: A .274 career hitter who played the outfield and pinch-hit for six clubs, later a hitting coach and instructor.

Pat Perry.blurb: A pitcher who worked from 1985 to 1990 for the Cardinals, Reds, Cubs and Dodgers.

Reggie Smith.blurb: A true five-tool player who switch-hit with power and average, ran well, played a fine center field and had maybe the best arm of his era. He broke in as a rookie on the 1967 Impossible Dream Red Sox and took a scientific, analytical approach to the game.

Tom Hall.blurb: At 6 feet and 150 pounds he was The Blade; a teammate said he wouldn't sink two inches walking on quicksand. Born in Thomasville, North Carolina, he became one of the game's most dependable relievers and helped four teams reach the postseason.

George Brett.blurb: The Royals' only Hall of Famer as the team hit 50: pine tar over batting gloves, chewing tobacco over bubble gum. He was the youngest of four brothers, and all four played pro baseball.

Thurman Munson.blurb: The scrappy catcher from Ohio who, with Bobby Murcer, bridged the old Yankee legends and the late-'70s champions.

Matt Nokes.blurb: A lefty-hitting catcher and DH who played 11 seasons, mostly with the Tigers and Yankees, and could also fill in at first, third and the corner outfield.

Bob Walk.blurb: The Whirly Bird went 105-81 over 350 games, mostly with the Pirates, and has been a Pirates broadcaster ever since.

Jerry Koosman.blurb: The legend goes that in 1966 three Mets farmhands, all named Jerry, wrecked their car on the way to spring training in Florida; the car's sleeping owner was Koosman, who wired home for money. He made it from there.

Chris Sabo.blurb: A third baseman who played mostly for the Reds from 1988 to 1996, and later coached the Akron Zips.

Darin Erstad.blurb: The first overall pick in 1995 won three Gold Gloves, two in the outfield and one at first base, a rare combo. From Jamestown, North Dakota, he has the most career WAR of any big leaguer born in the state.

Kelvim Escobar.blurb: From a Venezuelan coastal village whose Escobar family tree, started by a grandfather with 18 sons, has produced more than 20 pro players. Kelvim, with a blazing fastball and split-finger, may be the best of the bunch: 101 wins with Toronto and the Angels.

Eric Byrnes.blurb: All speed and hustle, a free-swinger with some power and one of the best defensive left fielders around, later an MLB Network analyst.

Norris Hopper.blurb: In three seasons with the Reds he hit .316 and made just one error, a .996 fielding percentage across all three outfield spots.

CC Sabathia.blurb: Finished second in Rookie of the Year voting behind Ichiro, won the 2007 Cy Young with Cleveland, and pitched 19 seasons for the Indians, Brewers and Yankees.

Jeff Bagwell.blurb: A unanimous MVP in 1994 who drove in 100+ runs eight times. Steroid-era suspicion, never backed by evidence, delayed his Hall of Fame election for six years. (You own three of the 111 copies of his LE card.)

Bruce Hurst.blurb: Best known for two wins and a Game 7 start on three days' rest in the 1986 World Series. From 1983 to 1992 he was the only big leaguer to win at least 10 games every season.

Aaron Rowand.blurb: Famous for running face-first into the center-field fence at full speed to make a catch for the Phillies, breaking his nose and dinging the ad on the wall.

Bill Hall.blurb: A utility player for six clubs from 2002 to 2012, mostly the Brewers.

Ryan Braun.blurb: A two-time All-American at Miami, Braun spent his whole career with Milwaukee, from 2007 to 2020, as a five-tool left fielder.

Deion Sanders.blurb: Prime Time is the only athlete to play in both a Super Bowl and a World Series. He won two Super Bowls, played nine MLB seasons, and is now Coach Prime at Colorado.

Brandon Phillips.blurb: Bounced between Cleveland and the minors for years before a 2006 trade to Cincinnati.

Brian Jordan.blurb: One of seven men to play both MLB and NFL since 1970, and his 1,456 big-league games are the most of any of them, more than Bo or Deion. A superb outfielder, and later an Emmy-winning analyst.

Troy Percival.blurb: The Angels' fiery closer, key to their 2002 World Series title.

Matt Williams.blurb: Matt the Bat played in a World Series for each of his three teams: the Giants, Indians and Diamondbacks. He's now managing in the new Women's Professional Baseball League.

John Bale.blurb: A lefty from Crestview, Florida, who went 11-2 with a 0.38 ERA as a high school senior and pitched for four big-league clubs.

James McDonald.blurb: An 11th-round pick by the Dodgers in 2002 who pitched for the Dodgers and Pirates. The card that's in more of your filters than any other.

Randy Choate.blurb: The original LOOGY: a sidearm lefty who hid the ball from lefty hitters and was used almost only against them. Won the 2000 World Series with the Yankees. Your lineups know the type.

Ernie Clement.blurb: Holds the record for most hits in a single postseason, 30, set in 2025 with Toronto, and made his first All-Star team in 2026.

Yasmani Grandal.blurb: A Cuban-American catcher and two-time All-Star who played for the Padres, Dodgers, Brewers, White Sox and Pirates.

Shane Victorino.blurb: The Flyin' Hawaiian, a three-time Gold Glover with the Phillies, switch-hit for most of his career until injuries in 2013 made him hit only right-handed.

Chris Taylor.blurb: CT3, the Dodgers' do-everything utility man: 2017 NLCS MVP and a World Series champion in 2020 and 2024.

Jeremy Affeldt.blurb: A lefty who bounced between the rotation and the pen in Kansas City before settling in as a reliever for the Rockies, Reds and Giants.

Santiago Espinal.blurb: A Dominican infielder, a 10th-round pick in 2016, who played for Toronto, Cincinnati and the Dodgers.

Sebastian Walcott.blurb: A Bahamian shortstop prospect in the Rangers system, born in 2006: one of the youngest cards you play.

Aaron Crow.blurb: A pitcher for the Kansas City Royals.

Nolan Arenado.blurb: The only infielder to win a Gold Glove in each of his first ten seasons, often called one of the best defensive third basemen ever.

Bryce Harper.blurb: One of the most hyped draft prospects ever: he left high school after his sophomore year, won the Golden Spikes Award in junior college, and went first overall in 2010. He debuted at 19.

Blake Snell.blurb: Won Cy Youngs in both leagues, with the Rays in 2018 and the Padres in 2023, and threw a no-hitter for the Giants in 2024.

Daniel Murphy.blurb: 2015 NLCS MVP who carried the Mets to the World Series, a three-time All-Star, and part of Team USA's first World Baseball Classic gold in 2017.

Edwin Diaz.blurb: A month after his debut he struck out 11 batters in a row, breaking Randy Johnson's Mariners record of 10. He's been a closer ever since.

Jett Williams.blurb: A shortstop and center fielder prospect in the Brewers system, born in 2003.

Jordan Montgomery.blurb: Jordan Montgomery goes by "Gumby" or "Monty." The Yankees drafted the South Carolina Gamecock in 2014, and after trades to St. Louis and then Texas he won his first ring with the Rangers in the 2023 World Series. After two years in Arizona, he went back to Texas for 2026.

Justin Verlander.blurb: Three Cy Youngs, an MVP and two World Series rings across 21 seasons. At Old Dominion he broke the school's and the conference's career strikeout records, and the Tigers took him second overall in 2004. He was the AL Rookie of the Year two years later.

Steve Pearce.blurb: Steve Pearce played for every team in the AL East, only the second man ever to do it, and he is the only player to hit two walk-off grand slams in a single week. In 2018 his power carried Boston past the Dodgers and made him World Series MVP.

Dave Stewart.blurb: Dave Stewart grew up in East Oakland, the son of a longshoreman and a cannery worker. When Reggie Jackson caught him sneaking into the Coliseum, Jackson offered him tickets, and Stewart washed Reggie's car to earn them. Down to his last chance years later, he came home to the A's and became a four-time 20-game winner and a World Series MVP.

Carl Hubbell.blurb: Carl Hubbell grew up on a pecan farm in Oklahoma and found his screwball while trying to make the ball sink. In his first big-league camp, Detroit's player-manager Ty Cobb told him to drop the pitch, and without it he lost his edge. He went on to become one of the top pitchers of the 1930s.

Old Hoss Radbourn.blurb: In 1884 Old Hoss Radbourn won 60 games for Providence, a record no one has come close to since. He led the league in ERA and strikeouts for the Triple Crown, then pitched every inning of all three games as the Grays won that fall's World Series.

Matt Clement.blurb: Matt Clement worked off a low-90s sinker and a hard slider. His win in Game 4 of the 2003 NLCS in Florida put the Cubs one game from the pennant, and from 2002 to 2005 hitters managed only a .233 average against him.

Jefferson Rojas.blurb: A Dominican second baseman and shortstop born in 2005, Jefferson Rojas is a prospect in the New York Mets organization.

Andruw Jones.blurb: From Curaçao, Andruw Jones won the Gold Glove every year from 1998 through 2007 with range and a strong arm to match. In the 1996 World Series he became the youngest player ever to homer in the postseason, and only the second to homer in his first two World Series at-bats.

Matt Carpenter.blurb: A 13th-round pick out of TCU, where he set the school records for games played and at-bats, Matt Carpenter became the first Cardinals second baseman to win a Silver Slugger after leading the majors in hits and runs. He moved around the infield, playing first, second and third.

Dave Stieb.blurb: Dave Stieb won more games than all but one pitcher in the 1980s, but he is remembered for near-misses: three times in twelve months he was one out from a no-hitter. On September 2, 1990 he finally got it, still the only no-hitter in Blue Jays history. In college at Southern Illinois he was an outfielder who hit .394 and pitched only 17 innings that season.

Cy Young.blurb: Cy Young holds two records nobody will touch: 511 wins and 749 complete games. He won 20 games sixteen times and 30 five times, threw the first pitch in World Series history in 1903, and is the only pitcher to win a game in both the old Temple Cup and the World Series.

Carlos Beltran.blurb: Rookie of the Year in 1999, Carlos Beltrán became a national star in the 2004 postseason, hitting .435 with eight home runs in 12 games. He is one of only five players with 400 homers and 300 steals, and his 435 home runs ranked fourth among switch-hitters when he reached the Hall of Fame in 2026. His last season brought a stain: he led the 2017 Astros' sign-stealing scheme.

Christy Mathewson.blurb: Matty threw four pitches with pinpoint control, his famous "fadeaway" (a screwball) among them, and was the greatest pitcher of the Deadball Era's first decade. He set modern National League records with 37 wins in a season, 373 in a career and 12 straight 20-win seasons. A handsome college man, he was the era's all-around hero.

Orel Hershiser.blurb: Orel Hershiser's 1988 was one of the great seasons: 23 wins, 15 complete games, 8 shutouts, a 2.26 ERA and the Cy Young. Then he was MVP of both the NLCS and the World Series, closing out Oakland with a nine-strikeout complete game to finish 2-0 with a 1.00 ERA in the Series.

Grover Cleveland Alexander.blurb: "Old Pete," also called "Alexander the Great," pitched from 1911 through 1930 for the Phillies, Cubs and Cardinals, and went into the Hall of Fame in 1938.

Russ Ortiz.blurb: Russ Ortiz pitched for six big-league clubs: the Giants, Braves, Diamondbacks, Orioles, Astros and Dodgers.

Jackie Robinson.blurb: When Jackie Robinson took the field for Brooklyn on April 15, 1947, more than 60 years of segregation in the majors ended. He won the NL's first official Rookie of the Year award, became the first Black player to win a batting title and an MVP and to reach the Hall of Fame, and was the first ballplayer of any color on a US postage stamp. Racism and the war kept him out until he was 28, yet he still hit .311 for his career.

Bret Saberhagen.blurb: Bret Saberhagen paired a blazing fastball with pinpoint control: two Cy Youngs, three All-Star games and a Gold Glove. He was MVP of the 1985 World Series as the Royals beat the Cardinals in seven, led the majors in wins and ERA in 1989, and threw a no-hitter in 1991.

Madison Bumgarner.blurb: MadBum won three World Series with the Giants (2010, 2012, 2014), plus two Silver Sluggers with his bat. He and Buster Posey debuted together in 2009 and became one of the best batteries in recent memory, and he has the most strikeouts of any lefty in Giants history.

Chad Billingsley.blurb: Chad Billingsley started for the Dodgers from 2006 through 2013, made the NL All-Star team in 2009, and finished with the Phillies in 2015.

Bob Miller.blurb: Bob Miller was the pitcher every club needed for something: he played for ten teams, tying a modern record, and in three different seasons he pitched for three teams in one year. Along the way he won three World Series, with the 1963 and 1965 Dodgers and the 1971 Pirates.

Shoeless Joe Jackson.blurb: A South Carolina mill-town boy who never learned to read or write much, Shoeless Joe is widely hailed as the greatest natural hitter who ever lived. His .408 in 1911 is still a Cleveland record and a rookie record, and he led the AL in triples three times. The 1919 Black Sox scandal ended his career in his prime, and he has never been given a plaque in Cooperstown.

Jered Weaver.blurb: The Angels took Jered Weaver 12th overall out of Long Beach State in 2004. He made three All-Star teams and twice led the American League in wins. His older brother Jeff pitched in the majors too.

Frank Viola.blurb: "Sweet Music" spent his early years beating himself, then became one of the best pitchers of his time: at least 34 starts every year from 1983 to 1992, 20-win seasons in both leagues, a Cy Young, and the win when it mattered most, Game 7 of the 1987 World Series.

Masahiro Tanaka.blurb: Masahiro Tanaka won 26 straight decisions for the Rakuten Eagles in 2012 and 2013, then signed with the Yankees for seven years and $155 million, at the time the fifth-largest deal ever for a pitcher. He pitched in New York from 2014 through 2020 before going home to Japan, where he now pitches for the Yomiuri Giants.

Nolan Ryan.blurb: The Ryan Express owns the records for strikeouts (5,714) and no-hitters, and only Cy Young started more games. He won a strikeout title and threw a no-hitter at 43, the oldest player in the game. The 1971 deal that sent him from the Mets to the Angels is called the best trade the Angels ever made and the worst in Mets history.

Curtis Granderson.blurb: "The Grandyman" played 16 seasons for seven clubs out of the University of Illinois Chicago, made three All-Star teams and won a Silver Slugger in 2011. He was just as known off the field: four Marvin Miller Man of the Year awards and the 2016 Roberto Clemente Award, much of it for his work with inner-city kids.

Billy Southworth.blurb: Billy Southworth hit .297 over 13 seasons and won the 1926 World Series as a Cardinals outfielder. As a manager he won pennants in 1942, 1943 and 1944 in St. Louis (two World Series) and another with the 1948 Braves, the last National League pennant Boston ever saw. His .642 winning percentage is the best of any Cardinals manager since 1900.

Dave Brown.blurb: A lefty, Dave Brown became one of the early pitching stars of the Negro National League with Rube Foster's Chicago American Giants. For decades his life story was as much legend as fact; research in 2023 finally pieced together much of the truth, which turned out to be even more twisting than the myths.

Kaelen Culpepper.blurb: A shortstop, Kaelen Culpepper was Minnesota's first-round pick in 2024 and made his big-league debut with the Twins in 2026.

Angel Genao.blurb: Ángel Genao is a Dominican infielder who made his major-league debut with Cleveland in 2026.

Ernie Banks.blurb: Ernie Banks, ever the glass-half-full type, opened 1970 three homers shy of 500 and a backup at first base. His daughter Jan asked him to "get it over with," and on May 12 he did, lining a pitch from Atlanta's Pat Jarvis into the left-field bleachers at Wrigley in front of 5,264 fans.

Dave Brain.blurb: Born in Hereford, England, Dave Brain didn't take up baseball until he was 19. He became an early home-run king on poor teams with a .252 career average, and at third and short he could make a spectacular play or a costly error, often both, over a seven-year career.

Eddie Plank.blurb: Eddie Plank fidgeted through a long ritual before every pitch, and from the seventh inning on he counted down the outs out loud. Hitters swung at anything just to move things along. He rarely bothered throwing over to first; he figured his arm had only so many pitches in it.

Chick Hafey.blurb: Chick Hafey was a line-drive hitter who batted for a high average year after year and won the World Series with the 1926 and 1931 Cardinals. He got the first hit in All-Star Game history in 1933, and the Veterans Committee put him in the Hall of Fame in 1971.

Francisco Lindor.blurb: "Mr. Smile" was born in Caguas, Puerto Rico, and moved to Florida at 12. Cleveland took him eighth overall in 2011; he hit over .300 in each of his first two seasons, and in 2016 he made his first All-Star team, reached the World Series and became the first Puerto Rican shortstop to win a Gold Glove.

Bob Feller.blurb: "The Heater from Van Meter" skipped the minors and debuted for Cleveland at 17. He was the first pitcher to win 24 games before turning 21, threw no-hitters in 1940, 1946 and 1951 plus 12 one-hitters, and gave up four prime years to Navy service aboard the USS Alabama.

Yadier Molina.blurb: Yadier Molina caught all 19 of his seasons for the Cardinals and is widely rated one of the greatest defensive catchers ever, with nine Gold Gloves and six Fielding Bible Awards for his blocking and throwing. He won two World Series and two World Baseball Classic silver medals with Puerto Rico.

Mickey Mantle.blurb: The Commerce Comet was raised by his father to be a ballplayer and trained to switch-hit from the start. Despite injuries that began with a knee in the 1951 World Series, he won three MVPs, hit 536 home runs and remains the only player with 150 homers from each side of the plate.

Jackie Jensen.blurb: Jackie Jensen starred in both football and baseball, and he is in the College Football Hall of Fame as well as being an American League MVP. He is best remembered for leaving baseball in mid-career because he could not bear to fly, part of a long struggle with anxiety.

Sherry Smith.blurb: A quiet lefty from Georgia, Sherry Smith narrowly lost a World Series game to a young Babe Ruth and missed a season serving in World War I. His daughter said he learned to pitch throwing balls of cotton at rabbits in the fields; he would only laugh when asked if it was true. After baseball he became a small-town lawman.

Jack Cust.blurb: Jack Cust was a designated hitter and outfielder for six clubs: the Diamondbacks, Rockies, Orioles, Padres, A's and Mariners.

Claude Grier.blurb: "Red" Grier, from Catawba County, North Carolina, pitched in the Negro leagues from 1924 to 1928, mostly for the Bacharach Giants, and threw a no-hitter in the 1926 Colored World Series.

Kevin Millwood.blurb: Kevin Millwood came up in the Braves' rotation alongside Maddux, Glavine and Smoltz, made the All-Star team in 1999 and helped Atlanta to that year's World Series. Later, with Cleveland, he led the American League with a 2.86 ERA, and in 2012 he reached 2,000 career strikeouts.

Danny Jackson.blurb: Hard-throwing lefty Danny Jackson pitched in three World Series for three teams, and in 1985 he struck out the side on nine pitches. His best year was 1988 with Cincinnati: 23-8, a 2.73 ERA, runner-up for the Cy Young. His slider broke late enough to trouble his own catchers.

Red Lucas.blurb: Red Lucas finished 204 of his 302 starts and had some of the best control of his day, walking just 18 batters in more than 219 innings in 1933. He could hit too, batting .281 with six seasons over .300, and filled in at second, short, third and left; but his teams were usually near the bottom, so few noticed.

Rube Marquard.blurb: In 1912 Rube Marquard won his first 19 decisions for the New York Giants, from his first start on April 11 until a loss on July 8, a single-season streak that still stands.

Brandon Beachy.blurb: Brandon Beachy pitched in the majors for the Atlanta Braves and the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Tanner McDougal.blurb: Tanner McDougal, born in 2003, pitches for the Chicago White Sox.

Rafael Furcal.blurb: A Dominican shortstop, Rafael Furcal played for the Braves, Dodgers, Cardinals and Marlins, and won the 2011 World Series with St. Louis over Texas.

Miguel Cabrera.blurb: Miggy won the Triple Crown in 2012, the first in 45 years and still the only one since 1968. Two MVPs, four batting titles and twelve All-Star teams later, he joined Hank Aaron and Willie Mays as the only players with a .300 average, 500 home runs and 3,000 hits.

Shane Mack.blurb: Shane Mack starred at UCLA, won a silver medal with the 1984 Olympic team and was a first-round pick of the Padres. Over 13 years he played for six big-league clubs and Japan's Yomiuri Giants.

Kevin Kiermaier.blurb: One of the best defensive center fielders of his time, Kevin Kiermaier won four Gold Gloves and a Platinum Glove. He won titles in high school in Indiana and at Parkland College, and debuted on September 30, 2013, in game 163, a wild-card tiebreaker.

Marco Scutaro.blurb: Marco Scutaro, from San Felipe, Venezuela, always had to fight to be noticed. As a boy his mother rode with him more than an hour each way to Barquisimeto so he could play against better competition, and he said everything he did, he did for her.

Hanley Ramirez.blurb: The 2006 NL Rookie of the Year and a three-time All-Star, Hanley Ramírez was an elite hitter in his prime, with a .289 career average and real power. Shortstop was never his best spot, left field went worse, but a move to first base in 2016 worked at the plate and in the field.

Branch Russell.blurb: Branch Russell, an Army corporal in World War I, debuted with the Kansas City Monarchs in 1922 and spent ten years with the St. Louis Stars, a good contact hitter who also managed the club for part of 1926.

Al Simmons.blurb: Born Aloysius Szymanski to Polish immigrants in Milwaukee, Al Simmons was the hard-hitting left fielder of Connie Mack's great Athletics from 1924 to 1932. He hit .360 or better at two minor-league stops on the way up, all from an unusual batting stance.

Aiva Arquette.blurb: Aiva Arquette, an infielder in the Miami Marlins system, played college ball at Washington and Oregon State.

Chase Utley.blurb: "The Man" was a six-time All-Star second baseman, won the 2008 World Series with the Phillies and was Sports Illustrated's second baseman of the 2000s. With Jimmy Rollins he formed one of the best middle-infield pairs in the National League.

Tommy Edman.blurb: Tommy Edman, who also plays for South Korea's national team, came out of Stanford as a Cardinals sixth-rounder and won a Gold Glove at second base in 2021. Traded to the Dodgers in 2024, he was NLCS MVP and won the World Series that fall.

Adam Cimber.blurb: Adam Cimber pitched for five clubs, one of the few big-league pitchers of his day with a true submarine delivery.

Bill Ricks.blurb: "Schoolboy" Ricks pitched for the Philadelphia Stars from 1944 to 1950. In 1949 he was MVP of the National Baseball Congress tournament, winning three games and striking out 30 in 26 innings.

Scott Spiezio.blurb: Scott Spiezio's three-run homer in Game 6 of the 2002 World Series sparked the Angels' comeback against the Giants, in his best full season. He added a second ring as a utility man with the 2006 Cardinals, and his father Ed played in the majors too.

Mark Fidrych.blurb: Mark Fidrych pitched only 58 big-league games, but in 1976 he came out of nowhere to become one of the best pitchers in baseball, and his antics and joy on the mound made him one of the game's most beloved players.

Marcus Semien.blurb: In 2021 Marcus Semien made the All-Star team and won a Gold Glove and a Silver Slugger with Toronto. Then he signed with Texas for seven years and $175 million and won the World Series there in 2023.

Carlos Delgado.blurb: No player born in Puerto Rico has hit more home runs than Carlos Delgado's 473. He grew up in Aguadilla idolizing Roberto Clemente, the son of a drug-and-alcohol counselor and a medical lab assistant, and both shaped him into a social activist as well as a slugger.

Hank Blalock.blurb: Hank Blalock played third base for the Texas Rangers and finished his career with Tampa Bay.

Willie McGee.blurb: Few Cardinals have been loved more than Willie McGee. A switch-hitter with quick hands and elite speed, he sprayed line drives everywhere and ran down fly balls, yet stayed humble through a World Series, an MVP, four All-Star teams and two batting titles. His father, a Navy-yard machinist and Pentecostal deacon, worked a second job as a janitor and brought the kids along to help.

Byron Buxton.blurb: Byron Buxton was called by some the most talented player in the 2012 draft, and the Twins took him second overall. Minor League Player of the Year in 2013, he has since won a Gold Glove, a Silver Slugger and made three All-Star teams.

Ben Zobrist.blurb: The original "super utility player," switch-hitting Ben Zobrist played mostly second base but also short and all over the outfield, and walked a lot. He won back-to-back World Series with the 2015 Royals and the 2016 Cubs, and was MVP of the second.

Josh Gibson.blurb: Walter Johnson said Josh Gibson could do everything: hit the ball a mile, catch as easily as sitting in a rocking chair, throw like a rifle. Called the Black Babe Ruth (some say Ruth was the white Josh Gibson), he was credited with a drive in Yankee Stadium that struck about 580 feet from home plate, and some accounts give him 800 to 1,000 home runs over a 16-year career.

Corey Kluber.blurb: A fourth-round pick out of Stetson who came to Cleveland in a three-team trade, Corey Kluber became a power pitcher with a hard sinker and a breaking ball somewhere between a slider and a curve, and he piled up strikeouts with it.

Roy Cullenbine.blurb: Roy Cullenbine walked in nearly 18 percent of his plate appearances, seventh-best ever, and once drew walks in 22 straight games, a record. In his day that skill was mistaken for laziness. A switch-hitter with power and a cannon arm, he was passed around to seven clubs in ten years.

Didier Fuentes.blurb: Didier Fuentes, a Colombian right-hander born in 2005, made his major-league debut with Atlanta in 2025.

Barry Larkin.blurb: Barry Larkin played all 19 of his seasons for his hometown Reds. At Archbishop Moeller High he hit .482, and he turned down the Reds as a second-round pick to go to Michigan on a football scholarship, with Bo Schembechler willing to let him play both sports.

Kyson Witherspoon.blurb: Kyson Witherspoon pitched at Oklahoma and was a Red Sox first-round pick in 2025; he is now in the Orioles organization.

Edgardo Alfonzo.blurb: "Fonzie" was an All-Star and a key part of the Mets' 2000 pennant winners, and his WAR as a Met ranks seventh in franchise history. After playing in Mexico and Japan, he went on to manage the Brooklyn Cyclones and entered the Mets Hall of Fame in 2020.

Pascual Perez.blurb: "He looked like a spider doing aerobics," one witness said of Pascual Pérez's delivery. The lanky right-hander rose from deep poverty in the Dominican Republic, showed fine control, started more than one bench-clearing brawl with inside pitches, and is perhaps best known for getting lost on the way to his own ballpark.

Bob Friend.blurb: "The Warrior" never spent a single day on the disabled list in 16 seasons. A workhorse with a heavy sinker, a hard curve and unusually good control, he led the 1960 Pirates in starts and innings and went 18-12, bouncing back from a rough 1959. He won 197 games in all.

Tris Speaker.blurb: Ty Cobb's friendly rival as the Deadball Era's best center fielder, Tris Speaker played famously shallow and still holds the records for putouts and double plays at his position. He hit .345 for his career and no one has topped his 792 doubles. Off the field he hunted, roped steers and taught Will Rogers how to use a lariat.

Kid Nichols.blurb: Kid Nichols was born in Madison, Wisconsin, in 1869, the son of a butcher, into a family full of ballplayers: his older brothers played for the town club before he was born. After the family moved to Kansas City he pitched the amateur Blue Avenue club, brothers and all, to a championship.

Roger Clemens.blurb: Roger Clemens's 24-year career ended where it began, against Cleveland: his last start, in the 2007 playoffs, came against the team he debuted against in 1984. A hamstring forced him out in the third inning, but not before he struck out the last batter he ever faced, Victor Martinez.

Steve Finley.blurb: A 13th-round pick who didn't reach the majors until 24, Steve Finley still played 19 years, collected over 2,500 hits, won five Gold Gloves and a World Series, and became one of the very few speed-and-defense center fielders with more than 300 home runs.

Dan Pasqua.blurb: Dan Pasqua played the outfield and first base for the Yankees and White Sox from 1985 to 1994, and later worked for the White Sox as a community representative.

Leodalis De Vries.blurb: Leodalis De Vries, a Dominican-Dutch shortstop born in 2006, is a prospect in the Athletics organization.

Scott Rolen.blurb: Seen as Mike Schmidt's heir when he came up with the Phillies, Scott Rolen became one of the best third basemen ever. Teammate Jonny Gomes said the clubhouse question was simply what would Scott do: never argue with umpires, run everything out, make every play.

Mickey Lolich.blurb: Mickey Lolich called himself "the beer-drinker's idol," and his portly build and easy manner made him a favorite in 13 seasons with Detroit. The son of a Portland parks director, he grew up outdoors throwing rocks at anything that moved, which built the arm.

Joc Pederson.blurb: The son of big-leaguer Stu Pederson, Joc was a Dodgers 11th-round pick who hit 30 homers and stole 30 bases to win the 2014 PCL MVP. He has won two World Series, made two All-Star teams, and played for Israel in two World Baseball Classics.

Justin Masterson.blurb: A 6-foot-6 sinkerballer born in Jamaica, Justin Masterson came out of San Diego State to the Red Sox and became an All-Star with Cleveland. He was the first Boston pitcher since Fenway opened in 1912 to make his first four starts there without a loss.

John Olerud.blurb: John Olerud wore a batting helmet in the field after nearly dying from a brain aneurysm in college. He had a gorgeous swing and a sure glove, never said a mean word about anyone, and won two World Series in 17 years.

Mel Ott.blurb: Mel Ott came from Gretna, Louisiana, the son of a cottonseed-oil plant worker, and joined the New York Giants at 17 as an apprentice rather than going to the minors. He stayed with them all 22 years of his career, a rags-to-riches star in the biggest city in the country.

Dock Ellis.blurb: Dock Ellis threw a no-hitter in 1970, then won 19 games, started the All-Star Game and won the World Series with the 1971 Pirates. Nicknamed "Peanut" and later "The Nut," he challenged old prejudices and both angered and amused people, and by his own account never pitched a big-league game without alcohol or drugs.

Albert Pujols.blurb: Albert Pujols's first 11 seasons in St. Louis were among the best stretches any player has had: a .328 average and, on average, 40 doubles, 40 homers and 120 RBIs a year. Later, slowed by age, he still reached 3,000 hits, 700 home runs and 2,000 RBIs.

Payton Tolle.blurb: Payton Tolle, born in 2002, pitches for the Boston Red Sox; he made his big-league debut in 2025.

Paul Goldschmidt.blurb: Lightly recruited out of high school and an eighth-round pick out of Texas State, Paul Goldschmidt became a seven-time All-Star and the 2022 NL MVP, with four Gold Gloves and five Silver Sluggers, the most ever by a first baseman.

Hank Thompson.blurb: Hank Thompson went from the Kansas City Monarchs to the majors, playing for the St. Louis Browns in 1947 and then third base for the New York Giants from 1949 to 1956.

Vladimir Guerrero.blurb: Vladimir Guerrero's rule was simple: see the ball, hit the ball, and he hit nearly anything. A five-tool player who did it all his own unconventional way, he had a cannon arm that never quite knew where the ball was going, and in one season he stole 40 bases while also leading the league in times caught.

Kenny Lofton.blurb: On an Indians club full of All-Stars, Jim Thome called Kenny Lofton the most talented player in baseball. He set the tone at the top of the order for those great Cleveland teams, and late in his career fans took to calling him the "Mayor of Cleveland."

Alfonso Soriano.blurb: Alfonso Soriano started his pro career with Japan's Hiroshima Carp before signing with the Yankees, where he was MVP of the 1999 Futures Game and won two pennants. He went on to play for the Rangers, Nationals and Cubs.

Colby Rasmus.blurb: Colby Rasmus played the outfield for the Cardinals, Blue Jays, Astros, Rays and Orioles, and also played for the US national team.

Mike Scioscia.blurb: A Dodgers first-round pick out of suburban Philadelphia, Mike Scioscia caught for 13 years, then managed the Angels, winning the 2002 World Series. He was the first manager to reach the playoffs in six of his first ten seasons.

Ryan Sloan.blurb: Ryan Sloan, born in 2006, is a pitcher in the Seattle Mariners system; Seattle drafted him 55th overall in 2024.

Seth Hernandez.blurb: Seth Hernandez, born in 2006, was the sixth overall pick of the 2025 draft and pitches in the Pittsburgh Pirates organization.

Milt Pappas.blurb: Milt Pappas's record stacks up with Don Drysdale's, and he argued that made him a Hall of Famer. Instead he is remembered for being the man traded for a superstar in one of the game's most famous deals, and for a reputation as a clubhouse lawyer he admitted to himself.

Kade Anderson.blurb: Kade Anderson won the 2025 College World Series with LSU and was named its Most Outstanding Player. Seattle took him third overall that summer, and he debuted with the Mariners in 2026.

Josh Johnson.blurb: "JJ" pitched for the Marlins from 2005 and finished with the Blue Jays in 2013.

Hank Aaron.blurb: On April 8, 1974, Hank Aaron hit number 715 off Al Downing and passed Babe Ruth as baseball's all-time home run king. As an African American breaking the game's most famous record, he carried the journey Jackie Robinson began in 1947 a giant step further, for the game and for the country.

Thomas White.blurb: Thomas White, born in 2004, is a pitcher in the Miami Marlins organization.

Kerry Wood.blurb: In just his fifth big-league start, on a drizzly May 6, 1998 at Wrigley, 20-year-old Kerry Wood struck out 20 Astros and allowed one hit, a single that glanced off his third baseman's glove. Many have rated it the most dominant pitching performance of the century. He won Rookie of the Year, then missed all of 1999 after Tommy John surgery.

Webster McDonald.blurb: Webster McDonald was an underhanded submariner who threw "56 varieties" of junk and saved his good fastball for when hitters weren't ready. He starred in the Negro Leagues and independent ball from 1918 to 1946, best remembered for beating white big-leaguers, and was respected everywhere he played and managed.

Hilton Smith.blurb: Hilton Smith was one of eight Negro League Hall of Famers from Texas, from Giddings, near where Rube Foster grew up. The oldest of six, he helped raise his siblings, which delayed his start in baseball, but he became a lights-out pitcher on the way to Cooperstown.

Toothpick Sam Jones.blurb: "Toothpick" Sam Jones pitched for six clubs from 1951 to 1964, among them the Indians, Cubs, Cardinals and Giants.

Catfish Hunter.blurb: Catfish Hunter threw the AL's first perfect game in 46 years in 1968, won 20 games five straight seasons, anchored three straight A's champions from 1972 to 1974 and won the 1974 Cy Young. When an arbitrator made him a free agent, the Yankees made him baseball's highest-paid player, and he won 23 games his first year in New York.

Willie Keeler.blurb: "Wee Willie" Keeler was one of the greatest contact hitters ever and nearly impossible to strike out: about 63 at-bats per strikeout, the best ratio in major-league history. He played on five pennant winners in Baltimore and Brooklyn.

AJ Pollock.blurb: A first-round pick out of Notre Dame in 2009, AJ Pollock was an All-Star and Gold Glove center fielder for Arizona in 2015 and later played for four other clubs.

Cool Papa Bell.blurb: Few legends have so many stories told about them, some true and some stretched, as Cool Papa Bell. Those who knew him remembered someone regal and gentle, never hurried, who signed every autograph and gave advice to anyone who asked. Judy Johnson said if everybody were like Cool, it would be a better world.

Ossie Bluege.blurb: Asked to rank third basemen, Joe Cronin always said you start with Ossie Bluege, his old Senators partner. Watching Brooks Robinson in 1970, Cronin called his plays "another Ossie Bluege play." A teammate said Bluege covered so much ground he was like two great infielders at once.

Jack Burdock.blurb: "Black Jack" Burdock was the premier second baseman of 19th-century baseball, chosen in 1885 by Harper's Weekly as the best at his position alongside King Kelly, Old Hoss Radbourn and Buck Ewing. Alcoholism cut his career short.

Darrell May.blurb: Darrell May bounced between several organizations and spent a stint in Japan before becoming the leader of a surprising team's pitching staff, then narrowly avoided a 20-loss season. Perseverance was his story.

Connelly Early.blurb: Connelly Early, born in 2002, debuted with Boston in 2025 and now pitches for the Washington Nationals.

Duke Snider.blurb: His father nicknamed him Duke for his swagger. Duke Snider was one of the great center fielders of the 1950s, with a strong, accurate arm, and his .300 average, 389 homers and 1,271 RBIs with Brooklyn and Los Angeles may make him the greatest Dodger hitter ever.

Mike Hampton.blurb: A pitcher who could really hit, Mike Hampton won five Silver Sluggers and a Gold Glove to go with two All-Star selections. He was MVP of the 2000 NLCS and pitched for the Mets in that year's World Series.

Yu Chang.blurb: Yu Chang played infield for the Guardians, Pirates, Rays and Red Sox; his 235 big-league games are the most ever by a player from Taiwan. He played for Chinese Taipei in the 2023 World Baseball Classic and now plays for the Fubon Guardians at home.

Rick Ankiel.blurb: Rick Ankiel was a young Cardinals pitcher until, in 2000, he suddenly could not throw strikes. He rebuilt himself as an outfielder in the minors and returned to St. Louis in August 2007, hitting 47 home runs as an outfielder for the Cardinals, plus two as a pitcher.

Brian Roberts.blurb: "B-Rob" was the Orioles' sparkplug leadoff man from 2001 to 2013, a two-time All-Star second baseman who led the AL in doubles twice (50 and 56) and in steals once (50). In 2005 he became the first switch-hitter with 45 doubles and 15 homers in a season.

Muddy Ruel.blurb: A skinny kid from the St. Louis sandlots, the son of a city policeman, Muddy Ruel became a big-league catcher who scored the winning run in Game 7 of a World Series, and later a general manager and a special assistant to the Commissioner.

Tom Glavine.blurb: Chipper Jones said Tom Glavine's poise and the way he went about his business won him more than 300 games. In Game 6 of the 1995 World Series, with Atlanta chasing its first title since the move from Milwaukee, the Braves put the ball in his left hand.

Red Faber.blurb: Red Faber was one of the last pitchers allowed to throw the spitball, a pitch he took up in the minors after throwing curves nearly ruined his arm. He spent all 20 years with the White Sox and won 254 games; his catcher Ray Schalk thought it might have been 300 if the Black Sox scandal hadn't gutted the team.

Phil Rizzuto.blurb: A Giants coach told Phil Rizzuto he was too small and should shine shoes. Instead the 5-foot-6 Brooklyn kid anchored Yankee infields that won nine pennants and seven World Series, won an MVP, made the Hall of Fame and spent forty years as the voice of the Yankees.

Doug Davis.blurb: Doug Davis pitched for the Rangers, Blue Jays, Brewers, Diamondbacks and Cubs.

Wade Boggs.blurb: Legend has it Ted Williams looked at a photo of 18-month-old Wade Boggs swinging a bat and said the kid had a perfect stance. He was right: Boggs won several batting titles on his way to the Hall of Fame. He grew up in a military family, the son of a Marine and Air Force pilot and a mail-plane pilot.

Chien-Ming Wang.blurb: With a hard sinker, Chien-Ming Wang won 19 games for the Yankees in both 2006 and 2007, leading the American League in wins the first year, before a foot injury in 2008 and later arm trouble slowed him.

Josh Beckett.blurb: The second overall pick in 1999, Josh Beckett won the 2003 World Series with the Marlins, where he was Series MVP, and the 2007 World Series with Boston, where he was ALCS MVP. He made three All-Star teams.

Andy McGaffigan.blurb: Andy McGaffigan pitched in the major leagues from 1981 to 1991.

Garrett Richards.blurb: Garrett Richards pitched for the Angels, Padres, Red Sox and Rangers.

John Kruk.blurb: John Kruk let his bat do the talking for ten years as a player, then made his wit the main attraction as a broadcaster. Born in Charleston, West Virginia, he grew up near the New Jersey Pinelands; when ESPN let him go in 2016 he joked he might become a fitness expert.

Jim Edmonds.blurb: "Jimmy Baseball" won eight Gold Gloves in center field and could hit too: a .284 average, 393 home runs and a .903 OPS over 17 seasons, most memorably with the Angels and Cardinals.

Roberto Clemente.blurb: Roberto Clemente was electrifying on the field: a bad-ball hitter with a rifle arm in right field who played with reckless but controlled abandon. Off it he was a role model in Puerto Rico and far beyond. Helping others was how he lived, and it was how he died.

Ernie Whitt.blurb: Ernie Whitt caught for 15 seasons, twelve with Toronto, and was the last player from the Blue Jays' first season of 1977 still on the team in 1989. An All-Star in 1985, he has managed Canada's national team since 2004.

Aaron Sanchez.blurb: A Blue Jays first-round pick, Aaron Sanchez was an All-Star in 2016 and led the American League in ERA. Traded to Houston in 2019, he threw the first six innings of a combined no-hitter in his very first start for the Astros.

Aaron Hicks.blurb: A Twins first-round pick in 2008, Aaron Hicks debuted in 2013, spent most of his career with the Yankees, and finished with the Orioles and Angels.

Jesse Barnes.blurb: Jesse Barnes of Circleville, Kansas, led the National League in wins in 1919 and made Baseball Magazine's All-American team beside Walter Johnson, Ty Cobb and Babe Ruth. He also won the fastest nine-inning game in big-league history.

Mark Langston.blurb: Mark Langston won 179 games and seven Gold Gloves, made four All-Star teams and led the American League in strikeouts three times. When he signed with the Angels he became the highest-paid player in baseball; he now broadcasts their games.

Jackie Bradley Jr..blurb: "JBJ" was Most Outstanding Player of the 2010 College World Series for South Carolina, an All-Star with the Red Sox in 2016, and MVP of the 2018 ALCS. These days he plays for the Banana Ball's Indianapolis Clowns.

Jim Deshaies.blurb: Jim Deshaies was a left-hander with sneaky-fast stuff who sometimes outshone his more famous rotation mates over 12 seasons before shoulder trouble ended it. He found a second career as one of the funniest color commentators in baseball, for the Astros and the Cubs.

Billy Wagner.blurb: At under 5-foot-10 and 170 pounds out of high school in Tannersville, Virginia, Billy Wagner drew few scouts. "Billy the Kid" became one of the most dominant closers of his time, mentioned in the same breath as Mariano Rivera, and like Rivera he came in to "Enter Sandman."

Willie Randolph.blurb: The son of South Carolina sharecroppers, Willie Randolph turned soft hands and a patient eye into 18 years at second base and six All-Star teams. Competing with Frank White and Lou Whitaker, he never won a Gold Glove. He later managed the Mets from 2005 to 2008.

George Klassen.blurb: George Klassen, born in 2002, made his major-league debut with the Angels in 2026.

John Lackey.blurb: In 2002 John Lackey became only the second rookie to start and win a World Series clincher, for the Angels. He went on to win rings with three teams (the Angels, Red Sox and Cubs) and 188 games, despite years of arm trouble. He grew up in Abilene, Texas, lettering in three sports.

Roy Halladay.blurb: "Doc," named by Blue Jays broadcaster Tom Cheek after the gunslinger Doc Holliday, led his league in complete games seven times, the most of any pitcher who started after 1945. An eight-time All-Star with Toronto and Philadelphia, he is regarded as one of the greatest pitchers of all time.

Dickie Thon.blurb: Dickie Thon was becoming one of the best young shortstops in the National League when a pitch hit him in the left eye and left him partly blind for good. We will never know how great he could have been; what he showed in coming back told everyone what kind of man he was.

Jakie May.blurb: "The Wee Carolinian," a short, round lefty from Wendell, North Carolina, once won 35 games in a single long minor-league season. In the last big-league game of his 14-year career, Game 4 of the 1932 World Series, he struck out Babe Ruth twice in a row. Then he went home to grow tobacco.

Danny Salazar.blurb: Danny Salazar, from the Dominican Republic, pitched for Cleveland from 2013 to 2019.

Mike Marshall.blurb: Mike Marshall did everything wrong by the book: he lifted weights, ran distance, threw a screwball, believed in pitching more rather than less, and mostly refused to sign autographs. "I'm an educator and baseball is my hobby," he said. In 1974 he pitched in a record 106 games for the Dodgers.

Mike Lowell.blurb: A Yankees prospect who beat the Yankees for the 2003 title with Florida, Mike Lowell was then dealt to Boston in a salary dump and won again in 2007 as World Series MVP. He holds the Red Sox records for best fielding percentage at third, season and career. His father pitched for Puerto Rico's national team.

Bobby Witt Jr..blurb: The second overall pick in 2019, Bobby Witt Jr. was the first shortstop with two 30-30 seasons (2023 and 2024). He has made three straight All-Star teams, with Gold Gloves, Silver Sluggers and a 2025 Platinum Glove along the way.

Michael Arroyo.blurb: Michael Arroyo, a Colombian infielder born in 2004, signed with Seattle in 2022, debuted with the Mariners in 2026 and also plays for Colombia's national team.

Jonathan Schoop.blurb: Jonathan Schoop, from Curaçao, was an All-Star second baseman for Baltimore in 2017 and also played for the Brewers, Twins and Tigers before moving to Mexico's Dorados de Chihuahua.

Dontrelle Willis.blurb: "The D-Train" kicked his leg sky-high and twisted away from the hitter, and it worked: he was the 2003 NL Rookie of the Year and won the World Series with the Marlins the same year. He now works as a broadcaster for the Dodgers and Fox.

Travis Sykora.blurb: Travis Sykora, born in 2004, is a pitcher in the Washington Nationals organization.

Frank Tanana.blurb: A first-round pick out of Detroit, Frank Tanana won 14 games as an Angels rookie, and with Nolan Ryan formed one of the toughest one-two punches in baseball. He led the AL in strikeouts in 1975, struck out 2,773 in all, and clinched division titles for the 1979 Angels and his hometown 1987 Tigers.

Joey Cantillo.blurb: A 16th-round Padres pick in 2017, Joey Cantillo was traded to Cleveland in 2020 and debuted with the Guardians in 2024.

Franklin Arias.blurb: Franklin Arias, a Venezuelan shortstop born in 2005, is a prospect in the Boston Red Sox organization.

Johan Santana.blurb: Johan Santana came from Tovar, a small town more than a mile up in Venezuela's Andes, where a sign at the ballpark now welcomes visitors to "the territory of Johan Santana." An electrician's son who dreamed of being an engineer, he wasn't even the best player in his own family; his older brother Franklin was.

Ed Morgan.blurb: Eddie Morgan crammed half of his 52 career home runs into one season, 1930 for Cleveland, when he drove in 136 runs. Mostly a first baseman who also played the outfield and third, he left the majors with a .313 average and a .398 on-base percentage.

Eddie Dixon.blurb: Eddie Dixon grew up in Bonifay, in the Florida panhandle, where his father and grandfather worked in turpentine factories, a fitting start for a pitcher whose career would lean on rosin bags and pine tar. Apart from his years in the Negro Leagues and in the Army during World War II, he lived his whole life in Florida.

Rickey Henderson.blurb: On May 1, 1991, Rickey Henderson stole third against the Yankees for career steal number 939, passing Lou Brock, and told the crowd he was now the greatest of all time. Boastful or not, he was right: Rickey is the greatest base stealer in history.

Rick Mahler.blurb: Rick Mahler pitched 13 seasons, mostly for the Braves, where he and his brother Mickey were teammates in 1979. The Austin native went 96-111 with a 3.99 ERA.

Larry Christenson.blurb: Larry Christenson spent his whole big-league career with the Phillies and won the 1980 World Series with them.

Alex Claudio.blurb: Puerto Rican lefty Alex Claudio pitched from an unorthodox sidearm angle for the Rangers, Brewers, Angels and Mets, and now pitches for Saltillo in the Mexican League.

Charlie Hickman.blurb: "Piano Legs" Hickman, all 215 pounds of him at 5-foot-9, had one of the Deadball Era's most powerful bats: in 1903 he hit one ball 100 feet over the left-field fence in Cleveland and another clean out of New York's Hilltop Park. A teammate said that with a lively ball, Hickman would have been one of five Babe Ruths.

Roy Campanella.blurb: Roy Campanella joined the Dodgers a year after Jackie Robinson and became their regular catcher in 1948. He was the first Black player to win two MVP awards and, when he died in 1993, the only one with three. He followed Robinson into the Hall of Fame as well.

Ryne Sandberg.blurb: On June 23, 1984, at Wrigley, with the Cubs down 9-8 to the Cardinals in the ninth and already three hits and four RBIs into his day, Ryne Sandberg lined a Bruce Sutter splitter into the last row of the left-field bleachers.

Vida Blue.blurb: A fireballing lefty, Vida Blue was a central figure on the A's teams that won five straight division titles and three World Series. His career, from 1969 to 1986, had high points and dark days, including a drug suspension and one of the most publicized contract holdouts ever.

Garret Anderson.blurb: Garret Anderson drove in the winning runs in the 2002 World Series and was MVP of the 2003 All-Star Game. Over 17 seasons, mostly with the Angels, he set franchise records for games, hits, runs, RBIs, doubles and total bases.

Cal Quantrill.blurb: Canadian right-hander Cal Quantrill came out of Stanford as a Padres first-round pick in 2016, debuted in 2019 and has pitched for six clubs since.

Corey Seager.blurb: Corey Seager was the 2016 NL Rookie of the Year and an All-Star in each of his first two full seasons. He was MVP of both the NLCS and the World Series as the Dodgers won the 2020 title, then signed a ten-year deal with Texas.

Jaxon Wiggins.blurb: Jaxon Wiggins, born in 2001, is a pitcher in the Chicago Cubs organization.

Carlos Guillen.blurb: At 6-foot-1 and 215 pounds, Carlos Guillén didn't look like a shortstop, and when he arrived from Venezuela at 19, teammates thought he looked more like a batboy. He played all four infield spots and left field, made three All-Star teams through eleven trips to the disabled list, and retired as one of the best shortstops in Tigers history.

Mike Zunino.blurb: Mike Zunino swept the Golden Spikes, Dick Howser and Johnny Bench awards at Florida and went third overall in 2012. He set franchise home-run records for catchers with both the Mariners and the Rays, and was an All-Star with Tampa Bay in 2021.

Gabby Hartnett.blurb: Gabby Hartnett was widely acknowledged as the best catcher in the National League in the 1920s and 1930s, a Hall of Famer for the Cubs who was on the field for several of that era's most famous moments.

Carlos Silva.blurb: Carlos Silva, from Venezuela, pitched for the Phillies, Twins, Mariners and Cubs from 2002 to 2010.

Steve Trout.blurb: "Rainbow" Trout pitched in the majors through the 1980s; his father, Dizzy Trout, was a big-league pitcher before him.

Joe Carter.blurb: As a boy in Oklahoma City, Joe Carter dreamed of stepping up as his team's last hope with the World Series on the line. On October 23, 1993, with Toronto trailing Philadelphia 6-5, he got the chance to live it.

Dick Allen.blurb: The Phillies' first Black superstar, Dick Allen was one of the most feared hitters of the pitching-dominated 1960s, launching some of the longest home runs anyone had seen. As a rookie in 1964, writers joked he was headed straight to the Hall of Fame; controversy soon followed him too.

Chick Stahl.blurb: A lifetime .305 hitter with power, Chick Stahl was one of the best center fielders of his day and was loved by his Boston teammates; catcher Lou Criger called him the squarest man he ever knew. His death at 34, in the spring of 1907, left the club grieving.

Alex Rodriguez.blurb: Like Babe Ruth or Muhammad Ali, A-Rod's fame went beyond his sport; the nickname alone is enough. A 2015 profile summed up the mix of stardom and his steroid suspension as part Babe Ruth, part Count Dracula.

Bob Gibson.blurb: The 1964 World Series was Bob Gibson's coming-out party: complete-game wins in Games 5 and 7 over the Yankees, the Cardinals' first title since 1946, and the Series MVP award. His manager Johnny Keane, his first manager in pro ball, had been his champion all along.

Bill Buckner.blurb: Bill Buckner was a gamer who played hurt and hated striking out; in nine seasons he ranked first or second in his league in at-bats per strikeout. Walter Alston said Buckner got the "red neck" a lot, and that he sort of liked it.

Brent Strom.blurb: Brent Strom pitched for the Mets, Indians and Padres in the 1970s and, by Tommy John's account, was the second pitcher ever to have Tommy John surgery. As Houston's pitching coach he helped guide the Astros to the 2017 title.

Jason Motte.blurb: Drafted by the Cardinals as a catcher in 2003, Jason Motte switched to pitching in 2006, saved five games in the 2011 postseason as St. Louis won it all, and led the NL with 42 saves in 2012.

Jake Peavy.blurb: Scouts called Jake Peavy "frail and wild," so the Mobile, Alabama high-schooler slipped to the 15th round in 1999. By 2001 his fastball, slider and changeup had made him the Padres' number-two prospect, and he debuted against the Yankees a year later.

Julio Lugo.blurb: Tall, slender and fast, Julio Lugo was built for the infield and played it for seven clubs, from Houston and Tampa Bay to Boston, St. Louis and Atlanta. He grew up in Barahona, a port town in the southwest of the Dominican Republic, one of the country's poorest communities.

Brody Hopkins.blurb: Brody Hopkins, born in 2002, made his major-league debut with the Tampa Bay Rays in 2026.

Arjun Nimmala.blurb: Arjun Nimmala, born in 2005, is a shortstop in the Los Angeles Angels organization.

Harvey Haddix.blurb: On May 26, 1959, Pittsburgh's Harvey Haddix threw 12 perfect innings against the Braves, retiring a record 36 straight batters, and still lost the game on an unearned run in the 13th. It is widely called the greatest game ever pitched. He was a three-time All-Star and won two World Series.

Matt Wieters.blurb: Matt Wieters went fifth overall out of Georgia Tech in 2007 and caught for the Orioles through 2016, making four All-Star teams and winning two Gold Gloves before stops in Washington and St. Louis.

Hubert Lockhart.blurb: Hubert Lockhart threw a no-hitter at Talladega College in 1923, then pitched six seasons for the Bacharach Giants, including the 1926 and 1927 Colored World Series. Afterward he coached sports at Alabama State for more than 40 years.

Dizzy Trout.blurb: Dizzy Trout attracted tall tales, and nobody is sure which are true. One goes that he struck out Ted Williams and asked him to sign the ball; Williams stormed off, then homered off him next time and called out that he'd sign that one if Trout could find it.

Kris Medlen.blurb: Kris Medlen pitched for the Braves, Royals and Diamondbacks, and now works as an analyst on Braves telecasts.

Brandon Webb.blurb: Brandon Webb, out of Kentucky, won the 2006 NL Cy Young with Arizona and made three All-Star teams. Shoulder injuries ended his career early, but his 142 adjusted ERA+ ranks 18th all time.

Will Clark.blurb: Will Clark arrived about as ready as a player can: World Series play at the Babe Ruth, American Legion and college levels, plus the Olympics. He helped make the Giants a contender again in his first five seasons and was briefly the highest-paid player in baseball before injuries wore him down.

Dean Stone.blurb: Dean Stone was the winning pitcher of the 1954 All-Star Game without officially facing a single batter, though he did throw to Duke Snider in front of 69,751 fans in Cleveland. Over parts of eight seasons he pitched for six teams.

Jack Coombs.blurb: For one season, "Colby Jack" Coombs was as good as anyone in the Deadball Era. In 1910 he went 31-9 with a 1.30 ERA for Connie Mack's A's, completed 35 starts and threw 13 shutouts, still the American League record.

Leon Durham.blurb: Leon "Bull" Durham, a lefty first baseman and outfielder, played 10 seasons, most of them with the Cubs, and later spent years as a minor-league hitting coach.

Tommy John.blurb: Tommy John never had overpowering stuff or the guile of a Perry or Niekro, just a good curve and a sinker, yet he won nearly 300 games and pitched into his 40s. His 26-year career is second only to Nolan Ryan's and Cap Anson's 27.

Eddie Cicotte.blurb: Eddie "Knuckles" Cicotte didn't invent the knuckleball, but he may have been the first big-leaguer to master it, throwing it about 75 percent of the time. The rest came from a cabinet of trick pitches, including the shine ball, the emery ball and a rising fastball he called the "sailor."

Pedro Martinez.blurb: The Dodgers traded a young Pedro Martínez, and an executive later regretted it: they gave up one of the best pitchers of the last 50 years, a three-time Cy Young winner with a 219-100 record and a 2.93 career ERA. He grew up in Manoguayabo, a poor town near Santo Domingo, the fifth of six children.

Larry Sherry.blurb: Larry Sherry was born with clubfeet and could barely walk until he was about twelve. After operations and the corrective shoes he wore for the rest of his life, he followed his athletic older brothers onto the ball field and all the way to the major leagues.

Andrew Miller.blurb: A 6-foot-7 lefty who struggled as a starter, Andrew Miller found himself in the bullpen, where his deceptive fastball and slider made him one of the game's most dominant relievers. He also helped the US win the 2017 World Baseball Classic.

Jose Canseco.blurb: Few players had more talent, or more erratic impulses, than José Canseco: Rookie of the Year in 1986, MVP in 1988, 462 home runs and 1,407 RBIs. His 2005 memoir admitted his own steroid use and named others, and his name turned up in the tabloids as often as the sports pages.

Al Leiter.blurb: Al Leiter pitched 18 years in both leagues, won two World Series rings and pitched in the Fall Classic for three teams. His charity work and his second career as a broadcaster have won him almost as much recognition as his pitching did.

Randy Jones.blurb: "The common man's pitcher," his manager called him: Randy Jones didn't look like much and threw nothing hard, and Mike Schmidt said he'd be embarrassed to take that stuff to the mound. Yet his junk baffled the best hitters in the league; Pete Rose, at 4-for-29 against him, tried switching sides.

Willie Bobo.blurb: Willie Bobo, from Tennessee, played first base in the Negro leagues from 1923 to 1930, mostly for the St. Louis Stars after starting with the Kansas City Monarchs. He died in 1931 at just 33.

Devin Williams.blurb: Devin Williams was the 2020 NL Rookie of the Year and Reliever of the Year with Milwaukee, then made two All-Star teams before stops with the Yankees and now the Mets.

Mike Trout.blurb: Many call Mike Trout the best player of his generation: three MVPs, four runner-up finishes, twelve All-Star teams and nine Silver Sluggers with the Angels. He captained Team USA in the 2023 World Baseball Classic.

Dan Bankhead.blurb: Until the Negro Leagues were recognized as major leagues in 2020, Dan Bankhead was on record as the first African American to pitch in the majors. He and four of his brothers all played in the Negro Leagues, but his big-league career was brief and he died at 55, before historians could record his story.

Teddy Higuera.blurb: Mexican lefty Teddy Higuera spent all nine of his big-league seasons with Milwaukee and is one of only four Brewers with 1,000 strikeouts.

Biz Mackey.blurb: As manager of the 1946 Newark Eagles, Biz Mackey built what was called the best pitching staff in Negro baseball and won a championship even with his ace hurting in the World Series. His shortstop Monte Irvin said that as a player, manager and person, Mackey was in a class by himself.

Milo Candini.blurb: After six years in the Yankees' farm system, Milo Candini debuted for Washington in 1943 and won his first seven decisions, hailed as the sensation of the league. Arm trouble dogged him for the rest of a 20-year pro career; he finished 26-21 in eight big-league seasons.

Tom Cheney.blurb: On September 12, 1962, Washington's Tom Cheney struck out 21 Orioles in a 16-inning, 2-1 win, the most strikeouts by any pitcher in a single major-league game.

Juan Uribe.blurb: Juan Uribe was spotted in the Dominican Republic by Jorge Posada's father and signed by the Rockies in 1997 as an undrafted free agent, starting his pro career that summer in the Dominican Summer League.

Alex Gordon.blurb: Alex Gordon swept the Golden Spikes, Dick Howser and Brooks Wallace awards at Nebraska and went second overall to the Royals in 2005. He debuted at third base, struggled, was sent down in 2010, and came back as a left fielder; he played his entire career in Kansas City.

Ivan Rodriguez.blurb: From the dirt fields of Puerto Rico, Pudge Rodríguez became perhaps the greatest all-around catcher ever: a decade of stardom in Texas, a World Series title with the Marlins, a revival in Detroit, and only the second catcher elected to the Hall of Fame on the first ballot.

Kyle Freeland.blurb: Kyle Freeland came out of Evansville as the eighth pick of the 2014 draft and pitched for his home-state Rockies after debuting in 2017.

Phil Niekro.blurb: Phil Niekro was born on April Fools' Day, 1939, fitting for a man who spent his career fooling hitters with a pitch most pitchers wanted nothing to do with. His grandparents came from Polish Russia to the West Virginia coal country.

Mike Schmidt.blurb: Mike Schmidt hit more home runs than anyone in the 1980s and is regarded as perhaps the greatest all-around third baseman ever. He charged bunts to make barehanded plays with submarine throws, and barehanded high choppers off the Veterans Stadium turf in one motion.

Tony Phillips.blurb: Tony Phillips played 18 seasons as the ultimate utility man: mostly second base, but plenty of short, third, both outfield corners and DH as well.

Jeff Kent.blurb: Jeff Kent won the 2000 MVP and a place in the Hall of Fame, but not many fans along the way; he was one of the most polarizing players of his time. "It's not arrogant; it's confident," he said of his old-school manner.
