Mark Bellhorn.blurb: Mark Bellhorn may be the most underrated member of the 2004 Red Sox. Next to Ortiz, Schilling and Dave Roberts he got little credit, but his clutch postseason play was a big reason Boston won that World Series.

Mike Napoli.blurb: "Porterhouse," or "the Beard," was a free-swinging power hitter who hit 267 home runs with a .346 on-base percentage over 12 seasons with the Angels, Rangers, Red Sox and Indians, and fans chanted his name in the big moments.

David Ross.blurb: David Ross caught for 15 seasons and seven clubs, won the World Series with the 2013 Red Sox and the 2016 Cubs, and managed the Cubs from 2020 to 2023.

Mack Eggleston.blurb: Mack Eggleston caught and played the outfield in the Negro leagues from 1919 to 1934 for more than a dozen teams, and managed the Wilmington Potomacs in 1925.

David Wells.blurb: On June 28, 1997, Yankee David "Boomer" Wells took the mound wearing a cap Babe Ruth had worn in 1934, which he'd bought for $35,000; Joe Torre made him take it off after one inning. Reverent about Yankee tradition, Wells was an iconoclast about nearly everything else.

Curt Flood.blurb: Curt Flood won seven straight Gold Gloves in center field, made three All-Star teams and hit over .300 six times, leading the league with 211 hits in 1964. He was also an activist, and he retired third in NL history in games played in center field.

Fernando Valenzuela.blurb: Of the 152 major-leaguers born in Mexico, Fernando Valenzuela stands above them all. With his trademark delivery and a superb screwball, he became in 1981 the only player to win Rookie of the Year and the Cy Young in the same season.

Heinie Manush.blurb: Heinie Manush mastered the line drive but never his temper, and he burst onto the scene with Detroit as one of the most feared hitters in the game. The son of German immigrants in Tuscumbia, Alabama, he was one of seven brothers, six of whom played pro ball.

Lew Burdette.blurb: One of the best control pitchers of the 1950s, Lew Burdette formed one of baseball's greatest pitching pairs with his roommate and best friend Warren Spahn. He was also a famous prankster: snakes in umpires' pockets, and posing as a lefty for his 1959 Topps card.

Cocaina Garcia.blurb: Manuel García, from Manacas, Cuba, was spotted pitching weekends at a sugar-mill team and went on pitching into the early 1950s. Short and stout, he was no power pitcher, and he became known as "Cocaína."

Paul Waner.blurb: A Pirates great, Paul Waner played before the TV era, and by 2005 his family found there was nothing at PNC Park to remember him by. His relatives set out to make sure his legacy wasn't lost.

Bill Lee.blurb: "Spaceman" Bill Lee pitched for the Red Sox and Expos and is in the Red Sox Hall of Fame, holding the club record for games by a lefty and the third-most wins by a Boston southpaw. At 65 he signed with an independent-league team, the San Rafael Pacifics.

Giancarlo Stanton.blurb: Known as Mike until 2012, the 6-foot-6 Giancarlo Stanton is the Marlins' all-time home-run leader and the only active player with more than 450 homers, now with the Yankees.

Kenta Maeda.blurb: Kenta Maeda won Japan's Sawamura Award twice with the Hiroshima Carp, then signed an eight-year deal with the Dodgers in 2016 and later pitched for the Twins and Tigers before returning home to the Rakuten Eagles.

Aroldis Chapman.blurb: "The Cuban Missile" earned the name with his fastball. A member of the 400-save club, Aroldis Chapman is the all-time strikeout leader among relievers, after starting out with Holguín back home.

Frank Robinson.blurb: Frank Robinson didn't want to be remembered as a pioneer, just as a ballplayer who did his job as well as it could be done. Jim Palmer called him the best player he ever saw, and Duane Kuiper called him the best manager he ever played for.

Brian Anderson.blurb: Brian Anderson pitched 13 seasons for five teams, then moved to the booth; he is now the color commentator on Rays telecasts.

Ben Brown.blurb: Ben Brown, born in 1999, pitches for the Chicago Cubs; he made his big-league debut in 2024.

Derrek Lee.blurb: "D-Lee" won the World Series with the 2003 Marlins and the NL batting title with the Cubs in 2005, along with three Gold Gloves at first base and two All-Star selections.

Steve Carlton.blurb: Lefty won 27 games in 1972 for a Phillies team that won only 59 in all. In 1980 he led the NL with 24 wins and the majors with 286 strikeouts and won the Cy Young in a landslide.

Josue De Paula.blurb: Josue De Paula, a Dominican-American outfielder born in 2005, made his debut with the Dodgers in 2026.

Randy Johnson.blurb: At 6-foot-10, "the Big Unit" was the tallest player in big-league history when he arrived, and his overpowering fastball and wicked slider kept him effective through 22 seasons, mostly with Seattle and Arizona, once he harnessed his early control problems.

Woodie Held.blurb: In the summer of 1963, Cleveland's Woodie Held started a record-setting parade: with two outs in the sixth he homered off the Angels' Paul Foytack, and pitcher Pedro Ramos, Tito Francona and Larry Brown followed with homers of their own, four in a row, a new league mark.

Eric Milton.blurb: Lefty Eric Milton started for several big-league clubs from 1998 to 2009, and now coaches high-school ball at Severna Park.

Charlie Sweeney.blurb: In 1884 Charlie Sweeney won 41 games for two teams in two different major leagues and struck out 19 in a nine-inning game; Tim Keefe called him the greatest pitcher who ever lived. His arm gave out that same year, drink took over, and he was out of the majors by 1887.

Mookie Betts.blurb: Mookie Betts won the 2018 AL MVP with Boston and has since added four World Series titles, eight All-Star games, seven Silver Sluggers and six Gold Gloves. He has played the outfield, shortstop and second base, and ranks among the top three active players in WAR.

Silver King.blurb: Named for his white-blond hair, Silver King (born Charles Koenig) won 32 games as a rookie for the 1887 pennant-winning Browns and at least 30 in each of his first four seasons, including a league-best 45 in 1888. Fiercely independent and often combative, he went 203-152 for seven teams.

Jim Bouton.blurb: Jim Bouton helped the Yankees win three pennants and a World Series, but his lasting mark came after he lost his fastball: his diary of the 1969 season as a struggling knuckleballer in Seattle, Ball Four, became one of the best-selling baseball books ever and changed how fans saw the game.

Mel Harder.blurb: After two decades on the mound, Mel Harder became a pioneering pitching coach, guiding the Indians' staff through a 111-win season when there was no how-to book for the job. He was writing it, nudging his pitchers toward discovering things for themselves.

Josh Donaldson.blurb: Drafted out of Auburn by the Cubs, Josh Donaldson debuted with Oakland in 2010 as a catcher, moved to third base and became an All-Star in 2014, then played for six more clubs over a 13-year career.

Ted Williams.blurb: Any argument over the greatest hitter ever includes Ted Williams; most narrow it to him and Babe Ruth. If the game is getting on base, nobody ranks above him. When asked, he listed Ruth, Gehrig, Foxx, Hornsby and DiMaggio as the top five, and left himself out.

Smoky Burgess.blurb: Smoky Burgess didn't look the part, and one book called him the fattest man ever to play pro ball. But Joe Garagiola said you could wake him at 3 a.m. on Christmas morning, throw him a curve, and he'd hit a line drive.

Carson Williams.blurb: Carson Williams, a Rays first-round pick in 2021, made his big-league debut at shortstop for Tampa Bay in 2025.

Richard Hidalgo.blurb: Richard Hidalgo hit in bursts: five straight games with a homer for the Mets, ten straight with an extra-base hit for Houston, and a .477 September in 2000, an Astros record for 17 years. That 2000 season he hit .314 with 44 home runs and 122 RBIs.

Juan Soto.blurb: Juan Soto signed with Washington at 16, finished second for Rookie of the Year in 2018 and was a key part of the Nationals' first World Series title in 2019. Six Silver Sluggers and five All-Star teams later, he plays for the Mets.

Johnny Niggeling.blurb: Johnny Niggeling wandered through ten leagues over nearly two decades before sticking in the majors at 36. His sidearm, one-finger knuckleball earned him a place with Cincinnati and later on Washington's famous mid-1940s staff of four knuckleballers.

Jimmy Crooks.blurb: Jimmy Crooks, born in 2001, is a catcher for the St. Louis Cardinals; he debuted in 2025.

Didi Gregorius.blurb: Born in Amsterdam, where his father played ball, Didi Gregorius moved to Curaçao at five and started in tee-ball. The Reds signed him as a teenager in 2007; he went on to play shortstop for Arizona, the Yankees and Philadelphia.

Jim Bunning.blurb: Jim Bunning struggled for nearly six seasons in the minors, then willed himself into a great pitcher: 224 wins and no-hitters in both leagues, the second a perfect game on Father's Day, 1964. He later served in the US Senate and was voted into the Hall of Fame.

Tim Raines.blurb: Tim Raines grew up in a competitive family in Sanford, Florida, racing his father until somebody could beat him; Tim did it first, at 15. A 2017 Hall of Famer, he has the best stolen-base percentage (84.7) of anyone with 400 or more steals since 1951.

Jim Brewer.blurb: Jim Brewer called himself a screwball, and he threw one; after three years of work, with help from a Hall of Famer, the pitch saved his career and made him the Dodgers' late-inning fireman for six years starting at age 30. He is also remembered for the sneak punch Billy Martin threw at him, which led to a long lawsuit.

Allen Craig.blurb: Allen Craig hit over .300 with 20-plus homers in every minor-league season, then batted .306 for the Cardinals through 2013. He was famous for hitting with runners on: .400 with runners in scoring position in 2012.

Ricky Bones.blurb: Puerto Rican right-hander Ricky Bones pitched from 1991 to 2001 for seven teams, including the Brewers, Yankees and Marlins, and now coaches pitchers for Monterrey in the Mexican League.

Jesse Petty.blurb: "The Silver Fox," from Olney, Texas, served as an infantry private in World War I and pitched in the majors from 1921 to 1930 for Cleveland, Brooklyn, Pittsburgh and the Cubs.

Randy Ready.blurb: Randy Ready was a big-league utility man from 1983 to 1995, played a season in Japan with Chiba Lotte, and later managed in the minors for the Tigers and Padres.

Adrian Beltre.blurb: Adrian Beltré reached the majors before he turned 20 and stayed 21 seasons, collecting 3,166 hits. One magazine called him almost boringly steady in the box score, but nothing about the way he played was boring.

Robby Snelling.blurb: Robby Snelling, born in 2003, made his major-league debut with the Miami Marlins in 2026.

Frank Grube.blurb: After four years out of the majors shoveling in the Chicago stockyards and working a Pennsylvania steel mill, Frank Grube made the 1941 Browns and said he'd learned what a fool anyone is to let baseball get away.

Placido Polanco.blurb: Plácido Polanco started two All-Star Games and retired with the best career fielding percentage ever at both second base and third base.

Willie Wilson.blurb: "Having Willie Wilson in center field is like having four outfielders," said his first minor-league manager, and Dwight Evans said he'd never seen anyone like him rounding second. Wilson grew up in Montgomery, Alabama, raised mostly by his grandmother.

Hod Lisenbee.blurb: Hod Lisenbee never touched a baseball until high school, at 21, and got cut. He still pitched professionally until he was 51, gave up home runs to both Babe Ruth and Jimmie Foxx, and Clarksville, Tennessee, later named a boulevard after him.

Jacoby Ellsbury.blurb: In Game 2 of the 2007 World Series, Boston rookie Jacoby Ellsbury stole second and won free tacos for the whole country through a sponsor's "Steal a Base, Steal a Taco" promotion, and millions learned his name that night.

Alex Rios.blurb: Alex Rios won a Fielding Bible Award in right field in 2007, made two All-Star teams, hit for the cycle and collected six hits in one game in 2013, and won the 2015 World Series with Kansas City. He played in three World Baseball Classics for Puerto Rico.

Bobby Shantz.blurb: Bobby Shantz won the 1952 AL MVP with the Philadelphia Athletics, took home eight straight Gold Gloves and won the 1958 World Series with the Yankees. He is the last living Philadelphia Athletic and the last surviving player from the 1940s.

Lance Parrish.blurb: "Big Wheel" kept the 1984 champion Tigers rolling, a catcher strong enough to wear the gear every day and still swing a powerful bat in the cleanup spot. He made eight All-Star teams.

Carl Pavano.blurb: Carl Pavano won the 2003 World Series with the Marlins and made the 2004 All-Star team, then signed with the Yankees, where injuries defined his four years. He also pitched for Montreal, Cleveland and Minnesota.

Sid Gordon.blurb: A powerfully built, well-liked Brooklyn native, Sid Gordon played wherever he was put, outfield or third base, for the Giants, Braves and Pirates. Brooklyn fans held a day for him at Ebbets Field even though he played for the rival Giants.

Tom Seaver.blurb: Tom Seaver was elected to the Hall of Fame on January 7, 1992, with a higher share of the vote than any player had ever received to that point.

Shin-Soo Choo.blurb: Shin-Soo Choo was MVP and best pitcher of the U-18 World Cup for South Korea, then became an outfielder for the Mariners, Indians, Reds and Rangers. He left MLB with the most home runs ever by an Asian-born player, 218, a record later passed by Shohei Ohtani.

Jimmy Rollins.blurb: "J-Roll" grew up in Alameda, California, was a Phillies second-round pick in 1996, and after most of five seasons in the minors debuted in September 2000. He quickly made his name as an excellent shortstop and played 15 seasons in Philadelphia.

Bobby Abreu.blurb: Known back home in Venezuela as "El Comedulce," Bobby Abreu combined power, speed and patience over 18 seasons: more than 2,400 hits, 400 steals and nearly 1,500 walks. The Phillies added him to their Wall of Fame in 2019.

Rogers Hornsby.blurb: Rogers Hornsby's .358 career average is second only to Ty Cobb's, and he is without much debate the greatest right-handed hitter ever. He won seven National League batting titles.

Cliff Lee.blurb: Cliff Lee, from Benton, Arkansas, won a Cy Young, made four All-Star teams, and pitched in back-to-back World Series in 2009 and 2010 for two different teams, the Phillies and the Rangers.

Greg Maddux.blurb: On August 26, 1995, Greg Maddux took a 5-0 lead into the third inning at Wrigley, chasing a record 16th straight road win. "This is like giving a 15-0 lead to a regular human being," one writer muttered in the press box, which said everything about how dominant he was in the 1990s.

Anderson Pryor.blurb: Anderson Pryor played second base in the first Negro National League, mostly for the Detroit Stars.

Al Kaline.blurb: Al Kaline's father, a Baltimore broom maker and semipro player, crouched and caught while his son worked on his pitches; by nine Al had a fastball, curve and changeup, and he once won ten straight for his grammar school. That arm made him one of the most complete players of his time.

Dale Murphy.blurb: Dale Murphy was the face of the Braves from 1978 to 1990, years when Atlanta mostly finished near the bottom of the division. He was known as a Boy Scout who didn't smoke or drink.

Tyler Anderson.blurb: An Oregon Duck and the 20th overall pick in 2011, lefty Tyler Anderson debuted with the Rockies in 2016 and has made two All-Star teams pitching for six clubs.

Tommy Harper.blurb: Tommy Harper played the outfield, third and second for seven franchises from 1962 to 1976, made an All-Star team and twice led the league in stolen bases.

Jake Bloss.blurb: Jake Bloss, born in 2001, debuted with Houston in 2024 and now pitches for the Toronto Blue Jays.

Roch Cholowsky.blurb: Roch Cholowsky played at UCLA and was the first overall pick of the 2026 draft, by the Chicago White Sox.

Pete Donohue.blurb: Texan Pete Donohue won 127 games for Cincinnati, three seasons of 20 or more, led the league with 27 complete games in 1925 and in wins in 1926, and is in the Reds Hall of Fame. He lost his edge by his late 20s and was done by 1931.

Alvin Davis.blurb: "Mr. Mariner" was Seattle's first homegrown star: Rookie of the Year in 1984, he anchored the lineup for eight seasons with a sharp eye and a powerful swing. He is remembered as much for his kindness and humility.

Aaron Heilman.blurb: Aaron Heilman, from Logansport, Indiana (also the hometown of Commissioner Kenesaw Mountain Landis), is forever linked with Yadier Molina by one postseason moment, the way Ralph Branca is tied to Bobby Thomson.

Stan Coveleski.blurb: Stan Coveleski threw one of the best spitballs ever and went to his mouth before every pitch, even when he went innings without throwing one, so hitters always had to look for it. He led the AL in strikeouts in 1920 but preferred getting outs in a few pitches.

Lonnie Smith.blurb: Lonnie Smith overcame drug problems to become one of the top base stealers of the 1980s, seventh-most in the decade, and played on five pennant winners, three of which won the World Series.

Mike Scott.blurb: The split-finger fastball turned Mike Scott from mediocre to ace, and he won the 1986 Cy Young with Houston. Hitters were sure he was scuffing the ball; it was never proven, and Scott liked them worrying about it.

Phil Douglas.blurb: "Shufflin' Phil" Douglas, 6-foot-3 out of Cedartown, Georgia, threw hard enough to draw Walter Johnson comparisons, and relied on a devastating spitball he learned from Ed Walsh in 1912.

Manny Ramirez.blurb: "Manny being Manny": one of the best right-handed hitters of the last 50 years, with 555 home runs plus a record 29 in the postseason, the 2002 AL batting title, the 2004 World Series MVP for Boston, 12 All-Star teams and nine Silver Sluggers.

Dave Harris.blurb: On August 5, 1932, Walter Johnson sent Dave Harris up to pinch-hit as the 27th batter against Detroit's Tommy Bridges, who was one out from a perfect game. Harris singled. He led the league with 14 pinch hits that year.

Dallas Braden.blurb: Dallas Braden threw a perfect game for Oakland on May 9, 2010, but ranks it a distant second. His favorite memory is a 2005 start for his hometown Stockton Ports, ten strikeouts deep into the ninth with only the ballpark's "beer batter" left to retire.

Zack Greinke.blurb: Gatorade's national high-school player of the year and the sixth overall pick in 2002, Zack Greinke pitched 20 seasons for six clubs and is considered one of the greatest pitchers of his generation.

Chris Sale.blurb: A 6-foot-6 beanpole of a lefty from Lakeland, Chris Sale struck out 300 batters in 2017 and anchored the 2018 World Series champion Red Sox rotation, after seven straight All-Star seasons.

Willie McCovey.blurb: Pitchers feared "Stretch" so much that teams shifted against his dead-pull line drives; the Giants slugger retired second only to Babe Ruth among lefty home run hitters and sailed into the Hall in 1986.

Orlando Hernandez.blurb: Banished from Cuban baseball, El Duque ended up a four-time World Series champion; the nickname was his father's first, earned playing for a toothpaste company team, and his half-brother Liván pitched seventeen seasons too.

Joe Mauer.blurb: Joe Mauer once rolled a 265 in bowling while just learning the sport, was an all-state point guard, and still chose baseball, going first overall to his hometown Twins and later winning an MVP.

Konnor Griffin.blurb: Barely out of his teens, Konnor Griffin went ninth overall in the 2024 draft, then reached the majors with the Pittsburgh Pirates in 2026 while still only twenty years old.

Gil Meche.blurb: Gil Meche's shoulder and back gave out so early that he walked away from baseball at just 32, after three straight Opening Day starts for Kansas City and a 2007 All-Star nod.

Ubaldo Jimenez.blurb: In 2010 Ubaldo Jiménez started the All-Star Game and threw the first no-hitter in Rockies franchise history, then won his 100th career game five years later as an Oriole.

David Freese.blurb: David Freese nearly quit baseball after high school, yet became the St. Louis hero who hit the walk-off homer in Game Six of the 2011 World Series, the exact daydream every kid has.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto.blurb: Yoshinobu Yamamoto won three straight Triple Crowns in Japan, threw two no-hitters, then landed a $325 million Dodgers deal, the biggest ever for a pitcher then, and won a ring as a rookie.

Barry Zito.blurb: Barry Zito did yoga in the outfield before games, played guitar, surfed, dyed his hair, and one winter danced a toy soldier in The Nutcracker; he also won a Cy Young Award.

Pop Lloyd.blurb: Monte Irvin called him the best black player of his time; Pop Lloyd played over twenty-five years for team after team, and in old age he and his wife watched Jackie Robinson play.

Tim McCarver.blurb: The Cardinals paid a Memphis linebacker-turned-catcher $75,000 to sign, and Tim McCarver helped win championships before talking his way into an even bigger second career in the broadcast booth.

Kendrys Morales.blurb: Kendrys Morales hit a walk-off grand slam, jumped on home plate with his teammates, broke his ankle, and missed nearly two years; he finally got his ring with the 2015 Royals.

Eppa Rixey.blurb: With the best name in the Hall of Fame, Eppa Rixey won 266 games, then laughed that he was glad Warren Spahn broke his lefty record because it reminded everyone he had set it.

Chad Bradford.blurb: A submariner who threw only mid-80s, Chad Bradford became a cult hero in Michael Lewis's Moneyball, and the movie version of him was played by actor Casey Bond.

Robin Yount.blurb: Robin Yount debuted as an 18-year-old shortstop, ran out every groundball at full speed for twenty seasons, and won MVP awards at two different positions before reaching 3,000 hits.

Jack Pfiester.blurb: After beating the Giants in 1908, one Chicago writer declared that nobody need struggle with Pfiester's name; he would simply be "Jack the Giant Killer," a lefty who went 15-5 against New York.

Ken Griffey Jr..blurb: With the sweetest swing ever seen and a 1,000-watt smile, Ken Griffey Jr. has two bricks behind Seattle's center-field wall, one reading "The House Their Father Built."

Rudy May.blurb: As a kid, Rudy May used to sneak into his catcher dad's gear in the car; years later, with the fastball gone, he joked an 85 on the corner beat a 95 down the middle.

Corey Koskie.blurb: The Canadian third baseman Corey Koskie played for the Twins, Blue Jays and Brewers, and in 2015 got the call to the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame.

Matt Holliday.blurb: A slugger who hit .300 eight times, Matt Holliday won the 2007 NLCS MVP award, carried Colorado to its first World Series, then got his own ring with St. Louis in 2011.

Rico Petrocelli.blurb: Boston loved the "Fenway Stroke" that dropped balls into the net atop the Green Monster, and Rico Petrocelli smacked 40 homers as a shortstop in 1969, a league record then.

Hank Greenberg.blurb: Hank Greenberg lost four prime years to World War II and still launched 331 homers, chased Babe Ruth's record in 1938, and posted an OPS topped then by only Ruth, Williams, Gehrig and Foxx.

Tony Watson.blurb: A ninth-round pick by Pittsburgh in 2007, Tony Watson made the 2014 All-Star team, then quietly piled up relief appearances until he became baseball's all-time leader in holds.

Sid Fernandez.blurb: A hefty, laid-back lefty who grew up surfing in Honolulu, "El Sid" baffled hitters and won 114 games, more than any other major leaguer born and raised in Hawaii.

Jim Tabor.blurb: Nicknamed "Rawhide," Jim Tabor was a lanky Alabama third baseman, 6-foot-2 and only 175 pounds, who played for the Red Sox through 1944 and the Phillies after the war.

Alex Bregman.blurb: Alex Bregman hit .678 as a high school junior, becoming the first prep player to win USA Baseball's Player of the Year, then starred at LSU and went second overall in 2015.

Lou Gehrig.blurb: Nearly 42,000 fans sat quietly at Yankee Stadium on July 4, 1939, to hear a gaunt Lou Gehrig, his uniform hanging loose, say goodbye after learning he had an incurable illness.

Mitchell Murray.blurb: Sometimes mistakenly listed as "Mitchell Murphy," this Ohio catcher spent fourteen Negro league seasons with the Dayton Marcos, St. Louis Stars, Chicago American Giants and Indianapolis ABCs.

Kyle Seager.blurb: Kyle Seager never wore another uniform: the third-round pick played all eleven big-league seasons for Seattle, grabbing both an All-Star spot and a Gold Glove in 2014.

Brett Butler.blurb: Diagnosed with cancer in May 1996, leadoff man Brett Butler beat it and was back on the field four months later, a four-time triples leader who then went on to manage Reno.

David Price.blurb: Just weeks after his debut, rookie David Price earned a save in Game 7 of the 2008 ALCS to send Tampa Bay to its first World Series, then won the 2012 Cy Young Award.

Dan Haren.blurb: Traded for Mark Mulder and later flipped for prospects, Dan Haren pitched for eight clubs, earned three All-Star nods, and now serves as a pitching strategist for the Diamondbacks.

Joe Dugan.blurb: Tens of thousands of fans were turned away from Game Five of the 1923 World Series at the brand-new Yankee Stadium, including the parents of Yankees third baseman Joe Dugan, locked out of their own son's game.

Sam Streeter.blurb: A Smithsonian exhibit once had a ten-year-old asking "Who the heck was Sam Streeter?" about an autographed ball; the answer was a Negro league lefty, once a Homestead Grays star and an early Pittsburgh Crawfords signing.

Von Hayes.blurb: Booed by Philadelphia fans after an infamous trade, Von Hayes shrugged that they could do whatever they wanted because he would still be eating steak every night, a stoic attitude that later won him cult fans.

John Donaldson.blurb: A sure-handed utility man from Charlotte, John Donaldson survived trades, demotions and releases across 405 big-league games with the A's and Seattle Pilots, and said he would happily do it all over again.

Dave Righetti.blurb: On the Fourth of July in 1983, Dave Righetti no-hit the Red Sox before 41,077 fans, the first Yankee no-hitter since Don Larsen's perfect game in 1956; he later saved 252 games and coached Giants pitchers for eighteen years.

Dustin Pedroia.blurb: Dustin Pedroia never wore another uniform: the Red Sox second baseman won Rookie of the Year in 2007 and AL MVP in 2008, plus World Series rings in 2007 and 2013.

Mickey Welch.blurb: Listed at just 5-foot-8 and 160 pounds, Mickey Welch won the Giants' first-ever NL game in 1883, strung together 17 straight wins in 1885, and became only the third pitcher to reach 300 victories.

Mickey Rivers.blurb: Known as "Mick the Quick," the speedy Yankees center fielder led off for the 1977 and 1978 World Series champions, both times beating the Dodgers, despite owning a below-average throwing arm.

Charles Johnson.blurb: Charles Johnson won four straight Gold Gloves behind the plate and once caught more than 100 games in a season without committing a single error, a feat achieved by only three catchers; he also won a 1997 ring with Florida.

Earl Webb.blurb: Waived twice and on his fifth club, Earl Webb smacked a record 67 doubles for the 1931 Red Sox, earning the nickname "The Earl of Doublin'" and a mark that still stands today.

Andy Pafko.blurb: Andy Pafko stood with his back to the left-field wall as Bobby Thomson's "shot heard 'round the world" sailed over his head in 1951, and later lost his Braves starting job to a kid named Hank Aaron.

Bob Veale.blurb: At 6-foot-6 and famously bespectacled, Bob Veale had a fastball and questionable vision that made hitters miserable; he led the NL with 250 strikeouts in 1964 and pitched in the first game started by an all-minority lineup.

Bruce Sutter.blurb: Bruce Sutter's split-fingered fastball seemed to roll along a table before the bottom dropped out, saving his moribund career and carrying him to 300 saves and Cooperstown; the Senators even drafted him as a 17-year-old.

Yogi Berra.blurb: A three-time AL MVP who appeared in 14 World Series as a player and five more as a coach or manager, Yogi Berra collected 13 championship rings, the son of Italian immigrants from St. Louis's "The Hill."

Chris Cannizzaro.blurb: The first big-league pitch Chris Cannizzaro ever called was a curveball to Wally Moon, which he missed and Moon crushed over the screen; he still lasted 13 seasons and became the Padres' first franchise All-Star.

Luis Arroyo.blurb: Nicknamed "Tite," Luis Arroyo was the first Puerto Rican to play for the Yankees, helped them win the 1961 and 1962 pennants, and was an All-Star in 1955 alongside Vic Power, another Puerto Rican first.

Rich Gossage.blurb: "Goose" Gossage threw 134 1/3 relief innings in 63 appearances for the 1978 champion Yankees and insisted it took three modern closers to do his job; Cooperstown agreed in 2008.

Eric Plunk.blurb: A 6-foot-5 reliever whose best moments always came at the end of games, Eric Plunk saved the September 17, 1996 win over the White Sox that clinched Cleveland's second straight division title.

Graig Nettles.blurb: With cat-like reflexes and range "as sweeping as a ten-foot leaf rake," Graig Nettles dove to snag a Reggie Smith smash in Game Three of the 1978 World Series, saving Ron Guidry and the Yankees.

Mike Piazza.blurb: In the first New York game after September 11, 2001, with the city still aching, Mike Piazza lined a two-run homer off Steve Karsay in the eighth inning to lift the Mets over the Braves.

Brock Holt.blurb: "The Brock Star" played every position except catcher, made the 2015 All-Star team, and hit for the cycle twice, including the only postseason cycle in major-league history.

Don Larsen.blurb: A carefree night owl who disliked training rules and had a mediocre career, Don Larsen still pitched the greatest game in World Series history, and later auctioned a prized keepsake to help pay his grandchildren's tuition.

Don Newcombe.blurb: Big Newk was the first African-American pitcher in an All-Star Game, then won Rookie of the Year, the first Cy Young Award and an MVP, a triple that no one matched until Justin Verlander in 2017.

Zack Britton.blurb: Drafted as a starter, Zack Britton became an Orioles closer who led the American League in saves in 2016 and, from September 2015 to August 2017, converted an AL record 60 straight saves.

Jeffrey Leonard.blurb: Five teams, four NLCS home runs and one famous "Flap-Down" strut: Jeffrey Leonard hit four homers in the 1987 NLCS for the Giants, who lost to the Cardinals anyway.

Whitey Ford.blurb: Nicknamed "the Chairman of the Board" by catcher Elston Howard, Whitey Ford won 236 games with the highest winning percentage of any 200-game winner since 1900 and once threw 33 2/3 scoreless World Series innings, breaking Babe Ruth's record.

Ruben Sierra.blurb: A can't-miss five-tool prospect who changed teams 31 times across nine clubs, Ruben Sierra still piled up over 300 homers, 1,300 RBIs and 2,100 hits, and in his thirties helped both the Rangers and Yankees.

Albert Belle.blurb: His mom said he was an Eagle Scout who could spell backwards at five; teammates said he threw coolers, shattered locker-room sinks and ripped thermostats off walls, a famously furious Albert Belle.

Arky Vaughan.blurb: Arky Vaughan nearly sparked a player strike in 1943 over Leo Durocher, quit, and sat out three years; before that he hit .385 in 1935, walked 937 times against only 276 strikeouts and made nine straight All-Star teams.

Alex Avila.blurb: Nicknamed "The Titanium Catcher" because foul tips seemed to find him, the son of Tigers general manager Al Avila caught Cy Young seasons from Justin Verlander and Max Scherzer despite repeated concussions.

Johnny Neun.blurb: Johnny Neun's hair went from thick and dark to thin and gray over a remarkable sixty-nine-year career, from 1920 to 1989, as a player, coach, manager, instructor and scout, and an excellent storyteller.

Magglio Ordonez.blurb: Magglio Ordóñez learned the game dodging windows and honking cars on the streets of Coro, Venezuela; mild off the field, a "Clark Kent" in street clothes, he hit 294 homers and .309 for the White Sox and Tigers.

Reid Detmers.blurb: Drafted tenth overall in 2020, Reid Detmers reached the Angels after just 14 minor-league games and, on May 10, 2022, threw a no-hitter, a big moment for a kid from tiny Nokomis, Illinois.

Dave Danforth.blurb: Dave Danforth was called the Forrest Gump of baseball for turning up in so many big events; teammates swore he did everything to the ball, and what exactly he threw remains an unsolved mystery.

Reggie Jackson.blurb: Hitting his way to the nickname "Mr. October" for postseason heroics, Reggie Jackson won three straight World Series titles with Oakland and two more with the Yankees, then entered the Hall of Fame in his first year eligible.

Ray Caldwell.blurb: Grantland Rice said Ray Caldwell could be another Walter Johnson; instead the talented pitcher loved nightlife so much that his escapades became legendary, even though Washington once offered Johnson himself for him.

Mark Buehrle.blurb: A St. Louis kid who grew up rooting for the Cardinals, lefty Mark Buehrle threw two no-hitters, one of them a perfect game, won four Gold Gloves and a World Series ring, and won 214 games.

Jacob Misiorowski.blurb: Known as "the Miz," Jacob Misiorowski set the record for the fastest pitch by a starter since tracking began in 2008, then became the first pitcher ever to throw 1,000 pitches of 100 mph or more in a season.

Don Mossi.blurb: Roommates as rookies on Cleveland's 1954 pennant winners, lefty control artist Don Mossi and flamethrower Ray Narleski formed one of the rare shut-down righty-lefty bullpens, though Mossi later became a top starter too.

Mark Littell.blurb: Nicknamed "Country" and "Ramrod," reliever Mark Littell led the 1976 Royals with 16 saves, but bone spurs in his elbow ended his career at 29, just before the Cardinals won the 1982 World Series.

Fred McGriff.blurb: Chris Berman christened him the "Crime Dog" after a cartoon police mascot, and Fred McGriff hit 30 homers for five different teams, led both leagues in home runs, and reached the Hall of Fame in 2022.

Khalil Greene.blurb: With cascading blond hair and a laid-back, surfer's look, Khalil Greene looked destined for stardom at shortstop, but social anxiety disorder drove him to quit baseball at just 30 and retreat into deep privacy.

Bert Cunningham.blurb: On September 15, 1890, Bert Cunningham threw five wild pitches in a single inning, a record Cardinals pitcher Rick Ankiel finally tied in a 2000 playoff game.

Henry Kimbro.blurb: Only 5-foot-8 and 175 pounds, Negro leagues leadoff man Henry Kimbro, a slap-hitting speedster for the Baltimore Elite Giants, also launched a ball over the roof of Detroit's Briggs Stadium, something few players ever managed.

Cecil Fielder.blurb: On the last day of the 1990 season, in front of only 13,380 fans in the Bronx, Cecil "Big Daddy" Fielder bashed his 50th and 51st homers, the first American Leaguer to reach 50 in 29 years.

Pretzels Getzien.blurb: Charles Getzien, the first German-born major leaguer, owned one of the best nicknames of his era, "Pretzels," and won an 1887 championship with the Detroit Wolverines, even though newspapers constantly misspelled his last name.

Eddie Yost.blurb: Known as "The Walking Man" for all the bases on balls he drew, Eddie Yost played more games at third base than anyone before him, mostly for the dreadful Senators, and later coached third for the Mets.

Jack Tobin.blurb: Everyone called him Johnny, but record books say Jack; in 1915, when St. Louis had three major-league clubs, Tobin was the only native St. Louisan on any of them.

Halley Harding.blurb: A Negro league shortstop who was also a football quarterback and punter and played pro basketball for the Harlem Rens, Halley Harding later became a sportswriter pushing for the integration of the Los Angeles Rams.

Todd Jones.blurb: A middle reliever turned closer, Todd Jones saved 319 games, 235 of them for Detroit, the most in Tigers history, and became the 21st member of the 300-save club on September 16, 2007.

Javy Lopez.blurb: Listed at 6-foot-3 and 185 pounds, Puerto Rican catcher Javy Lopez admitted his weight climbed to at least 248 during his career, but he still made three All-Star teams and won the 1995 World Series with Atlanta.

Wes Covington.blurb: Teammates with Hank Aaron on the 1952 Eau Claire Bears, Wes Covington looked so talented that Aaron wrote everyone would have assumed Covington was the one headed for the home run record, until injuries and outspokenness got in the way.

Dave Winfield.blurb: ESPN once ranked Dave Winfield the third-best all-around athlete in any sport; he won the 1992 World Series with a clutch hit for Toronto, wore number 31, and entered the Hall of Fame in 2001.

Greg Holland.blurb: Closer Greg Holland won the Mariano Rivera Award in 2014, helped Kansas City win the 2015 World Series, missed 2016 after Tommy John surgery, and then led the National League in saves for Colorado.

Joe Cronin.blurb: Joe Cronin spent fifty years in baseball without ever being fired or taking a year off, rising from star shortstop to manager, general manager and league president, and nearly became commissioner in 1965.

George Zettlein.blurb: A Civil War veteran who served in both the Army and Navy, pitcher George Zettlein surrendered the National Association's first home run in 1871 and its first grand slam that September.

Jack Stivetts.blurb: Jack Stivetts threw as hard as the "Hoosier Thunderbolt," hit as hard as anyone in the league, played every position except catcher, and in 1892 tossed the first no-hitter in Boston franchise history.

Jason Heyward.blurb: Called "J-Hey," Jason Heyward was named the best prospect in baseball in 2010, started on Atlanta's Opening Day lineup that year as a rookie, and made the All-Star team before playing sixteen seasons.

Harrison Bader.blurb: Nicknamed "Tots," Bronxville native Harrison Bader won a Gold Glove in center field for the Cardinals in 2021, then bounced through seven clubs, including the Yankees, Mets and Phillies.

Roy Partlow.blurb: One of the first African Americans signed by the Dodgers organization in 1946, Negro league pitcher Roy Partlow spent part of that season in Montreal alongside Jackie Robinson before being sent down to Trois-Rivières.

Kal Daniels.blurb: Pete Rose once saw the left-handed Kal Daniels as a possible MVP, and Reds hitting coaches were scared to tinker with his natural swing, which mixed patience, power, speed and all-field contact.

Tyler Glasnow.blurb: Dodgers righty Tyler Glasnow, an All-Star in 2024, won back-to-back World Series titles, beating the Yankees in 2024 and the Blue Jays in 2025, after earlier stops in Pittsburgh and Tampa Bay.

Jim Kaat.blurb: Bill James suggested Jim Kaat, who grew up in the Dutch-American town of Zeeland, Michigan, might be a Hall of Famer if only his best years had come closer together.

Tino Martinez.blurb: After Tino Martinez homered in Game 1 of the 1998 World Series, Yankees fans started calling him "The Bam-tino"; he finished with 339 home runs, six 100-RBI seasons, and a first-round draft pedigree from Tampa.

Tony Lazzeri.blurb: Scouts shied from Tony Lazzeri even after he hit .355 with 60 home runs in thin Salt Lake City air, partly because he was epileptic, yet Yankees scout Bill Essick kept watching and reporting back.

Mark Teixeira.blurb: One of baseball's most prolific switch-hitters, Mark "Tex" Teixeira won the 2000 Dick Howser Trophy at Georgia Tech, then led the American League in homers and RBI for the 2009 champion Yankees.

Joe Sambito.blurb: The Brooklyn-born lefty almost lost his career before it began, then spent five years as one of the National League's best relievers, with a nasty slider and a 1979 All-Star Game appearance.

Kenley Jansen.blurb: Signed as an undrafted catcher out of Curaçao, Kenley Jansen switched to the mound in the minors, then became the Dodgers' longtime closer and led the National League in saves in 2017 and 2022.

Jason Castro.blurb: A first-round pick (tenth overall) out of Stanford, catcher Jason Castro made the 2013 All-Star Game as a reserve, becoming the first Astro ever elected to play for the American League.

Cole Hamels.blurb: Nicknamed "Hollywood," Cole Hamels was a 17th overall pick from San Diego whose early minor-league years were derailed by injuries, including one from a bar fight, before he reached Philadelphia in 2006.

John Valentin.blurb: Told he was too small for Division I ball, John Valentin became a Silver Slugger shortstop and, in 1994, turned an unassisted triple play, only the tenth in major-league history.

Luke Appling.blurb: A happy-go-lucky hypochondriac, Luke Appling starred on some of the White Sox's leanest teams after the Black Sox Scandal and, sadly, retired just before Chicago finally reached a World Series.

Vada Pinson.blurb: Vada Pinson nearly chose music over baseball: a talented trumpet player in the McClymonds High band, he was steered toward sports by the same legendary coach who helped Frank Robinson and Curt Flood.

Jack Harshman.blurb: A slugging pitcher, Jack Harshman hit 21 career home runs on just 76 hits, a ratio no other player with that many had topped, and once threw about 245 pitches in a 16-inning shutout.

Ace Adams.blurb: Named Ace at birth as the eighth child, Giants reliever Ace Adams pitched over 60 games four years in a row and a record 70 in 1943, though he grumbled that "relieving was the low dog."

Ted Kluszewski.blurb: With famously huge 15-inch biceps, the 6-foot-2, 225-pound "Klu" from Argo, Illinois, was the original "Big Red Machine," a mountain of a slugger who powered Cincinnati in the mid-1950s.

Dwight Gooden.blurb: Doc Gooden was one of the biggest stars of the 1980s and also one of the game's great cautionary figures, the Tampa kid whose baseball-crazy father spent countless hours practicing with him.

Bill Henry.blurb: Teammates nicknamed the quiet lefty "Gabby"; in 1964, relief ace Bill Henry posted an 0.87 earned run average for the Reds, a season described as one of the great relief years ever.

Gregg Olson.blurb: Gregg Olson won the 1989 AL Rookie of the Year award as an Orioles closer, strung together 41 consecutive scoreless innings, and still holds Baltimore's career saves record.

Chris Hammond.blurb: Retired for four years, Chris Hammond came back in 2002 mainly so his kids could see him pitch, then posted a 0.95 ERA for Atlanta, joining Ferdie Schupp and Dennis Eckersley as the only sub-1.00 seasons.

Gary Carter.blurb: Nicknamed "the Kid" for his youthful enthusiasm, Gary Carter caught the 1986 Mets to a title, singling in the 12th inning to win NLCS Game 5 and starting the comeback rally in Game 6 of the World Series.

Hippo Vaughn.blurb: Hippo Vaughn pitched a double no-hitter against Fred Toney in 1917, though the lefty was really the best in the National League from 1914 to 1920, a career that came up just short of the Hall.

Lastings Milledge.blurb: The youngest player in the entire National League as a 2006 rookie with the Mets, Lastings Milledge later played in Washington, Pittsburgh and Chicago, and even starred in Japan for the Yakult Swallows.

Bruce Ruffin.blurb: Bruce Ruffin was called up in 1986 to take Steve Carlton's spot in the Phillies' rotation after the legend's release, and finished seventh in Rookie of the Year voting with a 2.46 ERA.

Matt Anderson.blurb: Detroit made reliever Matt Anderson the first overall pick of the 1997 draft; he debuted a year later and went on to pitch for the Tigers and the Rockies until 2005.

Kitty Bransfield.blurb: When Kitty Bransfield left Pittsburgh after 1904, the Pirates' search for a first baseman lasted decades and became known as "The Bransfield Curse"; he revived his career with the Phillies.

Walt Wilmot.blurb: During the Players League bidding war, outfielder Walt Wilmot reportedly earned an astounding $4,250 a season in Chicago, the highest salary in the National League and more than star teammate Cap Anson.

Joe Krakauskas.blurb: The Canadian lefty Joe Krakauskas is remembered for giving up the final hit, a double on July 16, 1941, in Joe DiMaggio's famous 56-game hitting streak.

Mark Belanger.blurb: Baltimore's wizard at shortstop used just two tiny black gloves a season, broke them in with spit and coffee, and hated anyone touching them; Sports Illustrated said he seemed to glide to every ball.

Al Spalding.blurb: A story worthy of Horatio Alger, Al Spalding went from a lonely Illinois boy who took up baseball against loneliness to star pitcher, club owner and sporting-goods tycoon, with a political career just beginning when he died.

Dennis Cook.blurb: Nobody recruited Dennis Cook out of high school; he went to a tryout camp for a junior college scholarship, was an 18th-round pick, and always considered himself a longshot who worked harder because he had nothing to lose.

Jake Daubert.blurb: Escaping the Pennsylvania coal mines, Jake Daubert became the Deadball Era's premier National League first baseman, a slashing chop hitter with two batting titles and a still-standing NL record of 392 sacrifices.

David Ortiz.blurb: "Big Papi" hit 541 home runs and 632 doubles, helped Boston break its 86-year World Series drought in 2004, won two more rings, and saw the Red Sox retire his number 34.

Tony Fernandez.blurb: Gangly and all limbs, the Dominican shortstop scuttled after grounders and pirouetted into an underarm throw; Tony Fernández won four straight Gold Gloves, and the Yankees' acquiring him in 1995 delayed Derek Jeter.

Mario Soto.blurb: A converted catcher who made the Reds on his fourth try, Mario Soto threw harder than any other Dominican pitcher of his day and became just the third from his country to win 100 games.

Vean Gregg.blurb: Only three years out of the deep bush of the Pacific Northwest, rookie lefty Vean Gregg won 23 games for the 1911 Cleveland Naps, led the league in ERA, and was called the best southpaw by Ty Cobb.

Alex Reyes.blurb: Baseball America's second-ranked prospect in 2016, Cardinals righty Alex Reyes set the major-league record for consecutive saves to open a career in 2021 and made the All-Star team that year.

Bret Boone.blurb: When the Mariners called up Bret Boone in 1992, the family founded a new category: three-generation big leaguers, with grandfather Ray, father Bob and, later, brother Aaron, who managed the Yankees.

Rynie Wolters.blurb: Born in the Netherlands, Rynie Wolters became the first professional ballplayer from his country, and on July 23, 1870, he threw the first shutout in baseball history, blanking the Chicago White Stockings 9-0.

Babe Adams.blurb: Babe Adams pitched three complete-game wins as a rookie to hand Pittsburgh the 1909 World Series, then spent 18 years with the Pirates walking just 1.29 batters per nine innings, second only to teammate Deacon Phillippe.

Darrell Porter.blurb: Darrell Porter leapt into Bruce Sutter's arms after the final out of the 1982 World Series and was named Series MVP, declaring that he had not had a drink in two and a half years.

Francisco Rodriguez.blurb: Francisco Rodríguez burst onto the scene in the 2002 playoffs at just 20 years old, and went on to collect 437 career saves, the fourth most in major-league history.

Bill Bray.blurb: A lefty reliever for the Nationals and Reds, Bill Bray was the only player from William & Mary ever selected in the first round of the draft, and the last first-round pick of the Montreal Expos.

Tetelo Vargas.blurb: Nicknamed "El Gamo Dominicano," the Dominican Deer, Tetelo Vargas was a Dominican star of the Negro leagues who played the outfield, shortstop and first base.

King Kelly.blurb: Also known as "$10,000 Kelly" for the price Boston paid for him, King Kelly was a player-manager three times, including leading the 1890 Boston Reds to the pennant in the Players' League's only season.

Johnny Bassler.blurb: Taught to hit by Ty Cobb, catcher Johnny Bassler had a .416 career on-base percentage, second highest in history for a catcher, and in 1924 hit .346, the best by an American League catcher up to then.

Drew Pomeranz.blurb: Nicknamed "Big Smooth," lefty Drew Pomeranz played for eight big-league clubs, made the 2016 All-Star team with the Padres, and won the 2018 World Series with the Red Sox.

Mickey Tettleton.blurb: One of the best-hitting catchers of his era, Mickey Tettleton twice hit homers over Tiger Stadium's right-field roof and in 1992 became the first player to reach Eutaw Street at Camden Yards.

Ray Dandridge.blurb: Nicknamed "Hooks" and "Squat," and "Mamerto" in Mexico, Ray Dandridge was a dazzling Negro leagues third baseman and high-average hitter, considered too old for the majors when integration came, but he reached the Hall of Fame in 1987.

Hank Aguirre.blurb: A two-time All-Star lefty for the Tigers who led the American League in ERA in 1962, Hank Aguirre later became a successful businessman in Detroit.

Rich Hill.blurb: Nicknamed "Dick Mountain," Rich Hill played for a record-tying fourteen teams, pitched in every season from 2005 through 2025, and was the oldest active player in the majors in 2024 and 2025.

Rafael Devers.blurb: A two-time Silver Slugger and member of Boston's 2018 championship team, Rafael Devers signed an eleven-year, $330 million extension before 2023, then was traded to the Giants in June 2025.

Lon Warneke.blurb: "The Arkansas Hummingbird" Lon Warneke hit the first triple and scored the first National League run in All-Star Game history in 1933, and he later became a major-league umpire and a county judge.

Ketel Marte.blurb: Arizona's starting second baseman in the 2019, 2024 and 2025 All-Star Games, Ketel Marte won the 2023 NLCS MVP award as the Diamondbacks claimed their first pennant since 2001.

Edgar Renteria.blurb: Edgar Rentería's unique World Series résumé: at 21 he hit the Game Seven walk-off single for the Marlins, at 28 he made the final out, and at 34 he homered his way to World Series MVP.

Fred Luderus.blurb: A pure fastball hitter who feasted on pitches between waist and shoulders, Phillies first baseman Fred Luderus was called "the most under-rated man in baseball" in 1915, despite leading the NL in first-base errors four times.

Dan Uggla.blurb: Dan Uggla is the only second baseman in major-league history to hit at least 30 home runs in five straight seasons, after winning both rookie of the year awards voted on by players and The Sporting News in 2006.

Carlos Lee.blurb: With 358 home runs, Carlos Lee is the all-time home run leader among players born in Panama, and his 17 career grand slams tie Ted Williams and Jimmie Foxx, more than Babe Ruth.

Koji Uehara.blurb: Koji Uehara owns the best strikeout-to-walk ratio in major-league history among pitchers with 100 innings, and he won the 2013 ALCS MVP before closing the final game of that year's World Series for Boston.

Daniel Hudson.blurb: Daniel Hudson was on the mound at the end of Game 7 of the 2019 World Series to clinch Washington's first championship, then won a second ring with the Dodgers in 2024, his final season.

Frank Schulte.blurb: Nicknamed "Wildfire," Frank Schulte slugged in right field for the great Cubs teams of 1906 to 1910 and outlasted Brown, Chance, Evers and Tinker, even playing under Tinker as manager by the end of his Chicago run.

Clint Thomas.blurb: Known as "The Hawk," Clint Thomas seemed to be at the center of every watershed moment in Black baseball, from the First Colored World Series to Yankee Stadium's first Black ball game, over a 19-year career.

Juan Pierre.blurb: Speedster Juan Pierre stole 614 bases, the most since 2000, and collected 2,217 hits, more than any other player who never made an All-Star team.

Octavio Dotel.blurb: Octavio Dotel pitched for 13 major-league teams, second most in history, helped throw a six-man combined no-hitter for the Astros in 2003, and won a ring with the 2011 Cardinals.

Robb Nen.blurb: The son of former first baseman Dick Nen, closer Robb Nen won the 1997 World Series with the Marlins, then saved 206 games for the Giants on the way to 314 career saves.

Eddie Murray.blurb: Never an MVP winner but top ten in the voting eight times, "Steady Eddie" Murray drove in more runs than any other switch-hitter, and his 996 RBI in the 1980s led all of baseball.

Kid Madden.blurb: Just 124 pounds on a 5-foot-7 frame, "Kid" Madden threw such a wide curve that people still marveled at it long after his tragically short career, with a Portland sportswriter calling his drops and curves puzzling.

Harry Heilmann.blurb: The Tigers asked Harry Heilmann to replace Hall of Famer Sam Crawford in right field, and he did, winning four batting titles, topping .400 and becoming one of the best right-handed hitters ever.

Bob Horner.blurb: After a record-setting career at Arizona State, Bob Horner skipped the minor leagues entirely, jumped straight to Atlanta, and won the 1978 National League Rookie of the Year award.

Darren Daulton.blurb: "Dutch" Daulton was a Phillies lifer whose teammate John Vukovich said he never saw a bigger leader in 32 years of baseball; he ranks first among Phillies catchers in walks.

Jose Altuve.blurb: Born and raised in Maracay, Venezuela, Jose Altuve is the only player still with the Astros who joined them when they were in the National League, and he is considered one of the best second basemen ever.

Warren Spahn.blurb: Warren Spahn lost prime years to Army service in World War II, yet still won 363 games, the most ever by a left-hander and the most by anyone who pitched his whole career in the live-ball era.

Eddie Collins.blurb: A brainy 5-foot-9 second baseman, Eddie Collins studied how pitchers held the ball and looked off runners, believing a runner steals off the pitcher and not the catcher, a master craftsman of the Deadball Era.

Lave Cross.blurb: Born Vratislav Kriz, Lave Cross played 21 seasons, mostly for Philadelphia teams in four different leagues, and retired fifth in major-league history in hits and RBI.

Hugh Daily.blurb: Nicknamed "One Arm," pitcher Hugh Daily had a surly disposition that executives disliked, so he played for seven teams in six seasons, yet fans loved him wherever he went.

Ty Cobb.blurb: Perhaps the most competitive personality ever to wear a big-league uniform, Ty Cobb won a record 11 or 12 batting titles, hit over .400 three times, and retired with 4,189 hits.

Bernie Williams.blurb: Bernie Williams played all sixteen seasons with the Yankees, won four World Series rings, a batting title and four Gold Gloves, and after baseball became a musician.

Jose Mendez.blurb: One of the first great national sporting heroes of Cuba, rawboned fastball ace José Méndez rose in a meteoric flash that has since become a murky legend of island baseball.

Al Oliver.blurb: Al Oliver hit .300 or better eleven times and, at one point or another, led a league in hits, doubles, RBIs, total bases, games and batting average; with the 1982 Expos he took the NL batting and RBI crowns in the same season.

Hal Woodeshick.blurb: Nicknamed "The Switchman" for his knack for turning out the lights on opposing batters, lefty Hal Woodeshick was the first closer in Astros history and a member of the 1967 champion Cardinals.

Brian Downing.blurb: Brian Downing started as a catcher, became an outfielder and designated hitter, helped the Angels win division titles in 1979, 1982 and 1986, and was the team's all-time offensive leader when he left.

Ichiro Suzuki.blurb: After seven straight batting titles in Japan, Ichiro Suzuki came to Seattle in 2001, put up ten straight 200-hit seasons, and set the single-season record with 262 hits in 2004.

Derek Lowe.blurb: In 2004, sinkerballer Derek Lowe won the clinching game of the Division Series, the ALCS and the World Series as Boston ended its 86-year drought; he also threw a no-hitter for the Red Sox in 2002.

Johnny Wright.blurb: Pitcher Johnny Wright, with a blazing fastball, sharp curve and good control, shares history with Jackie Robinson as one of the first two players to break the color line in the twentieth century.

Don Robinson.blurb: Don Robinson was the youngest member of the 1979 Pirates' World Series family in just his second year, and might have been a Phillie had they drafted him in 1975 as he expected.

Goose Goslin.blurb: Goose Goslin singled in the ninth inning to win the 1935 World Series for Detroit, ending a 34-year wait; Gabby Hartnett called it simply a "$50,000 pitch."

Rick Monday.blurb: The first player ever chosen in the inaugural 1965 draft, Rick Monday played 19 seasons, won the 1981 World Series with the Dodgers, and later became a broadcaster.

Javier Vazquez.blurb: Javier Vázquez had such rough luck at Yankee Stadium that a writer joked he must have fought for the Confederacy in a past life, yet he was a very good pitcher for the Expos and Yankees.

Kevin Bass.blurb: The Brewers traded 23-year-old outfielder Kevin Bass to Houston to land 37-year-old Hall of Famer Don Sutton for the 1982 World Series run, a deal that may have been Harry Dalton's worst; Bass later became an All-Star.

Judy Johnson.blurb: His father wanted him to be a boxer, but Judy Johnson never entered the ring; the quietly exuberant Negro league third baseman was pure finesse where Josh Gibson was sheer power.

Tarik Skubal.blurb: A ninth-round pick in 2018, Tarik Skubal won the 2024 pitching Triple Crown, the first American League pitcher to do so since 2011, and back-to-back Cy Young Awards in 2024 and 2025.

Luis Castillo.blurb: Raised in humble conditions in San Pedro de Macorís with two brothers and three sisters, Luis Castillo became so beloved in Miami that he was named a top-five candidate to have his Marlins number retired.

Paul Assenmacher.blurb: Detroit native Paul Assenmacher epitomized the LOOGY, the lefty one-out guy, building a long and profitable career out of entering a game, facing one or two left-handed batters, and leaving.

Jack Clark.blurb: Brash and feared, Jack Clark was called "the greatest fastball hitter of his era" by his own manager, powered teams to two World Series, and played in four All-Star Games.

Cody Bellinger.blurb: Cody Bellinger, son of former big leaguer Clay Bellinger, helped his Arizona team reach the 2007 Little League World Series at age 11 before becoming a Dodgers fourth-round pick in 2013.

Joey Votto.blurb: A one-franchise man, Joey Votto spent all 17 seasons with the Reds, won the 2010 NL MVP and seven Tip O'Neill Awards, and became the second Canadian after Larry Walker with 2,000 hits, 300 homers and 1,000 RBI.

Rick Wilkins.blurb: Rick Wilkins's 1993 season, with 30 homers, a .300 average and 150 OPS+, was one of only a dozen such seasons by a catcher and produced more WAR than any Cubs catcher, even Gabby Hartnett.

Max Fried.blurb: Taken seventh overall by the Padres in 2012, Max Fried threw six shutout innings in the final game of the 2021 World Series, helping Atlanta win its first championship in 26 years.

Felipe Alou.blurb: Felipe Alou arrived in the United States in 1956 knowing no one, speaking no English and unaware of racism, as the first Dominican in the majors, and became a respected All-Star and manager over five decades.

Mickey Moniak.blurb: Philadelphia took Mickey Moniak with the very first pick of the 2016 draft, and the outfielder has since played for the Phillies, the Angels and the Rockies.

Duane Ward.blurb: At 6-foot-4 with a 95-mph fastball and hard slider, Duane Ward was Toronto's steady setup man and closer for back-to-back World Series champions, regularly working 65 to 80 games a year, often for multiple innings.

Dillon Dingler.blurb: Tigers catcher Dillon Dingler debuted in 2024, won a Gold Glove in 2025, and was named to his first All-Star Game in 2026.

Chipper Jones.blurb: Atlanta picked Chipper Jones first overall in 1990, and he spent his entire career with the Braves, winning the 1995 World Series, the 1999 NL MVP award, and eight All-Star selections.

Buster Posey.blurb: Buster Posey played all twelve of his big-league seasons with the Giants, won gold with Team USA in the 2017 World Baseball Classic, and now runs San Francisco's baseball operations as president.

Davy Jones.blurb: A rare Deadball Era collegian with a law degree who later built a prosperous career in pharmacology, Davy Jones told Lawrence Ritter that baseball back then attracted smart guys, crazy guys, tough guys and hicks.

Jon Nunnally.blurb: Jon Nunnally homered in his very first big-league at-bat for the Royals in 1995, then did it again in 2000 in his first plate appearance in Japan, the only player ever to do both.

Gregg Jefferies.blurb: A phenom who became the first two-time winner of Baseball America's Minor League Player of the Year award, Gregg Jefferies later spent a fourteen-year career with the Mets, Phillies and four other clubs.

Cal Raleigh.blurb: Seattle's switch-hitting catcher, nicknamed "Big Dumper," won both the Gold Glove and the Platinum Glove in 2024 and was considered one of baseball's elite power hitters by the end of 2025.

Brook Fordyce.blurb: As an eighth grader in Connecticut, Brook Fordyce averaged 23 points a game for his basketball team, which went 15-1, in what turned out to be his last year of organized hoops before baseball took over.

Matty Alou.blurb: The second of three baseball-playing Alou brothers, Matty Alou finally left their shadow, became a batting champion, and was part of the first wave of Dominicans who changed American baseball in the 1960s.

Tom Henke.blurb: Tom Henke, a 6-foot-5 closer with a slow, easy delivery, drew praise from Dave Winfield, who said the fastball arrives with a "poof" and is very tough to hit.

Paul Blair.blurb: Considered one of the premier defensive center fielders of his era, Paul Blair played 1,947 games over seventeen seasons and, for a short time, even tried switch-hitting.

Dick Stuart.blurb: Dubbed "Dr. Strangeglove" for his fielding, first baseman Dick Stuart was once greeted by Henry Aaron before the 1963 Hall of Fame game with a cheerful "Hello, Stone-fingers."

Ryne Duren.blurb: Blazing fastball, terrible eyesight, and thick glasses made Ryne Duren so scary that few batters dared dig in, and Casey Stengel said he would not admire hitting against a pitcher who might hit you.

Josh Hader.blurb: A 19th-round pick of the Orioles who was traded twice before settling in as a star closer, Josh Hader became a six-time All-Star and a three-time National League Reliever of the Year.

Frank Howard.blurb: Gentle, humble Frank Howard was seen as a threat to Babe Ruth's 60-homer record while still in college and the minors, though in the end he was no match for Ruth.

Mickey Haefner.blurb: Standing no taller than 5-foot-7, a fact he confirmed himself in 1943, "Itsy-Bitsy" Mickey Haefner threw a sidearm knuckleball and won ten or more games five seasons in a row for the Senators.

Sandy Koufax.blurb: Dubbed "The Left Arm of God," Sandy Koufax became the first man to win three Cy Young Awards during a mythic five-year run from 1962 through 1966.

Joe Nuxhall.blurb: On June 10, 1944, Joe Nuxhall became the youngest man ever to play in the major leagues, a mark he still holds, in a game the Reds were losing badly.

Carl Crawford.blurb: Known as "the Perfect Storm," Carl Crawford spent nine years with the Rays and was considered one of the best baserunners in baseball before moving on to Boston and Los Angeles.

Spoony Palm.blurb: Catcher Clarence "Spoony" Palm had played for eight clubs since 1927 and joined the 1935 Pittsburgh Crawfords, who already had Josh Gibson and Bill Perkins behind the plate.

Larry Doby.blurb: On July 5, 1947, less than three months after Jackie Robinson, Larry Doby debuted for the Cleveland Indians as the first Black player in the American League and the second in the modern major leagues.

Shawon Dunston.blurb: Known for his remarkable throwing arm, Shawon Dunston anchored the Cubs' double play alongside Ryne Sandberg in the mid-1980s before injuries turned him into a journeyman.

Walter Johnson.blurb: Ty Cobb admitted Walter Johnson's fastball "made me flinch" and hissed with danger; the Senators ace debuted on August 2, 1907, losing 3-2, and later was called the greatest pitcher ever by Frank Graham.

Joe Crede.blurb: Joe Crede hit .289/.327/.622 with four homers and 11 RBI in the 2005 postseason and played lockdown defense at third base, building a case as MVP of the White Sox's entire championship run.

Kid Elberfeld.blurb: Called "the dirtiest, scrappiest, most pestiferous" ballplayer ever to stand on spikes, Kid Elberfeld modeled his fiery style on the 1890s Baltimore Orioles and believed an umpire should be kept in his place.

Lary Sorensen.blurb: Lary Sorensen pitched eleven seasons for seven teams and faced the 1978 All-Star Game lineup, but his toughest opponent was alcoholism, a battle his story compares to an amusement park ride.

George Davis.blurb: Known as "Gorgeous George" for his graceful play and blond locks, switch-hitting shortstop George Davis hit better than .300 every year from 1893 to 1901 and led his league in fielding percentage four times.

Jim Thome.blurb: When Jim Thome joined the 600 Home Run Club, the SABR writer imagined Henry, Willie, Babe and Junior in their clubhouse tree house, sliding over to make room.

Thornton Lee.blurb: Acquired by the White Sox at 30 as a hard-throwing but wild lefty with just 12 wins, Thornton Lee developed under Jimmy Dykes into one of the best southpaws and the anchor of Chicago's staff.

Dewey Creacy.blurb: Negro leagues third baseman Dewey Creacy played 13 of 15 seasons for teams called the Stars and won four championships, three with St. Louis and one with Philadelphia in 1934.

Roger Connor.blurb: Roger Connor's home run record stood until Babe Ruth passed him; he was also the player credited with making the New York Gothams become known as the Giants.

Al Rosen.blurb: His mother held her breath watching little Al Rosen gasp from asthma, and few expected a major leaguer, but the resolutely determined kid became a great athlete anyway.

Frank Miller.blurb: The hard-throwing Pirates righty valued himself so highly that he sat out two full seasons over salary; even Commissioner Landis visiting his Michigan dairy farm couldn't change that, but bad milk yields eventually did.

Dick Lundy.blurb: A 1952 Pittsburgh Courier poll ranked Dick Lundy the third-greatest shortstop in Negro league history behind Pop Lloyd and Willie Wells, and he was known as "King Richard" and "Sir Richard."

Andre Dawson.blurb: After more than a dozen knee operations and eleven years of being overlooked in Montreal, Andre Dawson's famously menacing scowl at the plate and sheer determination carried him to a place among the most well-rounded players ever.

Garry Templeton.blurb: Garry Templeton didn't learn until he was 12 or 13 that his father Spiavia had played in the Negro leagues, where Satchel Paige once remarked the young Garry looked just like his dad.

Leroy Matlock.blurb: Promoted as "the Black Carl Hubbell," lefty Leroy Matlock won 26 straight games through early 1936, including an undefeated regular season with the Pittsburgh Crawfords.

Chuck Knoblauch.blurb: Chuck Knoblauch was the best second baseman in the American League from 1991 through 1997, piling up 38 WAR, more than runner-up Roberto Alomar's 31.

Ryan Zimmerman.blurb: Ryan Zimmerman spent his whole 17-year career with the Washington Nationals, moving from third base to first in 2015, and was a member of the franchise's 2019 championship team.

David Cone.blurb: David Cone once said he'd stare down Tiger Woods or Wayne Gretzky at the plate thinking "You have no chance," the same bulldog attitude he needed in the bases-loaded jam of Game Three, 1996.

Stan Williams.blurb: A big, tall fireballer signed by the Dodgers out of high school, Stan Williams worked in pro baseball for more than 50 years, still on a major-league payroll as a scout into his 70s.

Tony Gwynn.blurb: No sports icon is linked to a city quite like Tony Gwynn is to San Diego: eight batting titles, a Hall of Fame career with the Padres, and twelve years coaching at his alma mater, San Diego State.

Garland Buckeye.blurb: Imagine your favorite team's right guard pitching for your favorite baseball club: "Gob" Buckeye opened holes for the Chicago Cardinals football team and threw fastballs for the Cleveland Indians.

Doug DeCinces.blurb: Doug DeCinces bridged two Hall of Fame infielders, Brooks Robinson and Cal Ripken Jr., first shaking off comparisons to Robinson, then getting traded to make room for Ripken.

Kent Tekulve.blurb: Told to abandon his sidearm delivery in the Pirates' 1970 camp, Kent Tekulve ignored the advice, and became a World Series hero for the 1979 "We Are Family" champions.

Candy Jim Taylor.blurb: Over a forty-year career, Negro leagues infielder and manager "Candy Jim" Taylor played for more than a dozen black clubs and made his final appearance at 58.

Eddie Joost.blurb: A career .239 hitter, Eddie Joost learned to work the walk, reaching base by walk or hit-by-pitch 1,076 times, and later became the last manager in Philadelphia Athletics history.

Sean Doolittle.blurb: Drafted in the first round in 2007 as a first baseman and outfielder, Sean Doolittle reinvented himself as a pitcher and debuted with Oakland in 2012, later closing for the Nationals.

James Shields.blurb: Nicknamed "Big Game James," starter James Shields pitched for the Rays, Royals, Padres and White Sox between 2006 and 2018 and made the 2011 All-Star team with Tampa Bay.

Rick Sutcliffe.blurb: A 6-foot-7 right-hander, Rick Sutcliffe was never mistaken for a wallflower; Rick Monday praised his guts and his willingness to challenge hitters even after making a mistake.

Pedro Guerrero.blurb: Bill James once declared Pedro Guerrero "the best hitter God had made in a long time," an opinion shared by many who watched the Dodgers star in the mid-1980s.

Buck Ewing.blurb: Buck's middle name "Buckingham" was invented by a sportswriter teasing his polished look; he led the league with 10 homers in 1883, and in 1889 caught 97 of his team's games with no chest protector or shin guards.

George Sisler.blurb: "Gorgeous George" began as a pitcher before moving to first base, set a modern record with 257 hits in 1920 that stood until Ichiro in 2004, then lost the whole 1923 season to a double-vision sinus infection.

Roger Bresnahan.blurb: "The Duke of Tralee" started as a pitcher until John McGraw asked if he wanted to catch, and in 1907 he became the first catcher to wear shin guards, enduring plenty of teasing.

Dan Brouthers.blurb: "Big Dan" Brouthers struck out only six times in 565 plate appearances in 1889, won five batting titles, never hit below .300 in a full season, and retired with a .342 average.

Fred Clarke.blurb: One of baseball's early "boy-managers," Fred Clarke led Pittsburgh while still playing left field in his twenties, preferring to keep his head in the game, and won pennants in 1901, 1902, 1903 and 1909.

Ed Delahanty.blurb: The eldest of five brothers to reach the majors, Ed Delahanty was the first big leaguer to hit over .400 three separate times, led the NL in steals in 1898, and once went 9-for-9 in a doubleheader.

Jesse Burkett.blurb: Teammates called him "The Crab" for his fiercely competitive style; Jesse Burkett started out going 39-6 as a minor-league pitcher and is one of only two players to bat over .400 twice.

Jack Chesbro.blurb: Cheerful "Happy Jack" Chesbro won a modern-record 41 games in 1904, a total that still stands, after taking up the spitball in 1902, the same year Pittsburgh won the pennant.

Johnny Evers.blurb: Just 5-foot-9 and 125 pounds, Johnny Evers relied on rules knowledge and scrappiness, became immortalized in a 1910 poem alongside Tinker and Chance, and hit .438 as the 1914 "Miracle Braves" swept the Athletics.

Joe McGinnity.blurb: Aptly nicknamed "Iron Man," Joe McGinnity averaged about 344 innings a season, led the league with 35 wins in 1904, didn't reach the majors until age 28, and kept pitching in the minors until 54.

Rube Waddell.blurb: The big, cheeky "Rube" once wrestled alligators as a stunt, struck out 349 batters in 1904, 110 more than the next best AL pitcher, and led the league in wins, strikeouts and ERA in 1905.

Ed Walsh.blurb: "Big Ed" Walsh threw his spitball about 90 percent of the time, owns the lowest career ERA in baseball history at 1.82, and in 1908 won 40 games, the last pitcher to reach that mark.

Mickey Cochrane.blurb: Nicknamed "Black Mike" for his fiery drive to win, catcher Mickey Cochrane won AL MVP awards in 1928 and 1934, and Lefty Grove said he shook off Cochrane's signs only five or six times.

Herb Pennock.blurb: The youngest player in the American League when he debuted with the Athletics at 18, Herb Pennock never lost a World Series decision, went 5-0, and later helped build the Phillies' 1950 "Whiz Kids."

Charlie Gehringer.blurb: "The Mechanical Man" played every inning of the first six All-Star Games at second base and in 1936 hit 60 doubles, one of just six times a batter has reached that mark.

Jimmie Foxx.blurb: Nicknamed "The Beast" for his booming swing but known as one of baseball's kindest players, Jimmie Foxx won the 1933 Triple Crown and three MVPs, and later managed the Fort Wayne Daisies in the women's league.

Dizzy Dean.blurb: Despite leaving school after second grade, "Dizzy" Dean went 30-7 and won the 1934 NL MVP for the champion Cardinals, then became a beloved broadcaster famous for mangling names and grammar.

Bobby Wallace.blurb: Bobby Wallace debuted in 1894 as a pitcher for the Cleveland Spiders before moving to the field, and thanks to smart play and defense stayed in the majors until age 44.

Rabbit Maranville.blurb: Standing only about 5-foot-5, defensive wizard Rabbit Maranville helped the 1914 Braves climb from last place in mid-July to a pennant, and was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1954, the year he died.

Jim O'Rourke.blurb: Known as "Orator Jim" for his long-winded speech, Jim O'Rourke won the 1884 NL batting title and, crediting clean living with no alcohol or tobacco, played one more game for the Giants at age 54.

Joe DiMaggio.blurb: "Joltin' Joe" and the "Yankee Clipper" is famous for a 56-game hitting streak in 1941, though he'd once hit in 61 straight in the minors; Paul Simon name-checked him in a hit song.

Ted Lyons.blurb: Ted Lyons skipped the minors entirely, going from Baylor to the majors at 22, and after arm injuries reinvented himself with knuckleballs and slow curves, once pitching 42 innings without a walk in 1939.

Ray Schalk.blurb: Nicknamed "Cracker," Ray Schalk stole 30 bases in 1916, a catcher's record that lasted until 1982, caught 151 of 154 games in 1920, and is credited with catching four no-hitters.

Sam Crawford.blurb: Named "Wahoo Sam" after his Nebraska hometown, Sam Crawford debuted at 19 and holds the major league record with 309 triples, many legged out in huge dead-ball-era ballparks.

Max Carey.blurb: Nicknamed "Scoops," Max Carey was once headed for the ministry before stealing 738 bases for a National League record, leading the league in steals ten times, and later managing the Milwaukee Chicks.

Billy Hamilton.blurb: "Sliding Billy" Hamilton thrilled crowds with head-first slides, held the career steals record until Lou Brock passed it in 1979, and crossed the plate 198 times in 132 games in 1894.

Edd Roush.blurb: Edd Roush swung a 48-ounce bat, among the heaviest ever used, with strength built on his Indiana family farm, won batting titles in 1917 and 1919, and helped Cincinnati beat the "Black Sox."

Elmer Flick.blurb: At 15 Elmer Flick jumped into a semi-pro game barefoot because only eight players had shown, earned the nickname "Demon of the Stick," and at 87 became the oldest living player ever elected to Cooperstown.

Sam Rice.blurb: Sam Rice began as a pitcher before moving to right field, set an AL record with 454 putouts in 1920, and retired 13 hits shy of 3,000, the closest anyone has come without reaching it.

Burleigh Grimes.blurb: One of 17 pitchers allowed to keep throwing the spitball after it was banned, Burleigh Grimes won 20 games five times and won both his starts in the 1931 World Series for the Cardinals.

Tim Keefe.blurb: Known as "Sir Timothy," Tim Keefe pitched underhand, won the 1888 pitching Triple Crown with a 19-game win streak that lasted 24 years, and once threw two complete-game wins in a single day.

Pud Galvin.blurb: His nickname "Pud" came from how pudding-like he made hitters look, and workhorse Pud Galvin won 92 games in 1883 and 1884 and became the first pitcher to reach 300 career wins.

Red Ruffing.blurb: After losing four toes in a childhood mining accident, Red Ruffing moved from the outfield to the mound, once hit a 10th-inning homer to win his own 1-0 shutout, and won seven of nine World Series decisions.

Lloyd Waner.blurb: "Little Poison" shared the Pirates outfield with brother Paul, "Big Poison"; at about 130 pounds, he nearly missed the 1927 roster, then banged out 223 hits as a rookie.

Joe Medwick.blurb: "Ducky" Medwick hit .379 in the 1934 World Series, won the 1937 NL Triple Crown and MVP, and in 1940 was traded to Brooklyn for four players and a reported $125,000.

Waite Hoyt.blurb: Signed by the Giants while still a Brooklyn high schooler, Waite Hoyt allowed no earned runs in 27 innings of the 1921 World Series yet finished 2-1, and later talked about Babe Ruth for two hours on air.

Lou Boudreau.blurb: Cleveland made Lou Boudreau a player-manager at 24, and he invented a defensive shift crowding the infield to one side to counter Ted Williams's pull hitting, before swapping the dugout for the radio booth in 1960.

Jesse Haines.blurb: Cardinals knuckleballer "Pop" Haines didn't play a full big-league season until 26 yet pitched 18 years in St. Louis, and in the 1926 World Series he shut out the Yankees in Game 3 and won Game 7.

Jake Beckley.blurb: Nicknamed "Eagle Eye," Jake Beckley bunted by gripping the thick end of the bat, hit three home runs in a 1897 game that no one matched until 1922, and holds the all-time record for first-base putouts.

Lefty Gomez.blurb: Famous for saying he'd rather be lucky than good, Lefty Gomez was far more talented than he let on; the Yankees paid $45,000 for him in 1929, and in 1937 he won a pitching Triple Crown.

Buck Leonard.blurb: Buck Leonard spent all 15 years with the Homestead Grays, played in a record 11 East-West All-Star Games, turned down a big-league contract at 45, and earned his high school diploma at 52.

Early Wynn.blurb: Ted Williams called Early "Gus" Wynn the toughest pitcher he ever faced, and at age 43 Wynn won his 300th game in 1963, becoming only the 14th pitcher ever to reach it.

Monte Irvin.blurb: Monte Irvin played pro ball under a fake name in college to protect his amateur status, won a Triple Crown in Mexico after the Newark Eagles denied his raise, and hit .458 in the 1951 World Series.

George Kelly.blurb: Nicknamed "High Pockets" for his 6-foot-4 frame, George Kelly reached the majors at 19, led the NL with 23 homers in 1921, and moved to second base in 1925 so Bill Terry could play first.
