Jim Bottomley.blurb: "Sunny Jim" Bottomley drove in 12 runs in a single nine-inning game in 1924, a record that stood 69 years, after a cab driver took him on a long scenic ride to his first St. Louis tryout.

Sam Thompson.blurb: "Big Sam" Thompson drove in 166 runs in 1887, a record until Babe Ruth, became the first to reach 20 homers and 20 steals in a season in 1889, and tripled at 46 after returning in 1906.

Earl Averill.blurb: Called "Rock" and the "Earl of Snohomish," Earl Averill reached the majors at 26, hit four homers in a doubleheader first, and Lefty Gomez joked he was glad Averill wasn't a twin.

Billy Herman.blurb: Billy Herman set the NL record for second-base putouts with 466 in 1933, led all of baseball with 227 hits and 57 doubles in 1935, and still reached 2,345 hits despite two years in the Navy.

Ralph Kiner.blurb: Ralph Kiner led the National League in home runs seven straight years, a first, hit 50 twice, homered in four straight at-bats twice, and dated Elizabeth Taylor and Janet Leigh.

Oscar Charleston.blurb: Buck O'Neil said Oscar Charleston combined Ty Cobb, Babe Ruth and Tris Speaker in one player, and he played center field so shallow that he nearly stood behind second base.

Freddie Lindstrom.blurb: "Lindy" was still a teenager in the 1924 World Series, the youngest player ever to appear in a Fall Classic, and in 1928 he became the first NL player with nine hits in a doubleheader.

Robin Roberts.blurb: Robin Roberts threw 28 straight complete games across 1952 and 1953, started five All-Star Games, tying the record, and had his number retired while he was still pitching.

Martin Dihigo.blurb: Known as "El Maestro" and later "El Inmortal," Martín Dihigo is the only person enshrined in the Halls of Fame of Cuba, Mexico and the United States, and threw the Mexican League's first no-hitter in 1938.

Joe Sewell.blurb: Joe Sewell used one 40-ounce bat his whole career, nicknamed "Black Betsy," struck out only once every 62.6 at-bats, and played 1,103 straight games between 1922 and 1930.

Eddie Mathews.blurb: Ty Cobb said he saw few perfect swings and Eddie Mathews owned one; he became the seventh player with 500 home runs, and his 47 in 1953 stood as the third-base record for nearly 30 years.

Chuck Klein.blurb: Playing shallow in Philadelphia's short-fenced Baker Bowl, Chuck Klein set a still-standing record of 44 outfield assists in 1930 and in 1936 became the first modern NL player to hit four homers in one game.

Rube Foster.blurb: The "father of black baseball," Rube Foster reportedly won 44 straight games in 1902 for the Philadelphia Cuban X Giants and believed smiling and looking relaxed could rattle hitters even with the bases loaded.

Travis Jackson.blurb: Nicknamed "Stonewall," Giants shortstop Travis Jackson dragged a bunt to lead off the 11th inning of Game 4 in the 1933 World Series and scored the winning run; Rogers Hornsby never saw him make a mistake.

George Kell.blurb: George Kell won the 1949 batting title by a mere .0002 over Ted Williams, denying Williams a third Triple Crown, then spent decades broadcasting Tigers games; Connie Mack later regretted trading him.

Juan Marichal.blurb: "The Dominican Dandy" took a no-hitter into the eighth inning in his 1960 debut, famously kicked his leg high like a ballet dancer, and in 1983 became the first Dominican-born Hall of Famer.

Don Drysdale.blurb: "Big D" Don Drysdale hit seven home runs in both 1958 and 1965, an NL pitcher record, and in 1968 threw 58.2 straight scoreless innings, a streak that stood 20 years.

Rick Ferrell.blurb: Of six North Carolina brothers, only Rick wanted a catcher's mitt, and he caught four knuckleballers for Washington in 1944 and 1945, leading the league in passed balls each year.

Harmon Killebrew.blurb: "Killer" earned his nickname from tape-measure homers and the start of his last name, led the American League with 42 at age 23, and joked off the field that his favorite hobby was washing dishes.

Pee Wee Reese.blurb: "The Little Colonel" earned his nickname as a childhood marbles champion in Louisville, and in 1947 he famously put an arm around Jackie Robinson as fans jeered him in Cincinnati.

Lou Brock.blurb: Traded by the Cubs for Ernie Broglio in a deal many called lopsided, Lou Brock helped the Cardinals win the 1964 pennant, then at 35 stole 118 bases in 1974 and later broke Ty Cobb's career record.

Enos Slaughter.blurb: "Country" Slaughter, named for Roxboro, North Carolina, sprinted through a stop sign to score from first on a hit-and-run in Game 7 of the 1946 World Series; color blindness had ended his dream of flying.

Hoyt Wilhelm.blurb: Hoyt Wilhelm pitched his entire career with World War II shrapnel in his back, didn't reach the majors until 29, kept throwing his unpredictable knuckleball into his late 40s, and threw a no-hitter in his third Orioles start.

Bobby Doerr.blurb: Bobby Doerr went 414 straight chances at second base without an error, an American League record, and Red Sox fans voted him the franchise's greatest second baseman in 1969.

Ernie Lombardi.blurb: Nicknamed "Schnozz" for his huge nose, Ernie Lombardi gripped his bat like a golf club, won two batting titles as the first catcher to do so, and caught both of Johnny Vander Meer's consecutive no-hitters.

Willie Stargell.blurb: "Pops" Stargell handed out "Stargell Stars" to teammates, won NLCS and World Series MVP in 1979 while sharing the NL MVP, and hit seven of the roughly 18 balls ever knocked out of Forbes Field's right field.

Johnny Bench.blurb: Taught to catch by his father in tiny Binger, Oklahoma, Johnny Bench reached the majors at 19 and won ten Gold Gloves and two MVPs; Sparky Anderson joked other catchers shouldn't be compared to him.

Red Schoendienst.blurb: Red Schoendienst led the National League in steals as a rookie, once went 320 straight chances at second base without an error, and wore a big-league uniform in parts of eight decades.

Joe Morgan.blurb: At 5-foot-7 and about 160 pounds, "Little Joe" Morgan powered the Big Red Machine, won back-to-back NL MVP awards in 1975 and 1976, then spent 21 years calling ESPN's Sunday Night Baseball.

Jim Palmer.blurb: Nicknamed "Cakes," Jim Palmer turned down a UCLA basketball scholarship for the Orioles, won World Series games in three different decades, and never gave up a grand slam in his entire career.

Gaylord Perry.blurb: Fans were sure Gaylord Perry threw a spitball, yet he wasn't ejected for doctoring the ball until his 21st season; he won Cy Youngs in both leagues and his 300th game at 43.

Hal Newhouser.blurb: A Detroit native, "Prince Hal" Newhouser had already signed with the Tigers when Cleveland offered a bigger bonus and a car, and in 1945 he won the Triple Crown and a second straight MVP.

Richie Ashburn.blurb: "Whitey" Ashburn was so fast that Leo Durocher called him quicker than Pete Reiser, became the first leadoff man to lead the league in average and walks, and was the lone All-Star on the 120-loss 1962 Mets.

Leon Day.blurb: Leon Day threw an Opening Day no-hitter in 1946 at Newark, once struck out 12 Kansas City Monarchs in a Negro World Series game, and relieved in a 1942 All-Star Game to retire the last seven batters.

Bill Foster.blurb: Rube Foster's younger half-brother Bill Foster won 26 straight games in 1926 counting league and non-league play, then beat Bullet Rogan twice in a playoff doubleheader to send his team to the pennant.

Willie Wells.blurb: Mexican League players called him "El Diablo," the Devil, because his fielding at shortstop made him so hard to hit against; he was picked for the East-West All-Star Game eight times.

Bullet Rogan.blurb: Named "Bullet" for his powerful right arm, Negro leagues two-way star Bullet Rogan started his career in his mid-20s after Army ball with the 25th Infantry and hit .338, often batting cleanup while pitching.

Don Sutton.blurb: Growing up, Don Sutton invented imaginary backyard friends named after future big leaguers like Mickey and Yogi; he never missed a scheduled start across 756 games and became a regular on TV's Match Game.

Carlton Fisk.blurb: Nicknamed "Pudge," Carlton Fisk played basketball at New Hampshire before the Red Sox drafted him, waved his 12th-inning homer fair in Game 6 of the 1975 World Series, and caught more games than anyone ever.

Bid McPhee.blurb: Bid McPhee played most of his 18-year career barehanded at second base, finally put on a glove at 36 and promptly posted the best fielding percentage ever for the position, and holds the record for putouts.

Tony Perez.blurb: Tony Pérez drove in 954 runs in the 1970s, second only to Johnny Bench, powered the Big Red Machine, won the 1967 All-Star MVP with a 15th-inning homer, and once learned just one English word eating chicken for a week.

Bill Mazeroski.blurb: Maz hit the walk-off Game 7 home run that ended the 1960 World Series, the first of its kind, won eight Gold Gloves, and still holds the record for double plays turned by a second baseman.

Kirby Puckett.blurb: The youngest of nine children raised a mile from Comiskey Park, Kirby Puckett had four hits in his 1984 debut and in Game 6 of the 1991 World Series robbed a Braves batter, then homered in the 11th.

Dennis Eckersley.blurb: Dennis Eckersley is the only pitcher with 100 saves and 100 complete games, and in 1992 he won both the AL Cy Young and MVP with 51 saves; Goose Gossage said he could hit a gnat.

Paul Molitor.blurb: Ted Williams compared Paul Molitor's game to Joe DiMaggio's; Molitor hit in 39 straight games in 1987, won the 1993 World Series MVP, and at 40 collected 200 hits in a season.

Cal Ripken Jr..blurb: "Iron Man" Cal Ripken played 2,632 straight games, passing Lou Gehrig in 1995, and as a 6-foot-4 shortstop that many doubted, he still won two Gold Gloves and two MVP awards.

Bert Blyleven.blurb: Born in the Netherlands and raised in Southern California, Bert Blyleven reached the majors as the youngest pitcher in the league, was so feared for his curveball that Brooks Robinson said it buckled knees, and set a record with eight straight 200-strikeout years.

Ray Brown.blurb: Ray Brown was so confident in his pitches that he'd throw a curveball on a 3-0 count, and in 1936 he went 21-4 in the Cuban Winter League while hitting .311.

Willard Brown.blurb: Josh Gibson gave Willard Brown the nickname "Home Run," and in Puerto Rico he hit .432 with 27 homers in 234 at-bats, then in 1947 became the first Black player to homer in the American League.

Andy Cooper.blurb: Andy Cooper once went 43 innings without a walk, threw a 17-inning playoff game against the Chicago American Giants in 1937, and managed the Kansas City Monarchs to three pennants.

Pete Hill.blurb: Pete Hill was so restless on the bases that he'd bounce around to coax pitchers into throwing to him; one historian placed him in an all-star pre-1920 outfield alongside Ty Cobb and Tris Speaker.

Louis Santop.blurb: The 6-foot-4, 240-pound catcher nicknamed "Big Bertha" for a German artillery piece would throw a ball over the center-field fence from behind the plate before games and once out-hit Babe Ruth in a 1920 exhibition series.

Mule Suttles.blurb: Mule Suttles hit the first home run in the East-West Classic All-Star Game in 1933, drawing crowds to batting practice just to watch his mammoth drives, and mentored young teammates like a father.

Ben Taylor.blurb: One of four baseball-playing Taylor brothers, first baseman Ben Taylor was nicknamed "Old Reliable" for his clutch hitting and steady glove, and Buck Leonard credited him with teaching him first base.

Jud Wilson.blurb: Nicknamed "Boojum" for the thud of his hits off outfield walls, the sturdy 5-foot-8, 190-pound Jud Wilson crowded the plate, got hit often, and was ranked by Satchel Paige among the finest hitters he faced.

Ron Santo.blurb: Diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes at 18, Ron Santo kept it private until 1971, became the first player to use the 10-and-5 rule to refuse a trade, and kept broadcasting Cubs games after losing both legs.

Deacon White.blurb: Deacon White caught barehanded, played all nine positions including two mound appearances, got the first National Association hit in 1871, and, born in 1847, is the oldest-born player elected to the Hall.

Frank Thomas.blurb: A two-sport star who caught passes as an Auburn tight end before committing to baseball, "The Big Hurt" won back-to-back AL MVP awards in 1993 and 1994, receiving every first-place vote in 1993.

John Smoltz.blurb: The only pitcher with 200-plus wins and 150-plus saves, John Smoltz switched from starter to closer and set an NL record with 55 saves; as a kid, he and his dad planted Tiger Stadium turf in the backyard.

Trevor Hoffman.blurb: Trevor Hoffman grew up with a single kidney after a damaged one was removed at six weeks old, began as a shortstop until a coach suggested pitching, and fooled batters with a famously silly changeup.

Alan Trammell.blurb: Debuting at 19, Alan Trammell hit 9-for-20 to win the 1984 World Series MVP and formed baseball's longest-running double-play duo with Lou Whitaker, 1,918 games together.

Harold Baines.blurb: Bill Veeck first followed Harold Baines from a Little League game at 12 until the draft; Baines played 1,643 games as a designated hitter and finished with 2,866 hits and 384 home runs.

Edgar Martinez.blurb: Edgar Martínez's cousin talked him into taking Seattle's $4,000 offer; despite an eye condition weakening his depth perception, he won two batting titles, and the league's DH award now bears his name.

Mariano Rivera.blurb: Signed by the Yankees for just $3,000 in 1990, Mariano Rivera saved 42 postseason games with a 0.70 ERA, and his unusually flexible fingers helped give his cutter its movement.

Lee Smith.blurb: Lee Smith was a high school basketball star until bad knees and a big arm pointed him to baseball, nearly quit when the Cubs made him a reliever, and was talked back by Billy Williams.

Derek Jeter.blurb: Raised a Yankees fan and drafted sixth overall in 1992, Derek Jeter made the famous flip play in a 2001 playoff game and played a record 158 postseason games, roughly an extra full season.

Ted Simmons.blurb: Ted Simmons was a standout high school football player with scholarship offers before choosing baseball, and in 1975 he collected 193 hits, the most by any catcher playing 150 or more games that year.

Larry Walker.blurb: Cut from junior hockey at 17 after serving as a third-string goalie, undrafted Larry Walker signed with the Expos in 1984 and won the 1997 NL MVP with 49 homers and a .366 average.

Minnie Minoso.blurb: Minnie Miñoso became the first dark-skinned Latin player in the AL or NL, earned his nickname in Cleveland, played across five decades, and once fractured his skull diving into a ballpark wall.

Todd Helton.blurb: Todd Helton once passed up a 1992 Padres draft pick to play quarterback at Tennessee, where a knee injury opened the job for Peyton Manning, then in 2003 was intentionally walked in the finale and missed the batting title by a sliver.

Dick Redding.blurb: Nicknamed "Cannonball" for his blazing fastball, Dick Redding claimed he once shattered a new ball against a building, struck out Babe Ruth three times on nine pitches, and reportedly impressed Casey Stengel more than Satchel Paige.

Newt Allen.blurb: Nicknamed "Colt" as the Monarchs' youngest player in 1922, Newt Allen played in the Negro World Series in both 1924 and 1942, nearly two decades apart, and once held a spiking grudge so long he beaned a Chicago rival.

Dobie Moore.blurb: "The Black Cat" hit .487 in the 1924-25 California Winter League, reportedly won a new suit for smashing a tailor's advertisement on the outfield wall, and was later called the Negro leagues' most overlooked star by Bill James.

Lazaro Salazar.blurb: Fans called him "El Príncipe del Belén" for his sharp style and gentle manners; Lázaro Salazar wore No. 17 for his patron saint, collapsed in the dugout in 1957, and Mexican baseball retired his number league-wide.

Bill Byrd.blurb: Younger players called him "Daddy," and his spitball got him banned in Puerto Rico, though he kept hitters guessing by pretending to throw it; his 1942 beaning of Willie Wells reportedly inspired an early batting helmet.

Hurley McNair.blurb: In May 1911, Hurley McNair hit three home runs and pitched a win in the same game, and the roughly 5-foot-6 outfielder earned the nickname "toy cannon" for his surprisingly powerful throwing arm.

John Beckwith.blurb: John Beckwith hit the first over-the-fence home run at Cincinnati's Redland Field in 1921, with fans showering him with coins, and reportedly kept pace with Babe Ruth's homers in 1928.

Roosevelt Davis.blurb: An Illinois paper nicknamed Roosevelt Davis "Duro" and ranked him just behind Satchel Paige; he taught Bill Byrd the spitball, reportedly scuffed balls with his fingernails and belt buckle, and later worked as a waiter.

Bingo DeMoss.blurb: Bingo DeMoss's nickname likely came from bunting a ball exactly where he wanted, which a catcher likened to a pool shot, and he once punched an umpire in 1915, landing in jail for a night.

Rap Dixon.blurb: Rap Dixon's nickname likely came from a high school batting display compared to William Tell's marksmanship; beaned in 1929, he returned the next day and rapped hits in 14 straight league games.

Alejandro Oms.blurb: Called "El Caballero" for his classy conduct, Alejandro Oms reportedly hit 40 home runs on a 1922 barnstorming tour and won MVP in 1928-29 with a 30-game hitting streak, a Cuban Winter League record.

Dave Malarcher.blurb: Despite being just 5-foot-7 and 150 pounds, "Gentleman Dave" Malarcher was a standout defensive third baseman who borrowed $75 from Rube Foster after Army service and took up poetry after his wife died in 1946.

Quincy Trouppe.blurb: Quincy Trouppe's 10th-inning homer won a 1947-48 Puerto Rico title game and briefly made him mayor of Caguas for a day; he later supplied nearly all the Negro leagues footage in Ken Burns's Baseball.

Jelly Gardner.blurb: Short, stocky Floyd Gardner got the name "Jelly Roll," shortened to "Jelly," and manager Rube Foster reportedly flashed him signs with pipe smoke, then whacked him with the pipe when he tripled instead of bunting.

Fats Jenkins.blurb: Fats Jenkins earned his nickname as a chubby kid though he was lean as an adult, made a leaping catch in 1930 while sprinting with his back to the infield, and in 1939 smashed a homer through a tin scoreboard.

Frank Duncan.blurb: Frank Duncan slipped into all-white music halls carrying an empty instrument case to watch singer Julia Lee, won Game Eight of the 1924 Negro World Series with a clutch single, and caught Dizzy Dean in 1934.

Ted Strong.blurb: A two-sport star who also played for the Harlem Globetrotters, where his oversized hands snagged passes with one hand, Ted Strong hit an inside-the-park homer in the 1937 East-West All-Star Game.

Sam Jethroe.blurb: Nicknamed "The Jet," Sam Jethroe ran 60 yards in 5.9 seconds in 1949 spring training, won the 1950 NL Rookie of the Year despite shaky defense, and decades later sold that award for $3,500.

Piper Davis.blurb: Piper Davis got his nickname when fans at a Fairfield basketball game cheered his hometown because they forgot his name; he played for the Globetrotters while starring for the Black Barons in baseball.

Spottswood Poles.blurb: Records spelled Spottswood Poles's first name many ways, and one census even listed him as "Spootsie"; he learned young by hitting tennis balls with a broom handle, and John McGraw reportedly ranked him first on his wish list.

Goose Curry.blurb: In 1939, Goose Curry crashed into a fence to rob Josh Gibson of an extra-base hit, then dove for the rebound; he also hit a ninth-inning grand slam in Atlanta and homered again in the nightcap.

Rufus Lewis.blurb: Rufus Lewis started Game Seven of the 1946 Negro World Series and pitched Newark to the title, was twice picked to start for the East in the East-West Game, and later toured with Satchel Paige.

Sal Maglie.blurb: "Sal the Barber" earned his nickname with chin-grazing fastballs, joined Brooklyn from Cleveland for just $100, threw a Dodgers no-hitter, and was the last player to wear uniforms for the Giants, Dodgers and Yankees.

Max Manning.blurb: Teammate Jimmy Hill dubbed him "Dr. Cyclops" after a 1940 movie because of his thick glasses; Max Manning reportedly fanned the first five Homestead Grays he faced in 1939 and returned to college at 33.

Luis Tiant.blurb: Reggie Jackson called Luis Tiant "the Fred Astaire of baseball" for his dancing windup; his 69-year-old father threw a ceremonial first pitch at Fenway in 1975, ending with a knuckleball that wowed the crowd.

Marvin Williams.blurb: Marvin Williams went 5-for-5 in a 12-11 Stars win over Newark in 1943, reportedly chose golf clubs over $50 in cash from Spalding after a huge 1952 season, and taught Frank Robinson to hit curveballs.

Booker McDaniel.blurb: Nicknamed "Cannonball" for his fierce fastball and "Balazo" by Mexican fans, Booker McDaniel became the first Black pitcher in the Pacific Coast League in 1949, and Satchel Paige called him a better hurler than himself.

Jim LaMarque.blurb: In 1942, Jim LaMarque nearly quit the Monarchs and tried to slip away until Satchel Paige drove him to the ballpark; he cooled his feet in an ice bucket between innings and was called "Libertad" in Puerto Rico.

Joe Greene.blurb: Joe Greene was called "Pig" for his huge appetite and then "Pea" for his powerful throws to second base; Buck Leonard gave him a 37-inch bat to reach curveballs, and his WWII Army unit reportedly found Mussolini's body.

Lester Lockett.blurb: Lester Lockett won the Negro National League batting title in 1948, the final season of his career, after playing in Canada, Mexico and Venezuela, and in 1997 was living at a Chicago YMCA with a briefcase of memorabilia.

Specs Clark.blurb: Morten "Specs" Clark was a left-handed-hitting shortstop who, nearly a decade after his death, still received votes in a 1952 Pittsburgh Courier poll of the greatest Negro leaguers; some papers even called him "Martin."

Sol White.blurb: As a teenager Sol White filled in for an injured teammate against future AL president Ban Johnson, wrote the first book on Black professional baseball in 1907 (only five copies are known), and was inducted in 2006.

Frank Grant.blurb: Called "The Black Dunlap" after the white second baseman Fred Dunlap because his fielding was judged the league's best, Frank Grant stood about 5-foot-7, 155 pounds, and a Buffalo reporter once called him "a Spaniard."

Double Duty Radcliffe.blurb: Ted "Double Duty" Radcliffe once caught one game, then pitched a shutout in the second game of a 1932 doubleheader, played for about 30 teams, and in 1934 reportedly became the first Black man to manage a white pro team.

Dizzy Dismukes.blurb: Dizzy Dismukes beat the reigning champion 1911 Pittsburgh Pirates 2-1 in an exhibition game, threw a 1915 no-hitter in Indianapolis, and reportedly taught submarine-style pitching to future major leaguer Carl Mays.

Wilson Redus.blurb: Wilson "Frog" Redus played 16 Negro league seasons from 1924 to 1940 with a long list of clubs, played in the East-West All-Star Game in 1936 and 1937, and led the Chicago American Giants in 1940 as player-manager.

Newt Joseph.blurb: Newt Joseph hit the first home run in the 1924 Colored World Series, and in 1923 Muskogee fans waited past midnight for the Monarchs' train and lifted him out of his berth; a Utah paper called him "the noisiest coach in baseball."

Tubby Scales.blurb: Over a 25-year Negro league career, Tubby Scales hit .320, and Buck Leonard reportedly called him the best curveball hitter he ever saw; after retiring from baseball in 1958 he became a stockbroker.

Willie Pope.blurb: Known as "Wee Willie," Willie Pope threw a 1947 no-hitter for the Homestead Grays against the New York Cubans and was part of the 1948 Grays team that won the Negro World Series.

Lennie Pearson.blurb: Nicknamed "Hoss," Lennie Pearson won the 1942 batting Triple Crown, topping his league in average, hits, homers and RBI, and even as a first baseman led the league in steals in 1946 with 17.

Satchel Davis.blurb: In 1940, Satchel Davis and Willie Hubert shared a no-hitter for the Baltimore Elite Giants against the Newark Eagles; that same year he also made two appearances in Mexico with the Diablos Rojos.

Herb Souell.blurb: Switch-hitting Herb Souell spent a decade with the Kansas City Monarchs, from 1940 to 1950, and was part of the 1942 Monarchs team that won the Negro World Series.

Earl Taborn.blurb: Earl Taborn debuted with the Kansas City Monarchs in August 1946, caught for several clubs in Mexico into 1961, and is buried at Fort Sam Houston National Cemetery in San Antonio.

Jack Matchett.blurb: Palestine, Texas-born Jack Matchett threw right-handed but batted left, helped the Kansas City Monarchs win the 1942 Negro World Series, and pitched for the Cincinnati Clowns that same year.

Sammie Haynes.blurb: Sammie Haynes shared a Kansas City Monarchs clubhouse with Jackie Robinson in 1945, later managed the reorganized Atlanta Black Crackers, and, though he lost his sight, founded a charity helping struggling former athletes.

Buck O'Neil.blurb: At age 94, Buck O'Neil signed with the Kansas City T-Bones for a 2006 Northern League All-Star Game and drew two intentional walks, the same year he posthumously received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Smokey Joe Williams.blurb: A giant of a man whose fastball seemed to drop off a mountaintop, Smokey Joe Williams was voted the greatest black pitcher ever in a 1952 poll, a single vote ahead of Satchel Paige, and owned the era's best emery ball.

Curt Schilling.blurb: Teammates loved Curt Schilling on the days he pitched and found him exhausting the other four: a loudmouth nicknamed "Red Light Curt" for his love of cameras, who rose to the big moment and shared the 2001 World Series MVP with Randy Johnson.

Scott Hatteberg.blurb: Hatteberg hit into a triple play and homered with the bases loaded in his next at-bat, then was played by Chris Pratt in Moneyball, a movie about a catcher learning first base.

Hyun-soo Kim.blurb: A Korean hitting machine who won the 2008 KBO batting title at 22 and pinch-hit the go-ahead single in Beijing's gold-medal run, he later crossed the Pacific to hit for Baltimore and Philadelphia.

Michael King.blurb: A Rhode Island high school phenom who once fanned three Red Sox on nine pitches, King grew into a strikeout ace for San Diego, flirting with postseason no-hitters and tossing a complete-game shutout against Colorado.

Charlie Condon.blurb: A Georgia slugger who walloped a record 37 homers in the 2024 college season, Condon swept the Golden Spikes Award, then signed with Colorado for a $9.25 million bonus, tying the largest in draft history.

Ed Cushman.blurb: Cushman threw a Union Association no-hitter in 1884, then lost a bid for a second one a week later to a ninth-inning single, and later struck out eight straight batters.

Adam Ottavino.blurb: A 6-foot-5 switch-hitting reliever who set a Colorado record with 37 straight scoreless outings after Tommy John surgery, Ottavino also became the first Yankee to wear number 0 and later pitched for Team USA.

Rich Aurilia.blurb: Aurilia hit the first interleague grand slam, set a postseason RBI record for National League shortstops, and appeared with his wife as jurors on the soap opera General Hospital in 2003.

Dolf Luque.blurb: Cuba's "Pride of Havana" reportedly told a heckler shouting "Lucky Luque!" he'd deal with him, with manager Wilbert Robinson's blessing, and he won a World Series game in relief at 43.

Ty Wigginton.blurb: Wigginton's most memorable delivery came in December 2006, when he caught his own son in a bedroom closet at home, with a 911 operator coaching and a shoelace standing in for the umbilical clamp.

Rich Harden.blurb: A Canadian flamethrower whose tumbling splitter was nicknamed the "ghost pitch," Harden struck out the side on nine pitches in 2008, pitched for Oakland, the Cubs and Texas, and entered the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame in 2023.

Marty Cordova.blurb: Cordova won the 1995 Rookie of the Year award, retired a day before 2005 spring training, and once tried to enter Canada without his passport on Dana White's private jet, on camera.

Ralphy Velazquez.blurb: A first baseman who helped the United States win the 2017 U-12 World Cup, Velazquez was Cleveland's first-round pick in 2023, reached Triple-A in 2026 after a hot start at Akron, and played in two Futures Games.

Bryce Rainer.blurb: A Harvard-Westlake two-way star who went 9-0 on the mound as a freshman and hit .505 as a senior, Rainer was drafted 11th overall as a shortstop by Detroit, signing for $5.8 million.

Fernando Abad.blurb: Abad throws an occasional 55 mph eephus that reportedly left Adrian Beltre on one knee, and he went 2,226 days between wins before earning his last one for Colorado in 2023.

Braden Montgomery.blurb: A two-way Stanford and Texas A&M star, Montgomery was drafted 12th overall by Boston and promptly dealt to the White Sox in the Garrett Crochet trade, then won his big-league debut with a walk-off homer.

Travis Wood.blurb: A Little Rock lefty who threw a 17-strikeout no-hitter at the Babe Ruth World Series, Wood nearly threw a perfect game in his third start, made an All-Star team, and homered in the 2016 playoffs on the way to a title.

Shane Bieber.blurb: A walk-on at UC Santa Barbara who became the 2020 AL Cy Young winner with a pitching Triple Crown, Bieber also took 2019 All-Star Game MVP honors and wore "Not Justin" on his jersey as a nickname.

Willson Contreras.blurb: He launched a home run on the first pitch of his first big-league at-bat, helped end the Cubs' 108-year title drought in 2016, and once crushed a 491-foot playoff blast, the longest Statcast has tracked in October.

Nico Hoerner.blurb: A glove-first Cubs second baseman who won Gold Gloves in 2023 and 2025, Hoerner hit the first homer of the 2022 season off a reigning Cy Young winner and swiped 40 bases, a Cubs high since 2006.

Johnny Markham.blurb: A right-handed Negro leagues pitcher from Shreveport, Louisiana, Markham worked seventeen seasons between 1930 and 1946, spending his best-known stretches with the Kansas City Monarchs and the Birmingham Black Barons before finishing with the Cincinnati Crescents.

Nolan McLean.blurb: A former Oklahoma State quarterback who passed on the Orioles to go back to college, McLean won his first four big-league starts for the Mets, started the 2026 World Baseball Classic final, and took a rookie Gold Glove.

Sterling Hitchcock.blurb: A lefty who became the 1998 NLCS MVP by winning both his starts for San Diego with a 0.90 ERA, Hitchcock also picked up the Game 5 win for the Yankees in the 2001 World Series.

Doug Fister.blurb: He shook off a line drive to the head in Game 2 of the 2012 World Series and kept pitching, after setting an American League record by striking out nine batters in a row earlier that summer.

Marco Estrada.blurb: Known to fans as "Estradabien," this soft-tossing right-hander took a perfect game into the eighth inning in 2015, dominated Kansas City in the ALCS, and made the 2016 All-Star team with Toronto.

Logan Henderson.blurb: A Texas junior-college arm picked in the fourth round, Henderson struck out nine over six innings while winning his 2025 Brewers debut, and later started a World Series game for Milwaukee.

Joe Judge.blurb: A slick-fielding Washington first baseman, Judge scooped Harry Hooper's liner to protect a Walter Johnson no-hit bid in 1920, hit .385 in the Senators' 1924 title run, and retired with a .993 fielding mark.

Colt Emerson.blurb: An Ohio shortstop taken 22nd overall in 2023, Emerson signed an eight-year, $95 million extension before ever playing in the majors, then debuted for Seattle in 2026 and collected four hits in one game.

Shawn Estes.blurb: A Mariners first-rounder who blossomed in San Francisco, Estes went 19-5 and made the 1997 All-Star team, later hit a home run off Roger Clemens and beat Randy Johnson on Rockies Opening Day 2004.

Trey Gibson.blurb: Suspended for an entire college season at Liberty and then ignored in the draft, Gibson signed with Baltimore as an undrafted free agent, and climbed to the majors, making his Orioles debut against the Yankees in 2026.

Liam Doyle.blurb: A New Hampshire flamethrower who went 15-2 with a 0.68 ERA in his last two high school years, Doyle transferred twice, won SEC Pitcher of the Year at Tennessee, and went fifth overall to St. Louis.

Jeffrey Hammonds.blurb: Baltimore took the Stanford speedster fourth overall in 1992 with the biggest bonus of that draft, and he finally broke through for Colorado in 2000, hitting .335 with 20 homers and an All-Star nod.

Erik Sabrowski.blurb: An Edmonton lefty who survived two Tommy John surgeries, one of them costing him all of 2022 after Cleveland grabbed him in the Rule 5 draft, Sabrowski finally reached the majors in 2024 and fanned two in his debut.

Doyle Alexander.blurb: His Toronto contract paid him while hurt only if he followed hunting regulations and wore an orange hunting jacket; Alexander also went 9-0 with a 1.53 ERA for Detroit in 1987 after the Smoltz trade.

Thomas Pannone.blurb: A well-traveled lefty who took a no-hitter into the seventh in his first big-league start, Pannone fanned the side on nine pitches in 2019, then threw a Triple-A perfect game for Nashville in 2026.

Jake McGee.blurb: Nicknamed "Clockhands" for his unconventional windup, McGee saved 31 games for the 2021 Giants and threw a scoreless inning for the champion 2020 Dodgers in the World Series.

Tex Hughson.blurb: A big University of Texas right-hander who led the American League with 22 wins and a 2.59 ERA in 1942, Hughson lost prime years to war service and later founded Little League baseball in San Marcos.

Ellis Burks.blurb: A Red Sox rookie who joined the 20-20 club in 1987, Burks later led the National League in runs and slugging for Colorado in 1996, finishing third in MVP voting with 352 homers overall.

Johnny Antonelli.blurb: Antonelli never played a minor-league game, went 21-7 after a trade for Bobby Thomson, and retired in 1961 rather than join the expansion Mets, saying he didn't like traveling.

Otto Briggs.blurb: Nicknamed "Mirror," this Negro leagues outfielder from North Carolina played from 1915 to 1934, mostly for Hilldale and the Bacharach Giants, managed both clubs, won the 1925 Colored World Series, and later owned the Philadelphia Black Meteors.

Zack Cozart.blurb: A Reds second-round pick whose first season ended with Tommy John surgery, Cozart roared back in 2017 with 24 homers and a .297 average, earned his first All-Star spot, and signed a three-year, $38 million Angels deal.

Frank Schwindel.blurb: Known as "Frank The Tank," he homered in his first at-bat for Oakland, then became a Cubs sensation with a go-ahead grand slam in a September 2021 game and earned NL Rookie of the Month honors.

Jesus Made.blurb: A switch-hitting Dominican shortstop signed at 16, Made made the Brewers' 2026 spring roster at 18, shared a clubhouse with Jackson Chourio, and was ranked the top prospect in baseball by MLB.com that May.

Tin Can Kincannon.blurb: A West Virginia-born Negro leagues pitcher nicknamed "Tin Can," Kincannon spent six seasons with the Pittsburgh Crawfords, took the mound for them at the 1934 East-West All-Star Game, and finished his career in 1939 with the team in Toledo.

Winston Santos.blurb: Signed out of the Dominican Republic for a mere $10,000 bonus in 2019, Santos rose through the Rangers system with a 2.80 ERA at High-A, started the 2024 Futures Game, and reached the majors in 2026.

Sam McDowell.blurb: Once moved to second base mid-game so another pitcher could face Frank Howard, "Sudden Sam" returned to the mound and finished with 15 strikeouts, and he later founded a program helping athletes overcome addiction.

Mike Sweeney.blurb: A Royals first baseman by accident, after a teammate's all-terrain-vehicle injury, Sweeney drove in a franchise-record 144 runs in 2000 and ended a 2003 Father's Day game with a two-out walk-off hit.

Brandon Wood.blurb: A first-round Angels prospect who hit a California League record 43 homers in 2005, Wood later revealed he fought near-daily panic attacks during his 2010 season, a secret he kept for fear of hurting his career.

JoJo Romero.blurb: Nicknamed by a grandfather who couldn't pronounce his given name, this lefty reliever struck out all three batters in his 2020 debut, then posted a 2.07 ERA for the Cardinals in 2025.

Chase DeLauter.blurb: A James Madison slugger who reached base in his first 15 college games, DeLauter became the seventh player to debut in a postseason game, then homered twice in his 2026 regular-season debut for Cleveland.

Dave Barnhill.blurb: A New York Cubans righty who fanned more batters than anyone in the Negro National League in 1941, Barnhill earned five East-West All-Star selections and helped the Cubans win the 1947 Negro League World Series.

Bubba Chandler.blurb: A Georgia quarterback and pitcher nicknamed by his older sisters, Chandler turned down football, taught himself a slider by studying Kumar Rocker, and saved his Pirates debut before earning his first win five days later.

Hod Eller.blurb: Eller threw a 1919 no-hitter and struck out six straight in a World Series shutout, and in the film Matewan a child preacher names him his favorite pitcher.

Blake Mitchell.blurb: A Texas high school star who hit .465 and won a state title as a junior, Mitchell also won the U-18 World Cup gold-medal game in relief before Kansas City made him the eighth overall pick.

Dwayne Hosey.blurb: After an MVP season in the American Association, this switch-hitting outfielder played just 52 big-league games, but exploded in Japan, where Yakult's Katsuya Nomura called him one of the greatest players ever to come over.

Jonny Venters.blurb: A 30th-round Braves pick with a 93-96 mph sinker, Venters made the 2011 All-Star team with a 1.84 ERA, endured three Tommy John surgeries, and won NL Comeback Player of the Year in 2018.

Jonah Tong.blurb: A Canadian seventh-rounder who skipped North Dakota State, Tong pitched 6 and 2/3 innings of a Double-A combined perfect game in 2025 and won his big-league debut for the Mets that August.

Dellin Betances.blurb: A towering Washington Heights native who slipped to the eighth round, Betances became a four-time Yankees All-Star and the only reliever ever to strike out 100 batters in five consecutive seasons.

Parker Messick.blurb: A Florida Mr. Baseball turned Seminole turned Guardians lefty, Messick took a no-hitter to the ninth inning in April 2026 before a single ended it, then made his first All-Star team.

Bip Roberts.blurb: A Rule 5 pickup who stuck with the 1986 Padres, Roberts made the 1992 All-Star team, tied an NL record with ten straight hits, and later broke up Pedro Martinez's extra-inning perfect game with a double.

Dave Bush.blurb: A reliable right-hander who flirted with three near no-hitters, Bush earned a spot in the Cape Cod League Hall of Fame after a 0.84 ERA there, later returning to baseball as a pitching coach in Boston and Texas.

Owen Caissie.blurb: A Canadian outfielder from Burlington, Ontario, Caissie was the first Canadian taken in the 2020 draft, debuted for the Cubs against Toronto, then walked off Colorado with a 2026 Marlins homer.

Matt Davidson.blurb: Davidson hit three Opening Day homers for the 2018 White Sox, then in Japan he struck a Kirin beer billboard at the Tokyo Dome, winning a million yen and a year's supply of beer.

Jakob Junis.blurb: A 29th-round Royals pick who passed on North Carolina State, Junis won at least nine games in each of his first three seasons, a feat last matched by Masahiro Tanaka.

Gene Tenace.blurb: Born Fiore Gino Tennaci and nicknamed "Steamboat" for his block-like build, Tenace hit four homers in the 1972 World Series and won Series MVP and a sports car for his trouble.

Walker Jenkins.blurb: A North Carolina outfielder who hit .527 as a high school junior, Jenkins went fifth overall to Minnesota in 2023 for $7.14 million, then collected his first big-league hit and homer within a week of arriving.

Brendan McKay.blurb: A two-way Louisville star who swept the Golden Spikes Award and the Dick Howser Trophy in 2017, McKay carried a perfect game into the sixth inning of an early Rays start before injuries struck.

Mitch Webster.blurb: A switch-hitting outfielder who led the National League with 13 triples in 1986, Webster played for both Canadian big-league clubs, Toronto and Montreal, then scouted for the Dodgers for fourteen years.

Adam LaRoche.blurb: The first player to lose a home run to video replay, LaRoche won a 2012 Gold Glove and Silver Slugger, then retired from the White Sox when they limited his teenage son's clubhouse access.

Trea Turner.blurb: A speedy shortstop who hit three cycles, stole 30 bases without being caught in 2023, and helped Washington win its first World Series in 2019, Turner later signed an 11-year, $300 million Phillies deal.

John Gant.blurb: A Mets 21st-rounder whose herky-jerky "false step" delivery confuses hitters, Gant led the majors with 11 relief wins in 2019, then won league MVP in Taiwan with a 1.49 ERA.

Russell Martin.blurb: A Canadian catcher who hit two homers in a 2013 Wild Card game for Pittsburgh, Martin pitched a ninth inning for the Dodgers in 2019 and was inducted into the Canadian Baseball Hall of Fame.

Logan Gilbert.blurb: Seattle's 14th overall pick in 2018 led the majors with 208 and 2/3 innings in 2024, made the All-Star team, and pitches under a game-day alter ego he calls "Walter."

Steve Ontiveros.blurb: A swingman who led the American League with a 2.65 ERA in the shortened 1994 season, Ontiveros hit a three-run double in his only career hit, later coaching China's pitchers at the Beijing Olympics.

Trey Yesavage.blurb: An East Carolina ace taken 20th overall, Yesavage struck out nine in his 2025 Blue Jays debut, a club record, then fanned 12 in World Series Game 5, a rookie record for the Fall Classic.

Tyler Bremner.blurb: A San Diego high school ace who posted a 0.90 ERA, Bremner went 11-1 at UC Santa Barbara and was drafted second overall by the Angels in 2025, weeks after losing his mother.

Lazaro Montes.blurb: Born in Havana, Montes defected with his father at 13, signed with Seattle for $2.5 million, won 2025 Northwest League MVP, and later blasted a 474-foot homer, the longest at T-Mobile Park in Statcast history.

Hunter Dozier.blurb: A Stephen F. Austin shortstop picked eighth overall by Kansas City, Dozier signed below slot and hit 26 homers in his best season, 2019, before the Royals released him in 2023 still owing millions.

Cherokee Fisher.blurb: Known for a fast fastball and heavy drinking, Fisher led the National Association in ERA twice and allowed the first home run in National League history, to Chicago's Ross Barnes, in 1876.

Jack Kramer.blurb: A New Orleans right-hander who won a complete game for the St. Louis Browns in the 1944 World Series, Kramer later went 18-5 for Boston and earned a save in the 1946 All-Star Game.

Lance McCullers Jr..blurb: A first-round Astros pick famous for his curveball, McCullers threw 24 straight breaking balls to close out the Yankees in Game 7 of the 2017 ALCS, then helped Houston win its first World Series.

Willy Adames.blurb: A Dominican shortstop who smashed 31 homers for the 2022 Brewers, a franchise record for the position, Adames later signed a seven-year, $182 million contract with San Francisco, the richest in that club's history.

Pee Wee Butts.blurb: A tiny Georgia shortstop of about 140 pounds, Butts joined the Atlanta Black Crackers at 17, spent nine years turning double plays with Junior Gilliam for the Baltimore Elite Giants, and was nicknamed "Cool breeze."

Garrett Cleavinger.blurb: An Oregon freshman who went 9-0 with a 1.24 ERA, Cleavinger was dealt by Baltimore for Jeremy Hellickson, pitched for the Phillies, Dodgers and Rays, and helped Team USA reach the 2026 World Baseball Classic final.

Alexi Ogando.blurb: Oakland signed Ogando as an outfielder under a false name, which they learned a year later; Texas then turned him into a pitcher, and he won his first three big-league appearances.

Gage Jump.blurb: A lefty who went 9-0 as a senior at JSerra, Jump passed on the Padres for UCLA, survived Tommy John surgery, and struck out J.P. Crawford, the first batter he faced, in his 2026 Athletics debut.

Danny Tartabull.blurb: The son of a major leaguer, Tartabull hit 43 homers and won MVP at Triple-A Calgary in 1985, signed a $25.5 million Yankees deal, and once proposed with fireworks spelling out the question.

Rob Murphy.blurb: A lefty reliever who posted a 0.72 ERA in 1986 for Cincinnati, the lowest among relievers with at least 50 innings then, Murphy later appeared 87 times in 1987, then left baseball to breed racehorses.

Royce Clayton.blurb: Clayton played for eleven teams, tying the record for position players, and later portrayed Miguel Tejada in the film Moneyball before turning to high school coaching.

Lonny Frey.blurb: Frey left school after grammar school, read the dictionary when bored, and earned the nickname "Leopard" from teammates for his birthmarks, after leading the majors in errors twice as a booed Brooklyn shortstop.

Brent Mayne.blurb: Mayne won a game for Colorado in 2000 as an emergency pitcher having never pitched at any level, and the avid surfer later wrote a 2008 book called The Art of Catching.

Curt Simmons.blurb: A 1947 "bonus baby" who missed the 1950 World Series for National Guard duty, Simmons baffled Hank Aaron, who called him his toughest opponent, and went 18-9 for the 1964 champion Cardinals.

Mark Koenig.blurb: The last survivor of the 1927 Yankees' lineup played himself in The Pride of the Yankees, and finally received his high school diploma in 1988, at age 83, after leaving at 16 for baseball.

Chad Qualls.blurb: Qualls is the only player to wear the uniforms of all four 1990s expansion teams, and in 2013 he went viral by celebrating a strikeout with a fist pump, then slipping on his own cleat.

Jack Wilson.blurb: A slick Pittsburgh shortstop who tallied 201 hits and tied for the NL lead with 12 triples in 2004, Wilson won a Silver Slugger and a Fielding Bible award, then became a coach.

Eli Willits.blurb: A switch-hitting Oklahoma shortstop and the son of former big leaguer Reggie Willits, he was the third-youngest player ever taken first overall, picked by Washington in 2025 after hitting .516 as a senior.

Tommy Troy.blurb: A Stanford infielder who hit .394 with 17 homers in 2023, Troy went 12th overall to Arizona, and he collected two doubles in his 2026 debut before hitting his first homer a week later.

Julio Cruz.blurb: "The Cruzer" stole more than 40 bases each year from 1978 to 1983 for Seattle, held the Mariners' career steals record until Ichiro passed him, and later became a team broadcaster.

Ricky Romero.blurb: A Cal State Fullerton College World Series champion picked sixth overall in 2005, Romero faced fellow first-rounder Rick Porcello in a historic 2009 debut and made the 2011 All-Star team for Toronto.

Brandon Sproat.blurb: A Mets prospect who debuted with six innings and seven strikeouts in 2025, Sproat was swapped to Milwaukee in the January 2026 Freddy Peralta deal and later fanned a career-high ten Reds.

Jordan Walker.blurb: A first-round Cardinals pick who tied a rookie hitting-streak mark for under-21 players in 2023, Walker became the first Cardinal to win the Home Run Derby, beating Kyle Schwarber 12-11 in 2026.

Joe Mack.blurb: A Marlins catcher taken 31st overall in 2021, Mack reached Miami in May 2026 and soon hit an inside-the-park home run, with his brother drafted too and his sister playing college softball.

Jesse Duryea.blurb: An Iowa-born pitcher dubbed "Cyclone Jim" by Ted Sullivan during a brief stint with the St. Louis Browns, Duryea debuted at age 29 and won 59 games across six seasons.

River Ryan.blurb: An 11th-round Padres pick who debuted with 5 and 1/3 strong innings in 2024, Ryan came back from Tommy John surgery 30 pounds heavier and was later traded to Detroit in a Tarik Skubal deal.

Cotton Tierney.blurb: Tierney played every inning of all three games in baseball's only tripleheader in 1920, and his great-great-nephew later honored him by naming a contracts website Cot's Baseball Contracts.

Kelvin Herrera.blurb: A Dominican flamethrower from Tenares who anchored Kansas City's bullpen, Herrera made the 2015 and 2016 All-Star teams, won the 2015 World Series, and retired by announcing it on Twitter.

Justin Smoak.blurb: Called "The Freak From Goose Creek" by a Seattle announcer, Smoak was the 2009 World Cup MVP, signed minutes before the draft deadline, and waited a record 2,317 plate appearances for his first triple.

Elmer Smith.blurb: An Indians outfielder who hit the first grand slam in World Series history off Burleigh Grimes in 1920, Smith later led the Pacific Coast League with 46 home runs in 1926.

Carlos Santana.blurb: A switch-hitting Dominican who caught the final out of the 2016 ALCS and won 2013 World Baseball Classic gold, Santana became the oldest position player ever to win a first Gold Glove, at 38.

Steve Farr.blurb: A Maryland-born closer who led Kansas City with a 1.98 ERA in 1990, Farr threw a single complete game, a five-hit shutout, and saved 30 games with a 1.56 ERA for the 1992 Yankees.

Brandon Lowe.blurb: A Rays slugger who hit two homers in Game 2 of the 2020 World Series, Lowe blasted 39 in 2021 and reached 100 career homers in 477 games, the fastest primary second baseman ever.

Solly Hemus.blurb: A four-year Navy veteran nicknamed "Mighty Mouse," this Cardinals shortstop led the National League with 105 runs and got hit by 20 pitches in 1952, then managed St. Louis through a turbulent stretch.

Johnny Hodapp.blurb: Once branded a "$40,000 lemon," this Cleveland second baseman turned into a peach in 1930, hitting .354 and leading the American League with 225 hits after a veteran fixed his pivot.

Bruce Dal Canton.blurb: Signed by Pittsburgh after an open tryout while teaching high school, this pitcher once struck out all but one batter in a seven-inning prep game; Myrtle Beach later retired his number 43.

Ken Caminiti.blurb: A 1996 unanimous National League MVP for San Diego, Caminiti played that season through a torn rotator cuff, made a diving play on his debut's first play, and later admitted steroid use before his sad death in 2004.

Ted Blankenship.blurb: A Texas right-hander who spent nine seasons with the White Sox, Blankenship won 17 games in 1925 with a 3.03 ERA and hit nine career home runs, an unusually handy bat for a pitcher.

Hunter Harvey.blurb: The 22nd overall pick in 2013 and son of ex-big league pitcher Bryan Harvey, Harvey debuted with two strikeouts against the Red Sox in 2019 and later signed with the Cubs for $6 million.

Joe Saunders.blurb: A 2002 first-rounder who lost a year to shoulder surgery, Saunders wore a Virginia Tech cap in a 2007 tribute game, became the AL's first nine-game winner in 2008, and won the first Wild Card Game.

Fernando Rodney.blurb: Rodney celebrated saves by miming an arrow shot into the sky, posted a 0.60 ERA in 2012, and won the 2019 World Series with Washington at age 42.

Elden Auker.blurb: A football injury ruined his shoulder, so Auker threw underhand, beat Satchel Paige to end the Monarchs' 33-game streak, and chose Detroit's $450 over a $6,000 offer from the Chicago Bears.

Trevor May.blurb: May announced his retirement on Twitch while criticizing the Athletics' Las Vegas plans, and he moonlights as an electronic music DJ under names such as DJ HEYBEEF and DJ MAZR.

Howard Johnson.blurb: A switch-hitter who won titles with the 1984 Tigers and 1986 Mets, "HoJo" became the first switch-hitter in the 30-30 club in 1987, then led the National League in homers and RBIs in 1991.

Kody Funderburk.blurb: A Twins lefty chosen in the 15th round, Funderburk debuted in 2023 with two perfect relief innings and a win, after losing a full minor-league season in 2020 to the pandemic.

Heath Bell.blurb: Bell rollerbladed to Mets spring training in 2005 to the displeasure of his pitching coach, and later credited Wii Fit for losing 30 pounds before leading the National League with 42 saves.

Eric Davis.blurb: He hit 37 homers and stole 50 bases in 1987, fell just short of a 40-40 season, battled a kidney injury and later colon cancer, and won Comeback Player of the Year in 1996.

Jimmy Ryan.blurb: Ryan hit for the cycle and won the same game as pitcher in 1888, owned 21 leadoff homers when he retired, and in 1892 attacked a newspaper reporter over a critical article.

Ken Holtzman.blurb: A Jewish lefty who threw two no-hitters, one without a single strikeout, Holtzman beat his boyhood idol Sandy Koufax on Yom Kippur 1966 and finished with 174 wins, nine more than Koufax.

Ken Sanders.blurb: In 1971 this reliever led the majors with 83 appearances, a record 77 games finished and 31 saves, then was traded twice within 32 days, and is one of four men to play for both Kansas City franchises.

Fernando Tatis Jr..blurb: The son of a big-league third baseman, Tatis signed a 14-year, $340 million Padres deal before 2021, then led the National League with 42 home runs while winning his second straight Silver Slugger.

Shohei Ohtani.blurb: Baseball's two-way phenomenon, Ohtani won the 2021 unanimous AL MVP, struck out Mike Trout to clinch the 2023 World Baseball Classic, became the first 50-50 player in 2024, and signed a $700 million Dodgers deal.

Mitch Williams.blurb: "Wild Thing" took his name from his walk-up song, and Earl Weaver called him more hazardous than smoking, yet he led the majors with 76 games in 1989 and saved 36.

Cody Allen.blurb: A hard-throwing Cleveland closer whose 141st save in 2018 broke Bob Wickman's franchise record, Allen also allowed the longest home runs of any big-league pitcher that year, one of 495 feet.

Aaron Robinson.blurb: A catcher who hit his lone grand slam off Bob Feller, Robinson once threw out Eddie Stanky so convincingly in the 1947 World Series that the umpire did not bother signaling, and went 2,189 plate appearances without a steal.

Noah Schultz.blurb: At 6 feet 10, the White Sox lefty is one of the tallest players in major-league history, with a delivery compared to Randy Johnson, and he earned his first big-league win five days after debuting in 2026.

Greg Harris.blurb: An ambidextrous pitcher with a custom glove that fit either hand, Harris finally threw left-handed in the majors in 1995, and once had a sore elbow blamed on flicking sunflower seeds at a friend in the stands.

Jose Leclerc.blurb: A Rangers closer who rebounded from Tommy John surgery, Leclerc saved the first seven games of Texas's 2023 postseason, an MLB record, and won a World Series game in extra innings.

Patricio Scantlebury.blurb: A Panamanian pitching pioneer, Scantlebury won the 1947 Negro World Series with the New York Cubans, won 24 minor-league games in 1953, and finally debuted for Cincinnati at age 38.

Evan Longoria.blurb: The third overall pick in 2006, Longoria was the unanimous 2008 AL Rookie of the Year and reached the World Series with Tampa Bay, then again 15 years later, the longest gap for a position player.

Jack McDowell.blurb: McDowell won the 1993 Cy Young Award with 22 wins, then in 1995 answered booing Yankees fans with a gesture that inspired the song "The Yankee Flipper."

Rich Garces.blurb: Teammates called him "El Guapo," after the villain in Three Amigos, and the Venezuelan reliever, signed at 16 with his mother signing for him, took part in a six-pitcher Red Sox spring perfect game.

Brandon Nimmo.blurb: Nimmo wanted to be a bull rider as a kid, became the highest-drafted player in Wyoming history, and in 2018 led off a game with an inside-the-park homer at Coors Field.

Daulton Varsho.blurb: Varsho is named for Darren Daulton, a teammate of his father's, and he caught Tyler Gilbert's no-hitter in 2021 before hitting a walk-off grand slam for Toronto in 2026.

Louis Varland.blurb: Varland prefers "Louie" but asked scoreboards to use "Louis" to honor his uncle, and in the 2025 postseason he appeared in 15 games, more than any pitcher in a single postseason.

Andrew Painter.blurb: A Phillies first-rounder drafted 13th in 2021, Painter lost a year to Tommy John surgery, still won Arizona Fall League Pitcher of the Year, and shut down Atlanta for three scoreless playoff innings in 2026.

Shigetoshi Hasegawa.blurb: A Japanese Rookie of the Year and Ichiro's Orix teammate, Hasegawa made the 2003 AL All-Star team with a 1.48 ERA, and holds the record for most MLB appearances by an Asian-born pitcher.

Al Hollingsworth.blurb: Nicknamed "Boots" after a first-base error, this pitcher went to Philadelphia in the 1938 deal for Bucky Walters, pitched for the 1944 pennant-winning Browns, and later coached the Cardinals' pitchers.

Cecil Cooper.blurb: A Brewers slugger who hit two grand slams in one inning with Don Money in 1980, Cooper later won the Roberto Clemente Award and became the Houston Astros' first African-American manager.

Kevin McGonigle.blurb: A Tigers shortstop who skipped Auburn for a $2.85 million bonus, McGonigle got four hits in his 2026 debut, signed an eight-year, $150 million extension, and made the All-Star team at 21.

Joel Zumaya.blurb: Zumaya's fastball hit 104.8 mph, but his injuries were stranger: Detroit blamed a sore wrist on Guitar Hero, he later called that a cover story, and a falling box in an attic hurt his shoulder.

Steve Barber.blurb: Barber wore unlucky number 13 for the Orioles, once walked ten in a combined no-hitter that Baltimore still lost 2-1, and later drove children with disabilities to school in Nevada.

Carlos Correa.blurb: The first Latin American-born number-one pick in 2012, Correa was the 2015 AL Rookie of the Year and the 2017 World Series champion with Houston, before returning to the Astros in a 2025 trade.

Jack Meyer.blurb: Meyer pitched bent over with his arms dangling in a "gorilla stance," held Brooklyn to a .103 average, and was named in Sports Illustrated as a member of the Phillies' late-night "Dalton Gang."

Anthony DeSclafani.blurb: A Florida pitcher who turned down a $200,000 bonus for college, DeSclafani came via a big Toronto-Miami trade, hit a rare grand slam for the Reds, and threw a 12-0 complete-game shutout.

Caleb Bonemer.blurb: A two-time Gatorade Michigan Baseball Player of the Year, Bonemer passed on Virginia for a $3 million White Sox bonus and won the 2025 Carolina League MVP award with ten homers and 27 steals.

George Hunter.blurb: Hunter and his identical twin Bill were the first twins in the majors, though they never played together, and George pitched one promising 1909 season before a one-inning outfield cameo ended his career.

Charlie Buffinton.blurb: A Fall River, Massachusetts pitcher with what a teammate called the greatest drop ball he ever saw, Buffinton went 48-16 in 1884 and won 233 big-league games.

Hideo Nomo.blurb: Nomo invented his corkscrew "tornado" windup in fifth grade to impress his father and confuse batters, then found a contract loophole to reach the Dodgers and no-hit both Colorado and Baltimore.

Andy Etchebarren.blurb: Etchebarren dove into a pool to rescue Frank Robinson, who couldn't swim, and was the last batter ever to face Sandy Koufax, while Addams Family fans called him "Lurch."

Manny Machado.blurb: The third overall pick in 2010, Machado signed a 10-year, $300 million Padres deal in 2019, then reached his 2,000th hit in 2025, one of only five active players with that many.

Evar Swanson.blurb: Swanson circled the bases in 13.2 seconds in 1931, a mark nobody has beaten, and he played NFL football in the offseason despite never having played it in high school.

Trevor Cahill.blurb: Called "Pterodactyl" or "Dactyl" since his Oakland rookie days, Cahill won Olympic bronze in 2008, made the 2010 All-Star team at 18-8, and earned a Cubs ring in 2016 without pitching in the postseason.

Joe Grzenda.blurb: Grzenda was the last pitcher in Washington Senators history, grounding out to a standing ovation before fans stormed the field, then 34 years later handed George W. Bush the first-pitch ball.

Home Run Baker.blurb: The Maryland farm boy earned his nickname with consecutive 1911 World Series homers, and at his 1955 Hall of Fame election said a rosebud while alive beats a whole bouquet after you're dead.

Lance Johnson.blurb: Nicknamed "One Dog" for his speed and number 1, Johnson led his league in triples four straight years, and remains the only player to lead both leagues in hits in back-to-back seasons.

Tyler Clippard.blurb: Clippard won the 2011 All-Star Game without retiring a single batter, a fitting result for a pitcher whose odd delivery makes him admit that strikeouts just kind of happen.

Pete Incaviglia.blurb: After Montreal traded the young slugger right after signing him, baseball adopted the Pete Incaviglia Rule against such deals, and he reached Texas in 1986 without playing a minor-league game.

Dmitri Young.blurb: Young hit three homers on Opening Day 2005, and also amassed roughly 500 mint rookie cards, many of which he auctioned to fund a foundation for underprivileged children in Ventura County, California.

Jose DeLeon.blurb: DeLeon went 2-19 in 1985 and was dubbed the best losing pitcher in baseball, but he bounced back to win 16 and lead the National League with 201 strikeouts in 1989.

Mark Eichhorn.blurb: A shortstop turned submarine reliever after a hotel-lawn tryout, Eichhorn learned of his 1992 trade back to Toronto from the manager during a card game on a flight.

Max Clark.blurb: Indiana's two-time Gatorade Baseball Player of the Year and a national Gatorade winner across all sports, Clark went third overall to Detroit in 2023 and collected three hits in his 2026 debut.

Noodles Hahn.blurb: Hahn claimed he never knew why he was called Noodles, though one story involved his father's noodle-soup lunch; he struck out 16 in a game in 1901 and later trained as a veterinarian.

Jack Glasscock.blurb: "Pebbly Jack" earned his nickname by picking stones off the infield and tossing them aside, and the "King of the Shortstops" won the 1890 batting title with a .336 average.

Cliff Floyd.blurb: A 14th overall pick by Montreal who homered off Greg Maddux as a rookie in 1994, Floyd won a ring with the 1997 Marlins and made his lone All-Star team in 2001.

Brice Turang.blurb: Turang's whole family played: father Brian reached the majors, mother Carrie won an NCAA softball title at Long Beach State, and four older sisters were athletes too. Milwaukee took him 21st overall in 2018, and he debuted on Opening Day 2023.

Cannonball Morris.blurb: No left-hander won more games in the 1800s than 'Cannonball' Morris: 171 victories from 1884 to 1890, plus 12 shutouts in 1886, still the single-season record for a left-hander. Injuries, drink and a fighting temper ended his career early.

Junior Caminero.blurb: Tampa Bay named Caminero its Minor League Player of the Year, and the very next day, September 23, 2023, he was playing in the majors. Cleveland had given him up in 2021 for pitcher Tobias Myers, a trade that aged poorly.

Ross Barnes.blurb: Barnes was the undisputed master of the fair-foul hit, a now-vanished art of bouncing balls into foul ground for safe hits. He batted .429 in the National League's first season, 1876, topping nearly every offensive category for champion Chicago.

Willie Hernandez.blurb: In 1984, Hernández won a reliever's impossible double: the American League Cy Young Award and the MVP, after saving 32 games with a 1.92 ERA for champion Detroit. He was the first player from Puerto Rico to win an MVP award.

Chris Davis.blurb: 'Crush Davis' was a play on Crash Davis of Bull Durham, coined as Davis tore up his 2008 debut with Texas. In 2013 he hit 53 home runs, leading the majors and breaking Baltimore's single-season record.

Duke Kenworthy.blurb: Kenworthy was named William Jennings, after William Jennings Bryan, and born on the Fourth of July, 1886. He won 24 and 22 games as a pitcher in 1909 and 1910, then reinvented himself as a slugging second baseman in the Federal League.

Fred Dunlap.blurb: They called Dunlap 'Sure Shot' for the lightning-quick, accurate throws he fired to first base. His 1884 season was absurd: a .412 average, .621 slugging and 13 home runs for the St. Louis Maroons of the short-lived Union Association.

Hughie Jennings.blurb: Jennings managed Detroit from 1907 while hollering 'Ee-yah!' from the coaching box and plucking the grass bare, a yell the Marines took into World War I in modified form. In the off-season, the same man was a respected trial lawyer in Scranton.

Jason Isringhausen.blurb: Isringhausen was a 44th-round pick and a charter member of the Mets' 'Generation K,' three hyped young arms who mostly broke down; his own career stalled with tuberculosis. Converted to closing, he tied Lee Smith's Cardinals record with 47 saves in 2004.

John McGraw.blurb: McGraw stood 5-foot-7 and hated both his nicknames, 'Mugsy' and 'Little Napoleon.' It hardly mattered: managing the New York Giants from 1902 to 1932, he won 10 pennants and three World Series, finishing first or second 21 times.

Arthur Rhodes.blurb: Rhodes waited until his 19th season, at age 40, to make his first All-Star team in 2010. He retired after winning the 2011 World Series with St. Louis, holding the career record with 231 holds, baseball's most anonymous record.

Augie Galan.blurb: As a boy, Galan fell out of a tree, broke his right arm, and hid the injury from his parents; the arm never healed right. He lasted 16 seasons and, in 1937, became the first National Leaguer to homer from both sides in one game.

Camilo Pascual.blurb: Pascual's curveball was rated among the finest ever thrown, but pitching for the wretched 1950s Senators he lost 18 games in 1956 alone. The franchise's move to Minnesota in 1961 turned him from one of the league's biggest losers into a winner.

Cesar Cedeno.blurb: Houston signed Cedeño at sixteen, and he was patrolling center field in the majors at nineteen in 1970. The five-tool original finished 17 seasons with 199 home runs and 550 stolen bases, winning five straight Gold Gloves from 1972 to 1976.

Daniel Palencia.blurb: Palencia's major-league debut, on July 4, 2023, ended with him as the winning pitcher in extra innings. By 2026 he was closing at the highest level, finishing Venezuela's 3-2 win over the United States to win the World Baseball Classic.

Darrell Evans.blurb: Bill James called Evans the most underrated player in baseball history, full stop. In 1973 Evans hit 41 home runs alongside Hank Aaron's 40 and Davey Johnson's 43, the first trio of 40-homer teammates ever. He scored on Aaron's record-breaking 715th homer in 1974.

David Wright.blurb: Wright captained Team USA at the 2013 World Baseball Classic, was its best player, and came home 'Captain America.' Days later the Mets made him the fourth captain in franchise history. His number 5 was retired in 2025.

Ed Williamson.blurb: Williamson hit 27 home runs in 1884, a record that stood until Babe Ruth, thanks to Chicago fences 180 feet away and a ground rule reclassifying doubles as homers. His contemporaries called him Ed; he only became 'Ned' decades later, posthumously.

George Springer.blurb: Springer turned the 2017 World Series into his personal fireworks show, tying the record with five home runs as Houston beat Los Angeles in seven games and taking home the MVP award. He later signed with Toronto before the 2021 season.

Grant Balfour.blurb: Balfour pitched for Australia at the 2000 Olympics in his hometown, Sydney, a year after saving three games at the 1999 Intercontinental Cup to deliver Australia's first gold medal in a major international baseball competition. He made the 2013 All-Star team as Oakland's closer.

Harry Steinfeldt.blurb: Steinfeldt is the forgotten fourth man of the Tinker-to-Evers-to-Chance infield; in the famous photograph of the trio, he is literally cropped out. In 1906 he led the league in RBIs for the 116-win Cubs, their unofficial most valuable player.

Ben Sheets.blurb: Sheets struck out 18 Braves on May 16, 2004, shattering the Brewers' franchise record of 14. A 1999 first-round pick and 2000 Olympic gold medalist, he was a four-time All-Star and the first Brewers pitcher to start an All-Star Game.

Elly De La Cruz.blurb: In 2024, De La Cruz became the first shortstop in major league history with at least 20 home runs and 60 stolen bases in a season. The Reds signed him in 2018; he debuted June 6, 2023 and hit for the cycle that month.

B.J. Ryan.blurb: On May 1, 2003, Ryan won a game without throwing a pitch, picking off Detroit's Omar Infante. The lefty reliever signed a five-year, $47 million deal with Toronto in 2005, earned the win in the 2006 All-Star Game, and had Tommy John surgery in 2007.

Gabriel Moreno.blurb: Venezuelan catcher Moreno was traded with Lourdes Gurriel Jr. from Toronto to Arizona for Daulton Varsho on December 23, 2022. He won a Gold Glove in 2023, when the Diamondbacks reached their first World Series since 2001.

Wade Davis.blurb: Davis posted a 1.00 ERA for the 2014 Royals, then became their closer in 2015 and won the Babe Ruth Award for that postseason: 18 strikeouts, no earned runs in 10⅔ innings. He led the NL with 43 saves for Colorado in 2018.

Ethan Salas.blurb: Padres catcher Salas signed in January 2023 for a record $5.6 million bonus. After reaching the majors in September 2026, he homered twice on September 16 and became the youngest catcher to play in a postseason game, at 20 years, 120 days.

Henry Davis.blurb: The Pirates took Davis first overall in the 2021 draft out of Louisville, signing him for a reported $6.5 million bonus. On April 14, 2025, he and Paul Skenes became the first battery of No. 1 overall draft picks.

Hong-Chih Kuo.blurb: After Tommy John surgeries in 2000 and 2003, Kuo became the first Taiwanese-born All-Star in 2010, when the Dodgers lefty posted a 1.20 ERA over 60 innings. In 2007 he became the first Taiwanese player to homer in the majors.

Kirby Yates.blurb: Yates led the NL with 41 saves for the 2019 Padres, posting a 1.19 ERA, an All-Star selection and All-MLB First Team honors. After a second Tommy John surgery in March 2021, he made the 2024 All-Star team with Texas.

Walker Cooper.blurb: Teammates called Cooper 'Muley' for his strength and endurance. The catcher hit .305 with 35 homers and 122 RBI in 1947, and on July 6, 1949 went six for seven with three homers and 10 RBIs against the Cubs.

Aaron Judge.blurb: Judge hit 62 home runs in 2022, breaking Roger Maris's 61-year-old AL single-season record, and won his first MVP. The Yankees drafted him 32nd overall in 2013; he was unanimous AL Rookie of the Year in 2017.

Armando Benitez.blurb: With the Orioles, Benítez yielded Jeffrey Maier's infamous 1996 ALCS home run, yet went on to 289 career saves. He saved 47 of 51 chances for the 2004 Marlins and won the NL Rolaids Relief Man Award in 2001.

Ben Rice.blurb: On July 6, 2024, Rice became the first Yankees rookie to hit three home runs in a game, and his seven RBIs matched Lou Gehrig's Yankees rookie record. A 12th-round pick in 2021 after Dartmouth, he debuted June 18, 2024.

Bryan Harvey.blurb: In 1991, Harvey became the first pitcher with 40 saves and 100 strikeouts in one season, leading the AL with 46 saves for the Angels. He later joined the inaugural 1993 Florida Marlins and was an All-Star that year.

Cade Smith.blurb: Born in Abbotsford, British Columbia, Smith pitched at Hawaii, went undrafted in 2020 and signed with Cleveland. He debuted March 30, 2024, then made the 2026 All-Star Game and tied for the league lead with 41 saves.

Cam Schlittler.blurb: A 7th-round Yankees pick from Northeastern in 2022, Schlittler debuted July 9, 2025. In that year's Wild Card Series he threw eight scoreless innings with 12 strikeouts and no walks, and his 1.95 ERA led the league in 2026.

Craig Kimbrel.blurb: Kimbrel won 2011 NL Rookie of the Year with all 32 first-place votes and a rookie-record 46 saves, then led the NL in saves four straight years. In 2018 he became the youngest pitcher to reach 300 saves.

Cristopher Sanchez.blurb: In 2026, Sánchez threw 50⅔ straight scoreless innings, ending June 3: fifth-longest in MLB history and the longest by a lefty. The Rays signed him at 16 in 2013; Philadelphia got him for Curtis Mead in November 2019.

Daisuke Matsuzaka.blurb: Boston won the rights to Matsuzaka with a $51,111,111.11 bid in November 2006. 'Dice-K' was MVP of the 2006 and 2009 World Baseball Classics and won the 2007 World Series, the first player to win both.

Dave Smith.blurb: Smith converted his first 21 save opportunities of 1989, an Astros club record. The reliever pitched for Houston from 1980 to 1990, was an All-Star in 1986 and 1990, and finished with 216 career saves.

Drew Rasmussen.blurb: As an Oregon State freshman on March 21, 2015, Rasmussen threw the only perfect game in the program's history. As a Ray, he carried a perfect game through eight innings against Baltimore on August 14, 2022.

Dylan Cease.blurb: Dylan Cease threw a no-hitter for the Padres on July 25, 2024, a 3-0 win over Washington. He finished second in the 2022 AL Cy Young vote with the White Sox and had five straight 200-strikeout seasons, 2021 to 2025.

Garrett Crochet.blurb: Garrett Crochet went from the 2020 draft straight to the majors without playing in the minors, debuting for the White Sox that September. In 2025 with Boston he went 18-5 with a 2.59 ERA and 255 strikeouts, the most in the majors.

Gavin Williams.blurb: Nicknamed "the Big Rig," Gavin Williams threw two straight no-hitters as a high school senior in 2017. After East Carolina, Cleveland took him 23rd overall in the 2021 draft, and he debuted on June 21, 2023.

Hideki Matsui.blurb: Nicknamed "Godzilla," Hideki Matsui won three Central League MVP awards with the Yomiuri Giants, then played 518 straight games to open his Yankees career. He was the 2009 World Series MVP, the first Japanese-born player to win it.

Ian Kinsler.blurb: Ian Kinsler hit for the cycle with six hits in one game for the Rangers on April 15, 2009. A four-time All-Star, he won the 2018 World Series with Boston and later managed Israel at the 2023 World Baseball Classic.

J.D. Martinez.blurb: The Astros released J.D. Martinez in March 2014; he signed with Detroit and broke out that season. On September 4, 2017, with Arizona, he hit four home runs against the Dodgers, and in 2018 he led the majors with 130 RBIs for Boston.

Zack Wheeler.blurb: Zack Wheeler went sixth overall to the Giants in 2009, then was traded to the Mets for Carlos Beltran in 2011. Tommy John surgery in March 2015 kept him off the mound until 2017. He was 2026 NL Comeback Player of the Year.

Julio Teheran.blurb: Julio Teheran started Opening Day for Atlanta every year from 2014 through 2019, tying Warren Spahn's franchise record. The Colombian right-hander was named an All-Star in 2014 and 2016, the second Colombian All-Star after Edgar Renteria.

Robinson Cano.blurb: Robinson Cano won the 2011 Home Run Derby and was MVP of the 2013 World Baseball Classic. A member of the 2009 champion Yankees, he signed a 10-year, $240 million deal with Seattle in December 2013 and was suspended 80 games in 2018.

Raisel Iglesias.blurb: Raisel Iglesias was caught hiding in the mountains of Cuba's Isla de la Juventud during a failed defection in September 2013, then succeeded that November. He signed with the Reds in 2014 for seven years and $27 million, debuting April 12, 2015.

Jeremy Pena.blurb: Jeremy Pena was the first rookie to win a Gold Glove at shortstop. In 2022 he won both ALCS and World Series MVP, the first American League player to do so in one year. His father Geronimo played in MLB from 1990 to 1996.

Jacob deGrom.blurb: Jacob deGrom started at Stetson as a shortstop before being converted to pitcher. He won NL Rookie of the Year in 2014 and back-to-back Cy Youngs in 2018 and 2019, the first with a 1.70 ERA and just 10 wins.

J.A. Happ.blurb: J.A. Happ was the opposing starter in Matt Cain's perfect game on June 13, 2012. He went 20-4 with a 3.18 ERA for Toronto in 2016, and retired in 2022 after 15 seasons and a 133-100 record.

Hagen Smith.blurb: Hagen Smith threw seven no-hitters as a high school senior in 2021, tying a Texas record, after Tommy John surgery earlier. He set Arkansas's career strikeout record with 360 and went fifth overall to the White Sox in 2024.

Mike Greenwell.blurb: Mike Greenwell, nicknamed "Gator" for wrestling alligators in Florida, hit for the cycle on September 14, 1988, and finished second to Jose Canseco in AL MVP voting that year. In 1989 he put together a 21-game hitting streak.

Roy Thomas.blurb: Phillies center fielder Roy Thomas led the National League in walks in seven of his nine full seasons and reportedly fouled off as many as 27 pitches in one at-bat. The NL adopted the foul-strike rule in 1901. He stole 244 bases.

Armando Rios.blurb: Armando Rios, a left-handed outfielder from Santurce, Puerto Rico, won silver with Puerto Rico at the 1991 Pan American Games and played at LSU from 1991 to 1993. He debuted with the Giants in 1998, then played for Pittsburgh and the White Sox.

Dutch Leonard.blurb: Knuckleballer Emil "Dutch" Leonard won 20 games in 1939 for a sixth-place Senators club that managed only 65 wins, Washington's first 20-game winner since 1933. In 1945 he went 17-7 with a 2.13 ERA, his career best.

Will Smith.blurb: Dodgers catcher Will Smith homered in four straight at-bats on July 6, 2024, tying the major league record. A 2016 first-round pick who debuted in 2019, he has won three World Series with Los Angeles (2020, 2024, 2025).

Jose Ramirez.blurb: Jose Ramirez is the first Guardians player with three 30-30 seasons (2018, 2024, 2025). Signed for a $50,000 bonus in 2009, he debuted in 2013 and agreed to a seven-year, $175 million extension in January 2026.

Jose Bautista.blurb: Jose Bautista led the majors with 54 home runs in 2010, a Blue Jays record, two years after Pittsburgh traded him to Toronto on August 21, 2008. His 2015 ALDS bat flip against Texas became a symbol of Toronto's first playoff run since 1993.

Aidan Miller.blurb: Aidan Miller, a Phillies shortstop from Florida, went 27th overall in the 2023 draft and signed for $3.1 million. Across Double-A and Triple-A in 2025 he hit .264 with 14 home runs and 59 stolen bases in 116 games.

Michael Wacha.blurb: Michael Wacha was the 2013 NLCS MVP as a rookie, winning both starts with a 0.43 ERA over 21 innings. That September 24 he carried a no-hitter into the ninth against Washington before Ryan Zimmerman's infield single.

Kevin Mitchell.blurb: Kevin Mitchell won the 1989 NL MVP for the Giants, leading the league with 47 home runs and 125 RBIs. In Game Six of the 1986 World Series he singled in the 10th for the Mets, then scored the tying run on a wild pitch.

B.J. Upton.blurb: B.J. Upton hit seven home runs in Tampa Bay's 2008 postseason, four of them against Boston in the ALCS. Taken second overall in 2002, he debuted in 2004 and hit 24 homers while stealing 22 of 30 bases in 2007.
