Sam Jones.blurb: Sad Sam Jones no-hit the Philadelphia Athletics 2-0 on September 4, 1923, without striking out a batter, in a 21-8 season for the Yankees. The Sad nickname began with a new sportswriter who knew him only from the press box.

Kevin Alcantara.blurb: Kevin Alcantara signed with the Yankees in 2018 and went to the Cubs in the July 2021 trade for Anthony Rizzo. He debuted September 25, 2024, and hit his first big-league homer on August 3, 2026, off Justin Wrobleski.

Andy Van Slyke.blurb: Andy Van Slyke won five straight Gold Gloves in center field for Pittsburgh, 1988 to 1992, and Three Rivers Stadium had a "Slyke Zone" named for his arm. In 1988 he hit 25 homers, drove in 100 and finished fourth in MVP voting.

Khal Stephen.blurb: Khal Stephen, a Mississippi State pitcher, went in the second round of the 2024 draft to Toronto, then was traded to Cleveland for Shane Bieber on July 31, 2025. After 12 starts for Akron in 2026 he needed ulnar collateral ligament surgery.

Joshua Baez.blurb: Joshua Baez homered in each of his first three plate appearances in his August 15, 2026 debut against the Cubs, the first player to do so, finishing 3-for-4 with five RBI. The Cardinals took him in the second round in 2021.

Jose Reyes.blurb: Jose Reyes won the 2011 NL batting title at .337, the first Met to do so. He led the NL in stolen bases in 2005, 2006 and 2007, and holds Mets career records for triples (113) and steals (408).

Tom Brown.blurb: Liverpool-born Tom Brown stole 106 bases for the 1891 Boston Reds and led the league that year with 21 triples, 177 runs and 189 hits. He also set the major league record of 490 errors committed as an outfielder.

Gary Gentry.blurb: Gary Gentry started Game 3 of the 1969 World Series and shut out Baltimore for 6 2/3 innings before Nolan Ryan finished it. That rookie year he went 13-12 with a 3.43 ERA and pitched the Mets' division clincher against the Cardinals.

Janson Junk.blurb: Janson Junk was a 22nd-round Yankees pick in 2017 who started at Seattle University as a walk-on. After going 6-4 with a 4.17 ERA in 21 appearances for the Marlins in 2025, he was named their fifth starter on March 20, 2026.

Joe Mays.blurb: Joe Mays made the 2001 All-Star team for Minnesota, going 17-13 with a 3.16 ERA. White Sox broadcaster Hawk Harrelson called him "Cy" Mays because he consistently beat Chicago. Tommy John surgery cost him all of 2004.

Livan Hernandez.blurb: A Cuban defector (1995), he struck out a postseason-record 15 in Game 5 of the 1997 NLCS and won both NLCS and World Series MVP for the Marlins. He led the NL in innings pitched in 2003, 2004 and 2005.

Carlos Pena.blurb: Released by the Tigers on March 26, 2006, he signed with the Rays in 2007 and hit a career-high 46 home runs with 121 RBI, setting Rays franchise records and winning AL Comeback Player of the Year.

Mark Grudzielanek.blurb: He hit for the cycle against the Brewers on April 27, 2005, during his one season with the Cardinals. A 1996 All-Star, he won the AL second base Gold Glove with the Royals in 2006 and finished with 2,040 hits.

Jarrod Parker.blurb: The ninth overall pick in 2007, he missed 2010 after Tommy John surgery. As an Athletics rookie in 2012 he took a no-hitter into the eighth against Texas and went 13-8, 3.47, finishing fifth in Rookie of the Year voting.

Bill Dahlen.blurb: Nicknamed "Bad Bill" for his ejections and umpire arguments (65 of them as player and manager), he hit safely in 42 straight games in 1894. In his second Chicago season, 1892, he hit .293 and stole a career-high 60 bases.

Bob Romby.blurb: A left-handed pitcher and right fielder, he spent his Negro leagues career, 1946 to 1950, with the Baltimore Elite Giants. He led the Negro National League in strikeouts in 1947 and was on Baltimore's 1949 Negro American League champions.

Leo Cardenas.blurb: Nicknamed "Mr. Automatic" for his glove, the Cuban-born shortstop won his only Gold Glove in 1965. In 1966 he hit 20 home runs, then a Reds record for shortstops, including four in a June 5 doubleheader against the Cubs.

Henderson Alvarez III.blurb: He threw a no-hitter against the Tigers on September 29, 2013, the first at Marlins Park, winning 1-0 on a ninth-inning bases-loaded wild pitch. In 2014 he went 12-7, 2.65 with a majors-best three shutouts and made the All-Star team.

Tony Pena Sr..blurb: Known for a low crouch with one leg fully extended, he won three Gold Gloves in seven Pittsburgh seasons and a fourth with Boston in 1991, the second catcher to win in both leagues. Pittsburgh traded him to St. Louis on April 1, 1987.

Javier Baez.blurb: Nicknamed "El Mago," he stole home in Game 1 of the 2016 NLCS and shared NLCS MVP with Jon Lester, hitting .318. The Cubs won that year's World Series. An All-Star in 2018 and 2019, he later signed with Detroit for six years, $140 million.

Bill Keister.blurb: His constant trash talk earned him the nickname "Wagon Tongue." He hit .312 over 621 games, though his fielding was described as terrible enough to cancel out his bat. On July 19, 1899 he fought Tommy Corcoran and both were ejected.

R.A. Dickey.blurb: Drafted 18th overall in 1996, he lacked an ulnar collateral ligament in his right elbow, which cut his first offer to $75,000. He later climbed Kilimanjaro in January 2012 and went 20-6, 2.73 for the Mets, winning the NL Cy Young Award.

Pedro Alvarez.blurb: A Vanderbilt freshman who set the school's single-season record with 22 home runs, he went second overall to the Pirates in 2008. In 2013 he tied Paul Goldschmidt for the NL lead with 36 homers, drove in 100 and won a Silver Slugger.

Javier Lopez.blurb: A sidearm lefty reliever, he was traded to the Giants on July 31, 2010 and went 2-0 with a 1.42 ERA in 27 games for them. He won four World Series rings: with Boston in 2007 and San Francisco in 2010, 2012 and 2014.

Triston McKenzie.blurb: Listed at 6'5" and just 165 pounds, Triston McKenzie struck out ten Tigers in six innings in his 2020 Cleveland debut. In 2022 he went 11-11 with a 2.96 ERA over 191.1 innings.

Manny Banuelos.blurb: Mariano Rivera said he believed Manny Bañuelos was the best pitching prospect he had seen. Signed out of the Mexican League in 2008, Bañuelos had Tommy John surgery in October 2012 and debuted in 2015 with Atlanta.

Pat Patterson.blurb: Pat Patterson doubled off Martin Dihigo and scored the winning run in Game Six of the 1935 championship series for the Pittsburgh Crawfords. He played in six East-West Games and later taught and coached at Houston's Jack Yates High School.

Tommy Hinzo.blurb: Tommy Hinzo won the 1986 College World Series with Arizona, then debuted for Cleveland on July 16, 1987, a day after the Indians traded Tony Bernazard. The second baseman hit .265 in 67 games that year.

Emmet Heidrick.blurb: Emmet Heidrick's father died in a shotgun accident on July 20, 1901, and he considered quitting baseball. He returned to the Cardinals and hit .339, sixth in the league. In 1899 he led the league with 34 outfield assists.

Steve Hamilton.blurb: Six-foot-six Steve Hamilton played two NBA seasons with the Minneapolis Lakers before 12 major league seasons. He threw a high, slow eephus known as the Folly Floater, and his lowest ERA was 1.39 in 1965.

Enrique Hernandez.blurb: In Game 5 of the 2017 NLCS, Kiké Hernández hit three home runs, including a grand slam, and drove in seven runs, tying the record for RBI in a postseason game. He has played every position except catcher in the majors.

Charlie Blackwell.blurb: Charles "Rucker" Blackwell was a left-handed outfielder who played in the Negro leagues from 1915 to 1929, mostly with the St. Louis Giants/Stars. Born in Brandenburg, Kentucky, he died in 1935 at age 40.

Felipe Lopez.blurb: Felipe López, Toronto's first-round pick in 1998, broke out in 2005 as the Reds' regular shortstop: 23 home runs, 15 steals and a .291 average. He made the NL All-Star team that season.

Dick Lines.blurb: Montreal-born reliever Dick Lines fractured his left big toe in December 1965 after dropping frozen spare ribs on it, yet made the Washington Senators that April. He went 7-7 with a 2.83 ERA and six saves over 1966 and 1967.

George Walker.blurb: George Walker holds the lowest known single-season WHIP across all major professional leagues, 0.7347 with the 1940 Kansas City Monarchs. The Waco, Texas native also led the Negro American League in wins in 1939.

Red Howard.blurb: Herman "Red" Howard, a left-handed pitcher from Birmingham, Alabama, pitched in the Negro leagues from 1937 to 1946. His teams included the Birmingham Black Barons, Memphis Red Sox and Chicago American Giants.

Francisco Alvarez.blurb: Nicknamed El Troll, Francisco Álvarez signed with the Mets in July 2018. In 2023 he hit 25 home runs, broke the Mets record for a rookie catcher, and was only the second 21-year-old catcher to reach 20 in a season.

Enmanuel De Jesus.blurb: Venezuelan lefty Enmanuel De Jesus signed with the Red Sox at 16 in 2013, later pitched in Korea for Kiwoom in 2024 and KT in 2025, and was on Venezuela's 2026 World Baseball Classic team that won the country's first title.

Elmer Rodriguez.blurb: Elmer Rodríguez is a Puerto Rican right-hander the Red Sox traded to the Yankees for Carlos Narváez in December 2024. He went 11-8 with a 2.58 ERA across three levels in 2025, then debuted April 29, 2026, losing to Texas.

Justin Bruihl.blurb: Justin Bruihl, an undrafted lefty signed by the Dodgers in 2017, struck out the first batter he faced in his August 8, 2021 debut and pitched in that year's NLCS. He earned his first save September 18, 2022, and joined the Cardinals in January 2026.

Tim Corcoran.blurb: His first big-league hit was a two-run homer in 1977. His career year came with the 1984 Phillies: mostly a pinch-hitter, he played every day when Len Matuszek broke a finger and finished at .341 with a .440 on-base percentage.

Jim Weaver.blurb: At just under 6 feet 7, he went 57-36 in eight seasons without a losing year, and said he missed three pennants by one year. In 1934 he went 11-9 for the Cubs, including a 1-0 win over the Cardinals.

Adolis Garcia.blurb: Adolis García is a Cuban-born outfielder nicknamed El Bombi. In 2023 he set a record with 15 RBIs in a postseason series, won ALCS MVP and hit a walk-off homer in World Series Game 1 as Texas won in five. Phillies signee for 2026.

Kevin Brown.blurb: Kevin Brown threw a no-hitter for the Marlins on June 10, 1997; the only Giants baserunner reached on a hit by pitch. He led baseball with a 1.89 ERA in 1996, then went 18-7 with 257 strikeouts for the 1998 Padres.

Steve O'Neill.blurb: Tenth of 13 children, he worked the coal mines from age ten; his older brothers Mike and Jack formed the first brother battery in the majors. The Cleveland catcher hit .289 with 35 doubles in 1919, then .321 in 1920, catching 149 of 154 games.

Reed Garrett.blurb: Reed Garrett, a reliever taken fifth in the 2018 Rule 5 draft by Detroit, pitched in Japan for Saitama Seibu in 2020-21. For the 2024 Mets he went 5-0 with 41 strikeouts from April 4 to May 19, finishing with a 3.77 ERA.

Brooks Raley.blurb: Brooks Raley, a lefty drafted by the Cubs in 2009, pitched for the KBO's Lotte Giants in 2015-19. He posted a 2.68 ERA for the 2022 Rays and 2.80 in 66 games for the 2023 Mets, then traded to the Phillies August 3, 2026.

C.J. Wilson.blurb: C.J. Wilson, a lefty, founded and owns the racing team CJ Wilson Racing. He went 16-7 with a 2.94 ERA for the 2011 Rangers, led the league with 34 starts, then signed a five-year, $77.5 million deal with the Angels in December 2011.

Thayron Liranzo.blurb: Thayron Liranzo led the California League with 24 home runs in 2023. The catcher and first baseman went from the Dodgers to the Tigers in the July 2024 Jack Flaherty trade, and was added to Detroit's 40-man roster in November 2025.

Luis Pena.blurb: Luis Peña, a Dominican shortstop, stole 39 bases in 44 games in his 2024 debut season in the Dominican Summer League after signing with the Brewers in January 2024. He reached Double-A Biloxi late in 2026.

Jonny Farmelo.blurb: Jonny Farmelo went 29th overall to the Mariners in 2023 with a $3.2 million bonus, then tore his ACL chasing a pop-up in 2024. In 2026 he hit 17 home runs and stole 41 bases between Everett and Arkansas.

Zyhir Hope.blurb: Zyhir Hope was an 11th-round Cubs pick in 2023, traded to the Dodgers in 2024. In 2026 he hit .293 with 23 home runs at Tulsa, then went to Detroit on August 2 in the Tarik Skubal trade.

Roldy Brito.blurb: Roldy Brito, a switch-hitting Dominican second baseman and outfielder, signed with the Rockies as an international free agent in January 2024. In 2025 he was named Arizona Complex League MVP and the Rockies' Doug Million Minor League Player of the Year.

Jacob Reimer.blurb: Third baseman Jacob Reimer was drafted by the Mets in the fourth round in 2022 and debuted that year with the FCL Mets. He hit 17 home runs in 2025 and was rated the Mets' sixth-best prospect by MLB.com.

Eduardo Quintero.blurb: Venezuelan outfielder Eduardo Quintero signed with the Dodgers as an international free agent in January 2023. In 2025 he hit .293 with 19 home runs, earning Branch Rickey Player of the Year and California League MVP honors.

Jose Fernandez.blurb: Jose Fernandez defected from Cuba on his fourth try in 2007, at 15, diving in to save his mother when she fell overboard. He won 2013 NL Rookie of the Year and set a Marlins season record with 253 strikeouts in 2016.

Jarlin Susana.blurb: Jarlin Susana was part of the Juan Soto trade package that sent him from San Diego to Washington on August 2, 2022, after he signed with San Diego on January 15, 2022. In 2025 he went 1-4 with a 3.51 ERA in 14 starts.

Eduardo Tait.blurb: Eduardo Tait, a Panamanian catcher, signed with Philadelphia on January 15, 2023, and was named Florida Complex League player of the month for June 2024. In July 2025 he was traded to the Twins with Mick Abel for Jhoan Durán.

Josuar Gonzalez.blurb: Signed out of the Dominican Republic in the 2025 international period, Josuar Gonzalez was FanGraphs' top non-Sasaki prospect in that class. The Giants shortstop switch-hits, hit .288/.404/.455 in the DSL, and scouts see a lock to stay at short.

Yolfran Castillo.blurb: Yolfran Castillo signed with the Rangers out of the Dominican Republic in the 2024 international period. FanGraphs calls him the latest in a line of young, athletic, ultra-projectable middle-of-the-diamond players, and thinks he could be a good shortstop.

Christian Oppor.blurb: Christian Oppor was a fifth-round pick of the White Sox in 2023 out of Gulf Coast CC. In 2025 the starter earned a High-A promotion after a month and finished with 116 strikeouts, 42 walks and a 3.08 ERA over 87.2 innings.

Jack Wenninger.blurb: Jack Wenninger, a sixth-round pick out of Illinois in 2023, is a Mets righty who sits 93-96 mph and tops out at 98. His changeup grades 60, and FanGraphs projects him as a no. 4 starter just about ready for the majors.

Caden Scarborough.blurb: Caden Scarborough, a 2023 sixth-round pick from Harmony HS in Florida, was signed away from Dallas Baptist by Texas for $515,000. FanGraphs lists him at 6-foot-5 and describes an 80-84 mph sweeper with plus horizontal action.

Edward Florentino.blurb: Edward Florentino signed with Pittsburgh out of the Dominican Republic in the 2024 international period and ranks fourth in the Pirates system. FanGraphs notes his knack for catching the ball out front and elevating to his pull side, and sees a future right fielder.

Dax Kilby.blurb: Dax Kilby went 39th overall in the 2025 first round out of Newnan HS in Georgia, signing with the Yankees for just shy of $2.8 million despite a Clemson commitment. FanGraphs calls his prep contact rate excellent and says he looks passable at shortstop.

Michael Forret.blurb: Michael Forret was a 14th-round pick of Baltimore in 2023 from State College of Florida Manatee. In FanGraphs' June 26, 2026 Rays list he ranked fifth, a strike-thrower with fantastic feel for location and mid-rotation projection.

Felix Hernandez.blurb: Nicknamed "King Félix," Hernández threw the first perfect game in Mariners history on August 15, 2012, a 1–0 win over Tampa Bay. He debuted at 19 in 2005 and won the 2010 AL Cy Young Award despite a 13–12 record.

Jayson 'Werewolf' Werth.blurb: Jayson Werth stole second, third and home in one inning on May 12, 2009, becoming the ninth player in MLB history to do so. He won the 2008 World Series with the Phillies, batting .444 in the series, and finished with 229 home runs.

Walbert Urena.blurb: Signed as an international free agent by the Angels on March 31, 2021, Walbert Ureña reached Double-A and Triple-A in 2025. The Angels added him to the 40-man roster November 18, 2025, and he debuted on Opening Day 2026 against Houston.

Harry Salmon.blurb: Harry "Beans" Salmon pitched in the Negro leagues from 1920 to 1935, spending most of that time with the Birmingham Black Barons. He also pitched for the Pittsburgh Keystones, Memphis Red Sox and Homestead Grays.

A.J. Pierzynski.blurb: Pierzynski caught Mark Buehrle's 2007 no-hitter and Philip Humber's 2012 perfect game. A 1994 Twins third-round pick, he won the 2005 World Series with the White Sox and finished with 2,043 hits and 188 home runs.

A.J. Burnett.blurb: A.J. Burnett threw a no-hitter for the Marlins on May 12, 2001, a 3-0 win over San Diego, despite walking nine. He pitched 17 seasons, 1999 to 2015, and won the 2009 World Series with the Yankees.

Big Jeff Pfeffer.blurb: Big Jeff Pfeffer threw a 6-0 no-hitter against Cincinnati on May 8, 1907, for Boston. He tore a tendon in his pitching arm that June and was never the same, finishing 31-39 over 1905-1911.

Carlos Marmol.blurb: In 2010, Carlos Marmol averaged 16.0 strikeouts per nine innings, 138 in 77⅔ innings, a record for pitchers with at least 50 innings. The Cubs reliever was named closer on August 18, 2009, and made the 2008 All-Star team.

J.T. Snow.blurb: Snow's 2004 was a comeback: after hitting .246 across 2002 and 2003, he batted .327 for the Giants. A first baseman, he won six straight Gold Gloves from 1995 to 2000, and his father was NFL player Jack Snow.

Barney Morris.blurb: Barney Morris, a right-handed pitcher, led the Negro Southern League in strikeouts in 1932, his debut season. He later pitched for the New York Cubans from 1942 to 1948, after earlier stops in the Negro leagues.

Emil Morales.blurb: Spanish shortstop Emil Morales signed with the Dodgers as an international free agent in January 2024, then won Dominican Summer League MVP honors that year, hitting .342 with 14 home runs. He began 2026 at Ontario and was promoted to Great Lakes on May 19.

Abner Uribe.blurb: Abner Uribe, a Dominican pitcher, signed with the Brewers in 2018 and debuted July 8, 2023, with a 1.76 ERA over about 30⅔ innings. In 2026 he appeared in four World Series games without allowing a run as the Brewers won the title.

Jonathan Loaisiga.blurb: Born in Managua, Loáisiga was the first Nicaraguan to play for the Yankees, debuting June 15, 2018, with five scoreless innings. On June 25, 2021, he became the first Yankees reliever to strike out four batters in one inning.

Rainiel Rodriguez.blurb: Born in 2007, this Dominican catcher said he signed with the Cardinals out of fondness for Albert Pujols, receiving $300,000 on April 1, 2024. He hit 20 home runs across 84 games in 2025 and was promoted to Double-A Springfield on May 11.

Eric O'Flaherty.blurb: Eric O'Flaherty became the first reliever in major league history to post an ERA below 1.00 in a season with at least 70 appearances, doing it for Atlanta in 2011. The lefty later had Tommy John surgery in 2013.

Jeff Francis.blurb: In 2007, Jeff Francis won 17 games in his first 200-inning season and led Colorado to the postseason. He was the first Canadian starting pitcher to win a postseason game, beating Philadelphia in NLDS Game 1.

Tyler Matzek.blurb: Matzek, an 11th overall pick in 2009 who struggled with control, posted a 2.57 ERA over 69 relief appearances for Atlanta in 2021. He won NLCS Game 6 against the Dodgers with two perfect innings, striking out the side as Atlanta clinched the pennant.

Luis De Leon.blurb: Orioles lefty Luis De León, signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2021, sits 95-98 mph and tops 99 with a plus slider. FanGraphs ranked him third in Baltimore's system in May 2026, flagging his unusual delivery and relief risk.

Josue Briceno.blurb: Josue Briceño became the Arizona Fall League's first Triple Crown winner and was named league MVP in 2024. The Tigers first baseman-catcher signed in 2022, was promoted to Double-A Erie in July 2025, and announced wrist tendon surgery in March 2026.

Carlos Martinez.blurb: Nicknamed "Tsunami," Carlos Martínez signed with the Cardinals in 2010 after Boston's 2009 deal was voided over questions about his name and date of birth. He debuted May 3, 2013, and was an All-Star in 2015 and 2017.

Austin Meadows.blurb: Austin Meadows was the ninth overall pick in 2013 and reached the majors with Pittsburgh in 2018. Traded to Tampa Bay that July, he made the 2019 All-Star team with 33 home runs and a .291 average.

Chris Archer.blurb: Archer struck out 252 batters in 2015, a Rays single-season record, and made the All-Star team that year. He led the majors with 19 losses in 2016 and was traded to Pittsburgh in July 2018.

Justin Nicolino.blurb: Nicolino was a Blue Jays second-round pick in 2010 and one of seven players sent to Miami in the 2012 Buehrle, Johnson and Reyes trade. He debuted June 20, 2015, with seven shutout innings for the Marlins.

Glenn Davis.blurb: Glenn Davis hit 31 homers with 101 RBIs and finished second in 1986 NL MVP voting for Houston. After 1990 he was traded to Baltimore for Steve Finley, Pete Harnisch and Curt Schilling, a deal many call the Orioles' worst.

Jake Latz.blurb: Lefty Jake Latz, a Toronto 11th-round pick in 2014 out of an Illinois high school, turned down a $1 million bonus and went to LSU. Texas drafted him in 2017's fifth round; he debuted in 2021 and made his first All-Star team in 2026.

Robert Suarez.blurb: Robert Suarez won two Japan Series titles with SoftBank (2018, 2019) and led the Central League in saves with Hanshin in 2020 and 2021. In 2025 he led the National League with 40 saves for San Diego.

Charlie Grimm.blurb: "Jolly Cholly" Grimm played banjo and sang for fans before games. A first baseman who led the NL in fielding percentage seven times between 1920 and 1933, he hit .290 and managed the Cubs to pennants in 1932, 1935 and 1945.

Bill Sweeney.blurb: Bill Sweeney hit .344 with 99 RBI for the 1912 Boston Braves, his best year alongside 1911. He played 1907 to 1914 for Boston and the Cubs, collecting 1,004 hits, and later coached Boston College baseball in 1916 and 1917.

Sam Wise.blurb: Shortstop Sam Wise made a league-leading 88 errors in 1883, yet Boston won the pennant; in 1884 he led the National League in strikeouts. Cincinnati's failed bid to stop him breaking his contract was pro baseball's first court case.

Clay Holmes.blurb: Clay Holmes, a ninth-round Pirates pick in 2011, became the Yankees' closer in 2022 and set a franchise record for consecutive scoreless appearances. He made the All-Star team in 2022 and 2024, then moved to starting with the Mets.

Mike Grady.blurb: Grady was best known for a story he told for years, that he committed four errors on one play, though no contemporaneous record exists. The catcher hit .363 as a Phillies rookie in 1894 and played until 1906.

Damaso Marte.blurb: Marté's 2003 season was a standout: a 1.58 ERA with 11 saves and 87 strikeouts for the White Sox. He won Game 3 of the 2005 World Series with 1 2/3 hitless innings, then pitched for the champion 2009 Yankees.

Lefty O'Doul.blurb: Lefty O'Doul began as a pitcher but became a hitter, winning batting titles in 1929 (.398, with 254 hits) and 1932 (.368). His .349 career average ranks fourth all-time. He later helped build professional baseball in Japan.

Jim Brown.blurb: Catcher Jim Brown played for the Chicago American Giants, who won five Negro National League pennants with him and the 1926 and 1927 Negro League World Series. He managed them in 1929-1930 and hit .292 in nine games in 1931.

Marc Rzepczynski.blurb: Nicknamed "Scrabble," Marc Rzepczynski was a lefty reliever on the 2011 champion Cardinals, striking out three of four batters faced in two World Series games. He later posted a 2.74 ERA in 73 games for Cleveland in 2014.

Todd Walker.blurb: Walker was a second baseman who hit five postseason home runs for the 2003 Red Sox, still a franchise record. That year he hit .283 with 13 homers and a career-high 85 RBIs, and tied the Orioles with a ninth-inning homer.

Frank Snyder.blurb: Frank "Pancho" Snyder, a strong-armed catcher, was a player or coach on every New York Giants club that won a pennant between 1921 and 1937. His 16 major league seasons, 1912 to 1927, began and ended with the St. Louis Cardinals.

Joe Harris.blurb: Joe Harris signed a 1918 letter "Sergeant Moon," and suffered a skull fracture when an ambulance overturned in France. He hit .375 for Cleveland in 1919 and .440 with three home runs for Washington in the 1925 World Series.

Wilson Alvarez.blurb: Wilson Álvarez no-hit Baltimore on August 11, 1991, in his second major-league start, the first Venezuelan pitcher to do so. A 1994 All-Star with the White Sox, he finished with 102-92 in 14 seasons.

Steve Sax.blurb: Steve Sax won 1982 National League Rookie of the Year with the Dodgers and set a team rookie record with 49 steals. He stole 56 in 1983, hit .332 in 1986, and was an All-Star with the Yankees in 1989.

Marquis Grissom.blurb: Grissom caught the final out of the 1995 World Series for Atlanta. He led the majors in stolen bases in 1991 (76) and 1992 (78) with Montreal, and won four Gold Gloves from 1993 to 1996.

Freddy Galvis.blurb: Galvis debuted on Opening Day 2012 at second base, the first Phillies player to do so in 42 years. He became their shortstop, played all 162 games in 2017, and hit 18 home runs for Toronto in 2019.

Mark Davis.blurb: Mark Davis won the 1989 NL Cy Young Award as a Padres reliever, going 1.85 ERA and leading the league with 44 saves. A left-hander, he pitched from 1980 to 1997 for six teams.

Hector Carrasco.blurb: Reliever Hector Carrasco, from the Dominican Republic, debuted with the Reds in 1994. On April 15, 2000, he gave up Cal Ripken's 3,000th hit. His best year was 2005 for Washington: 5-4, 2.04 ERA.

Carl Lundgren.blurb: Carl Lundgren's 1907 for the Cubs: 18 wins, 207 innings without allowing a home run, seven shutouts and a 1.17 ERA. He later coached Michigan and then Illinois (1921 until his death in 1934), winning eight Big Ten titles combined.

Charlie O'Brien.blurb: O'Brien adapted a hockey-style goalie mask for catching after foul-tip headaches, and the helmet-style mask later spread widely. In 1989 Chris Bosio asked for him as his personal catcher, and he won a 1995 World Series with Atlanta.

George Harper.blurb: Outfielder George Harper hit .303 with 91 home runs in 1,073 games between 1916 and 1929. On September 20, 1928, he homered three times in one game against the Giants, and he played in that year's World Series for the Cardinals.

Jonny Gomes.blurb: Jonny Gomes played outfield in the majors from 2003 through 2015 for seven clubs, including the Rays, Reds, Athletics, Red Sox and Braves. He is the Arizona Diamondbacks' minor league outfield and baserunning coordinator.

Robin Ventura.blurb: Robin Ventura hit a 58-game college hitting streak at Oklahoma State in 1987, then won Olympic gold in 1988. A six-time Gold Glove third baseman, he hit two grand slams in one game on September 4, 1995.

Josh Willingham.blurb: On July 27, 2009, Willingham hit two grand slams in one game for Washington. In 2012 he hit a career-high 35 home runs for the Twins and won the American League outfield Silver Slugger Award.

Bob Allison.blurb: Allison won 1959 AL Rookie of the Year with 30 home runs. On July 18, 1962, he and Harmon Killebrew became the first teammates to hit grand slams in the same inning. His diving catch in the 1965 World Series drew Killebrew's praise.

Trei Cruz.blurb: Trei Cruz is the son of José Cruz Jr. A third-round pick from Rice in 2020, the switch-hitter batted .279/.411/.456 at Erie and Toledo in 2025, and FanGraphs' February 2026 Tigers list ranked him 32nd.

Dave LaRoche.blurb: Dave LaRoche was best known for his own eephus pitch, which he called "La Lob." Closing for Cleveland, he saved 17 games in 1975 and 21 in 1976, when he made the All-Star team.

Matt Garza.blurb: Matt Garza threw the first no-hitter in Rays history, beating Detroit on July 26, 2010. Two years earlier he was MVP of the 2008 ALCS, winning Game 7 against Boston. Chicago traded for him in January 2011.

Jose Rijo.blurb: Rijo was MVP of the 1990 World Series, winning Game 4 for the Reds with 8⅓ innings of one-run ball. In 1993 he won 14 games and led the league in strikeouts; in 1994 he was 9-6 with a 3.08 ERA.

Shawn Green.blurb: On May 23, 2002, Shawn Green of the Dodgers hit four home runs, a double and a single at Miller Park for 19 total bases, a mark no other player has reached. Across 1993 to 2007 he hit 328 homers.

Carlos Gomez.blurb: Nicknamed "Go-Go" by Twins manager Ron Gardenhire in 2008, Carlos Gómez hit for the cycle that May and later won the 2013 NL Gold Glove in center field with Milwaukee, the first Brewer to do so since Robin Yount in 1982.

Jason Varitek.blurb: Jason Varitek is one of only three men to play in a championship game of the Little League, College and Major League World Series. The switch-hitting catcher spent all 15 seasons, 1997-2011, with Boston, winning in 2004 and 2007.

Chuck Finley.blurb: Chuck Finley, a 6-foot-6 lefty, won 200 games and struck out 2,610 batters across 1986 to 2002. He spent 14 years with the Angels, holding team records for starts (379), wins (165) and innings pitched (2,675).

Ryan Waldschmidt.blurb: Waldschmidt tore his ACL during a Cape Cod League stint, then hit 14 home runs for Kentucky in 2024 and went 31st overall to Arizona. He debuted May 8, 2026, and hit his first homer July 22.

Andrew Bailey.blurb: Bailey, a Wagner College product taken by Oakland in 2006, won the 2009 AL Rookie of the Year Award with 26 saves and a 1.84 ERA. He was an All-Star in 2009 and 2010 and later became Red Sox pitching coach.

Carter Jensen.blurb: Carter Jensen, a third-round pick from Park Hill High in Missouri in 2021, debuted with the Royals in September, hitting three homers in 20 games. FanGraphs' April 2026 Royals list ranked him first, projecting a power-and-OBP catcher.

Bobby Lowe.blurb: On May 30, 1894, Boston's Bobby Lowe hit four home runs in one game against Cincinnati, with 17 total bases, a record then. He had gone 0-for-6 that morning. Boston won 20-11.

Sean Casey.blurb: Sean Casey was nicknamed "The Mayor" for his friendly, outgoing style. The lefty-hitting first baseman batted .302 over 12 seasons, made three All-Star teams with the Reds (1999, 2001, 2004), and hit .529 in the 2006 World Series.

Marcus Giles.blurb: Giles was a right-handed second baseman who made the 2003 All-Star Game and hit 49 doubles that year, a Braves single-season record. He played for Atlanta from 2001 to 2006, and his older brother Brian was an outfielder.

Stu Miller.blurb: Reliever Stu Miller baffled hitters with a changeup writers compared to a moth or butterfly, helped by a head snap he said was involuntary. He was relief ace for two pennant winners during a 16-year major league career.

Tom Williams.blurb: Nicknamed "Cyclone," Tom Williams threw two no-hitters for Morris Brown College in 1914, then went 13-2 for Rube Foster's Chicago American Giants in 1917. In the Negro National League's first season, 1920, he went 12-4 with a 1.83 ERA.

Tyler O'Neill.blurb: Canadian outfielder Tyler O'Neill won National League Gold Glove awards in left field in 2020 and 2021 with the Cardinals. He hit 34 home runs in 2021 and 31 for Boston in 2024.

Alec Burleson.blurb: Alec Burleson led the majors in RBI in 2026 for the Cardinals. A second-round pick from East Carolina in 2020, he debuted in 2022, became a regular in 2023, and won a Silver Slugger as a utility player in 2025.

Jurrangelo Cijntje.blurb: Cijntje is a Curaçaoan switch pitcher who can throw proficiently with either arm. Mississippi State's second-team All-American in 2024, he went 15th overall to Seattle that year and was traded to St. Louis in February 2026.

Frankie Pytlak.blurb: Pytlak set a major-league record by handling 575 consecutive chances without an error, from September 1938 to September 1940, passing Gabby Hartnett's 452. The Buffalo native caught for Cleveland from 1932 to 1940 and hit .321 in 1936.

Tim Salmon.blurb: Nicknamed King Fish, Tim Salmon spent his entire 1992 to 2006 career with the Angels. He helped them win the 2002 World Series and retired with a then-franchise-record 299 home runs, later passed by Mike Trout.

Jose Lima.blurb: Showman Jose Lima's rally cry was "It's Lima Time!" He went 21-10 with a 3.58 ERA for the 1999 Astros, his only All-Star year. His career mark was 89-102, and he died in 2010 at age 37.

Tony Fossas.blurb: Tony Fossas was a LOOGY, a left-handed one-out guy: in 166 of his 567 games he faced just one batter. Born in Havana, he left Cuba as a boy in 1968 and pitched in the majors from 1988 through 1999.

Slade Cecconi.blurb: Cecconi was drafted 33rd overall by Arizona in 2020 out of Miami and debuted in 2023. Traded with a draft pick to Cleveland for Josh Naylor in December 2024, he went 7-7 with a 4.30 ERA in 23 starts in 2025.

Drake Baldwin.blurb: Atlanta catcher Drake Baldwin won 2025 National League Rookie of the Year after starting on Opening Day, hitting .274 with 19 home runs and 80 RBI in 124 games. A third-round pick from Missouri State in 2022, he made his first All-Star team in 2026.

Jesse Orosco.blurb: Jesse Orosco pitched in 1,252 games, more than any other major-league pitcher, across 24 seasons from 1979 to 2003. He was on the mound for the final out of Game 7 of the 1986 World Series for the Mets.

Ron Hansen.blurb: Ron Hansen turned an unassisted triple play for the Washington Senators on July 30, 1968, against Cleveland, the first in the majors in 41 years. He had won AL Rookie of the Year in 1960 with Baltimore.

Dan Quisenberry.blurb: Dan Quisenberry, an undrafted submariner, set the major-league record with 45 saves in 1983 and finished with 244. He walked just 1.4 batters per nine innings and helped Kansas City reach the World Series in 1980 and 1985.

John Maine.blurb: As a 2006 Mets rookie, Maine threw a complete-game shutout against Houston. In 2007 he went 15-10 with 180 strikeouts and struck out 14 over 7⅔ scoreless innings against Florida on September 29.

Greg Gagne.blurb: On October 4, 1986, Gagne hit two inside-the-park home runs in one game against the White Sox. A defensive standout at shortstop, he played on the Twins' 1987 and 1991 World Series winners and homered in Game One of 1991.

Carlos Zambrano.blurb: Nicknamed El Toro and Big Z, Carlos Zambrano was a three-time All-Star who led the Cubs in wins above replacement during the 2000s. The Venezuelan right-hander was famously feisty, often throwing at hitters and arguing with umpires.

Bill North.blurb: Switch-hitting center fielder Bill North led the American League in steals in 1974 with 54, then led the majors in 1976 with 75 for Oakland. He won two World Series rings with the A's, in 1973 and 1974.

Hunter Greene.blurb: In his second major league start, April 17, 2022, Hunter Greene threw 39 pitches at 100 mph or faster, a major league record. The Reds took him second overall in the 2017 draft, and he made the 2024 All-Star team.

Dan Spillner.blurb: Bill James called Spillner the worst-hitting pitcher of the 1970s; he batted .077 for his career. On the mound, he went 12-10 with a 2.49 ERA and 21 saves as a Cleveland reliever in 1982.

Jeff Francoeur.blurb: Nicknamed "Frenchy," Jeff Francoeur hit .360 with a 1.067 OPS in his first 37 games after his July 2005 debut, earning a Sports Illustrated cover calling him "The Natural." He won a Gold Glove in 2007.

Roger Wolff.blurb: Roger Wolff threw his knuckleball with an unorthodox three-finger grip, and in 1945 he led the Washington Senators with a career-high 20 wins. A skilled butcher from Chester, Illinois, he started throwing the pitch as a boy.

Jorge Posada.blurb: Jorge Posada played 17 seasons for the Yankees, 1995-2011, on five World Series champions, and won five Silver Sluggers. His best year was 2007, hitting .338 with 90 RBIs; he finished with 275 career home runs.

Sonny Gray.blurb: Sonny Gray was Oakland's first-round pick from Vanderbilt in 2011 and debuted in 2013. He was an All-Star in 2015, 2019 and 2023, and finished second in 2023 American League Cy Young voting.

Bob Fothergill.blurb: Nicknamed "Fatty," Fothergill reportedly did a front flip onto home plate after a Fenway Park homer. He hit .325 over 12 seasons, including .359 for the 1927 Tigers, and set a pinch-hit record of 76.

Craig Reynolds.blurb: Reynolds was the only shortstop picked for both leagues' All-Star teams in consecutive seasons, with the Mariners in 1978 and the Astros in 1979. On May 16, 1981, he tied the major-league record with three triples in one game.

Lee Thomas.blurb: Lee Thomas batted .285 with 24 homers for the expansion 1961 Angels, then made the 1962 All-Star team with career highs of .290, 26 homers and 104 RBI. He later served as Phillies general manager.

Sammy Sosa.blurb: In 1990, Sammy Sosa hit .233 with 15 home runs and 32 steals for the White Sox. He later became the only man to hit 60 homers three times, won the 1998 MVP, and finished with 609 home runs.

Sandy Alomar Sr..blurb: Sandy Alomar Sr. played 648 consecutive games for the Angels between 1969 and 1973, earning the nickname "Iron Pony." The switch-hitting second baseman made the 1970 All-Star team and fathered Sandy Jr. and Hall of Famer Roberto.

John Anderson.blurb: Born in Sarpsborg, Norway, "Honest John" Anderson earned the nickname by rarely protesting umpires' calls. In 1901 for Milwaukee he hit .330 with 46 doubles, an American League record for a switch-hitter that stood over 100 years.

George Lombard Jr..blurb: Yankees shortstop George Lombard Jr., a 2023 first-round pick, debuted on August 4, 2026 with a solo home run in a 2-0 win over the Cardinals. On September 9 he hit his first grand slam, against the Rockies.

Ed Holley.blurb: Ed Holley pitched with a sidearm delivery during four National League seasons: the Cubs in 1928, then the Phillies and Pirates from 1932 to 1934. He went 25–40 with a 4.40 ERA and 169 strikeouts. Born in Benton, Kentucky, he died in 1986.

Alex Vesia.blurb: Alex Vesia went undrafted in 2014, pitched at Cal State East Bay, and was a 17th-round Marlins pick in 2018. Traded to the Dodgers in 2021, he went 5-0 with a 2.15 ERA in 63 games in 2022.

Charlie Smith.blurb: Charles "Chino" Smith batted .464 with 23 home runs for the 1929 New York Lincoln Giants, leading the American Negro League. Satchel Paige called him one of the two most dangerous hitters in Negro league history. He died of yellow fever in 1932.

Larry Gardner.blurb: Gardner won four World Series, three with Boston (1912, 1915, 1916) and one with Cleveland in 1920. His sacrifice fly ended the 1912 Series. He hit a career-best .319 with 120 RBIs in 1921.

Shawn Armstrong.blurb: Armstrong, an 18th-round Cleveland pick in 2011, debuted August 8, 2015. In 2023 he posted a 1.38 ERA with 54 strikeouts in 52 innings over 39 appearances for Tampa Bay, returning June 3 from the 60-day injured list.

Gary Sheffield.blurb: Gary Sheffield's swing was said to be quick enough to turn on a .38-caliber bullet. He led the NL in batting in 1992 and hit 509 homers over 22 seasons, playing for eight teams.

JJ Wetherholt.blurb: JJ Wetherholt hit .449 with 16 homers at West Virginia in 2023, earning Big 12 Player of the Year. St. Louis took him seventh overall in 2024; he homered for his first hit on March 26, 2026.

Chris B. Young.blurb: In 2007, Chris Young became the first rookie in major league history with 30 home runs and 25 stolen bases. The Diamondbacks outfielder made the 2010 NL All-Star team, and later played for Oakland, the Mets, Yankees, Red Sox and Angels.

Jim Todd.blurb: Todd was Oakland's secondary closer behind Rollie Fingers in 1975, setting career bests with 8 wins, 12 saves and a 2.29 ERA. He even received five AL MVP votes that year, as the A's won the West.

Fergie Jenkins.blurb: Fergie Jenkins was the first pitcher with more than 3,000 career strikeouts and fewer than 1,000 walks, finishing with 3,192 strikeouts and 997 walks. The first Canadian-born Hall of Famer, from Chatham, Ontario, he starred for the Cubs from 1966 to 1973.

Pedro Feliciano.blurb: Nicknamed "Perpetual Pedro," Puerto Rican pitcher Pedro Feliciano worked nine major-league seasons, all with the New York Mets (2002–04, 2006–10, 2013), plus 2005 in Japan with the Fukuoka SoftBank Hawks.

Dave Henderson.blurb: Dave "Hendu" Henderson is best remembered for a two-out, two-strike ninth-inning home run in Game 5 of the 1986 ALCS. He helped his teams reach the World Series four times, winning with Oakland in 1989, and later broadcast Mariners games.

Diamond M. Pipkins.blurb: Robert "Diamond" Pipkins was a left-handed Negro league pitcher, also called "Black Diamond." Born in Adams County, Mississippi, in 1907, he debuted with the Birmingham Black Barons in 1929, played for the Cleveland Cubs in 1931, and finished back in Birmingham in 1942.

Adam Kennedy.blurb: Kennedy hit three home runs in Game 5 of the 2002 ALCS against Minnesota and was named series MVP. The Angels second baseman then won the World Series that year, hitting .312 in the regular season.

Tom Herr.blurb: In 1985, Herr hit .302 with 8 home runs and 110 RBI for the Cardinals, the first player since George Kell in 1950 to drive in 100 with fewer than 10 homers. The switch-hitter made the All-Star team.

Walker Buehler.blurb: Walker Buehler earned the series-clinching save in the Dodgers' 2024 World Series win, after also winning in 2020. A Vanderbilt product and 2015 first-round pick, he made his debut in 2017 and was an All-Star in 2019 and 2021.

Maury Wills.blurb: Maury Wills stole 104 bases in 1962, a record then, and won the NL MVP. In 1965 he stole 94, hit .286 and scored 92 runs as the Dodgers won the pennant. He finished with 586 career steals.

Mike Lamb.blurb: Mike Lamb hit the first World Series home run in Astros history, in 2005. The Yankees acquired him in February 2004 and traded him to Houston that March, before he played a game for New York. He attended Cal State Fullerton.

Pablo Sandoval.blurb: Nicknamed "The Panda," Sandoval hit .315 with 23 home runs in 2011, made the All-Star team, and hit for the cycle on September 15. A year later he hit three homers in World Series Game 1.

Claude Osteen.blurb: Claude Osteen debuted at 17 and went on to win 196 games. In Game Three of the 1965 World Series, with the Dodgers down two games to none, he threw a 4-0 shutout, and Los Angeles won in seven.

Troy Glaus.blurb: Troy Glaus won World Series MVP honors in 2002 and was a four-time All-Star who played for the Angels from 1998 to 2004. He also won baseball bronze at the 1996 Olympics with the U.S. team, after lettering at UCLA.

Cristian Guzman.blurb: Cristian Guzman's speed was the focus of a 2001 Twins commercial in the "Get to Know 'Em" series. He led the AL in triples three times, but as a boy in the Dominican Republic he preferred basketball to baseball.

Juan Padron.blurb: Juan Padrón, a left-hander born in Key West in 1892, pitched in the Negro leagues from 1915 to 1926, including 1924 and 1925 with the Chicago American Giants. In 1931 he threw a ten-inning complete game for a Grand Rapids All-Star team against the Cardinals.

Ken Williams.blurb: In 1922 Williams became the first major leaguer with 30 homers and 30 steals, leading the American League with 39 homers and 155 RBIs. He also hit three home runs in a game on April 22.

Bobby Bonilla.blurb: Bonilla was a six-time All-Star with three Silver Sluggers as a Pirate, and won the 1997 World Series with Florida. His 1999 Mets buyout pays him $1,193,248.20 every July 1 from 2011 through 2035.

Travis Bazzana.blurb: Australian second baseman Travis Bazzana was the first overall pick of the 2024 draft by the Guardians. He debuted in the majors in 2026 and made his first All-Star Game the same year.

Mark Vientos.blurb: Nicknamed "Swaggy V," Mark Vientos hit 27 home runs for the 2024 Mets. In that postseason he drove in 14 runs, a Mets record, including a grand slam in Game 2 of the NLCS against the Dodgers.

Mark Huismann.blurb: Reliever Mark Huismann pitched in the majors from 1983 to 1991 but usually spent more time in the minors. In 1985 he set an American Association record with 33 saves for Omaha and won the league's Most Valuable Pitcher Award.

Devon White.blurb: Born in Kingston, Jamaica, White was a human highlight reel in center field, with seven Gold Gloves. His speed helped Toronto win the 1993 World Series; in the 1993 ALCS he hit .444, with 12 hits.

Tully Sparks.blurb: Right-hander Tully Sparks pitched 12 major league years with a 2.82 career ERA over 314 games, including three exceptional seasons from 1905 through 1907. He was born December 12, 1874, in Etna, Georgia.

Carlos Lagrange.blurb: Pitcher Carlos Lagrange signed with the Yankees as an international free agent in 2022. In June 2026 he moved to the bullpen, and on July 4 was shut down six weeks with a capsular sprain in his throwing shoulder.

Johnny Dickshot.blurb: Nicknamed "Ugly," Johnny Dickshot earned the name by declaring himself the ugliest man in baseball. The Waukegan, Illinois left fielder reached the majors with Pittsburgh in 1936 and played for the White Sox in 1944 and 1945.

Sean Marshall.blurb: Sean Marshall, nicknamed "Big Smooth," was a sixth-round Cubs pick in 2003 out of Virginia Commonwealth. He made 24 starts as a rookie in 2006 and later pitched for Cincinnati. His twin brother Brian also played baseball.

Rats Henderson.blurb: Henderson pitched in the Negro leagues from 1922 to 1931, mostly for the Bacharach Giants. He tied Nip Winters for the Eastern Colored League lead in wins in 1923 and led it in strikeouts in 1923 and 1925.

Josh Vitters.blurb: The Cubs drafted Vitters third overall in 2007. He reached the majors August 5, 2012, and hit his first home run August 20, finishing that year at .121. He retired from pro baseball in June 2021.

Al Grabowski.blurb: Al Grabowski was a Cardinals pitcher who hit far better than most of his kind, batting .327 (16-for-49) with four doubles, a triple and six RBI across 39 games pitched in his brief major league stint.

Phil Garner.blurb: Nicknamed "Scrap Iron" for his gritty play, Phil Garner hit .500 (12-for-24) in the 1979 World Series for the Pirates. He was an All-Star in 1976 and 1980, and later managed Houston to its first pennant in 2005.

Bobby Byrne.blurb: Bobby Byrne, a scrappy, pint-sized Pirates third baseman, stole second, third and home in one inning on June 10, 1911. In 1910 he led the National League with 43 doubles and hit .296.

Vinnie Chulk.blurb: Chulk, a relief pitcher of Cuban heritage, pitched in the majors for Toronto, San Francisco, Cleveland and Milwaukee. He joined Japan's Hiroshima Toyo Carp in 2010, debuting August 1, and made his last MLB appearance on May 18, 2012.

Johnny Kling.blurb: Catcher Johnny Kling, called arguably one of the most overlooked stars of the Deadball Era, was a key part of the Chicago Cubs dynasty of 1906 to 1910. At 14, in 1890, he pitched the Haverlys to an amateur league title.

Tony Gwynn Jr..blurb: Tony Gwynn Jr., son of Baseball Hall of Famer Tony Gwynn, played outfield for the Brewers, Padres, Dodgers and Phillies. He works as a Padres radio broadcaster and afternoon sports talk host.

Mason Miller.blurb: Mason Miller threw the fastest pitch in All-Star Game history, 103.6 mph, as a 2024 rookie closer for Oakland. Traded to San Diego in July 2025, he tied for the NL lead with 38 saves in 2026.

Fred Pfeffer.blurb: Fred Pfeffer, nicknamed "Dandelion," was one of the last barehanded fielders and the first player to foil a double steal by cutting off the catcher's throw. He played second base from 1882 to 1897, mostly for Chicago.

Roger Mason.blurb: Mason's first Tigers appearance, September 4, 1984, was eight innings of relief, a Tigers record for a nine-inning game. He pitched for seven major-league teams over nine seasons, including the 1993 Phillies in the World Series.

Felnin Celesten.blurb: Felnin Celesten, a switch-hitting shortstop signed out of the Dominican Republic in 2023, lost nearly all of that year to a hamstring tear, then played only 32 games in 2024 amid a wrist issue that required surgery. FanGraphs' June 2025 Mariners list ranked him sixth.

Josh Tomlin.blurb: Josh Tomlin was known for his low walk rate. Drafted by Cleveland in the 19th round in 2006, he debuted in 2010, lost the 2016 World Series with the Indians, then won the 2021 title with Atlanta.

Aaron Loup.blurb: Lefty Aaron Loup retired all six batters he faced in his 2012 debut for Toronto, and was named the Blue Jays' Rookie of the Year. In 2013 he went 4-6 with a 2.47 ERA and 53 strikeouts.

Joe Ryan.blurb: Joe Ryan was pitching for Team USA at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, winning silver, when Tampa Bay traded him to the Twins in July 2021. He debuted that September and was an All-Star in 2025 and 2026.

Ed Karger.blurb: Karger threw a seven-inning no-hitter for the 1907 Cardinals, retiring all 21 batters in a 4-0 win over Boston on August 11 that ended by prior agreement. That year the lefty went 15-19 with a 2.04 ERA and six shutouts.

Jon Garland.blurb: Jon Garland, a 6-foot-6 righty from Granada Hills, California, went 10th overall in the 1997 draft to the Cubs, turning down a USC scholarship. In June 1998 Chicago traded him to the White Sox for Matt Karchner.

Duffy Dyer.blurb: A light-hitting, good-fielding catcher, Duffy Dyer became a Mets fan favorite with a pinch-hit three-run homer on Opening Day 1969. In 1972 he set career highs of 94 games, 8 homers and 36 RBIs.

Dick Rudolph.blurb: At just 5-foot-9½ and 160 pounds, Dick Rudolph was a large part of George Stallings' "Big Three" as the 1914 Boston Braves won a miraculous pennant and swept the World Series. He relied on a great curveball and spectacular control.

Tiny Bonham.blurb: Ernie Bonham was nicknamed "Tiny" despite standing 6'2" and weighing well over 200 pounds. One of the few masters of the forkball, an ancestor of the split-fingered fastball, he was born in 1913 in Ione, California.

Al Hrabosky.blurb: Nicknamed "the Mad Hungarian," Al Hrabosky led the National League with 22 saves in 1975 and won The Sporting News Fireman of the Year. He pitched for the Cardinals, Royals and Braves across 13 seasons.

Andres Torres.blurb: Andrés Torres was a track star at Miami-Dade Community College who did not begin playing baseball until later. The switch-hitting center fielder was drafted by Detroit in 1998, debuted in 2002, and later played for the Rangers, Mets and Giants.

Darryl Strawberry.blurb: The Mets took Darryl Strawberry first overall in 1980 straight out of high school. He won 1983 NL Rookie of the Year, then hit 39 homers with 104 RBIs and 36 steals in 1987, and collected four World Series rings.

Eric Chavez.blurb: Eric Chavez won six straight Gold Gloves at third base (2001–2006) with the Oakland Athletics, adding a Silver Slugger in 2002. He later played for the Yankees and Diamondbacks, and the Athletics inducted him into their Hall of Fame in 2022.

Josh Bell.blurb: Josh Bell's $5 million signing bonus in 2011, a record for a player taken outside the first round, bought him out of a Texas scholarship. The Pirates' second-round pick played for them 2016 through 2020 and was an All-Star in 2019.

Chase Burns.blurb: Chase Burns signed with the Reds in 2024 for a then-record $9.25 million bonus after setting Wake Forest's single-season strikeout record with 191. In his June 2025 debut he struck out the first five Yankees he faced.

Broderick Perkins.blurb: Broderick Perkins was a first baseman whose only full-time season came in 1982, when he played 125 games for the Padres and batted .271. That year San Diego traded him and Juan Eichelberger to Cleveland for Ed Whitson.

Chris Hoiles.blurb: Chris Hoiles hit two grand slams in one game for Baltimore on August 14, 1998. His best year came in 1993, when he hit .310 with 29 homers and a 1.001 OPS.

Paul DeJong.blurb: Paul DeJong, a fourth-round Cardinals pick in 2015, led National League shortstops in home runs with 25 in 2017. In 2019 he made the All-Star team and led NL shortstops in assists, putouts and double plays.

Bobby Bonds.blurb: Bobby Bonds was the first player with more than two 30-homer, 30-steal seasons, doing it a record five times, matched only by son Barry. A right fielder from 1968 to 1981, he hit a then-record 35 leadoff homers.

Cedric Mullins.blurb: Cedric Mullins became the first Oriole to join the 30-30 club in 2021, hitting 30 homers and stealing 30 bases. That year he was an All-Star starter and won a Silver Slugger.

Ryan Zeferjahn.blurb: University of Kansas right-hander Ryan Zeferjahn was a third-round Red Sox pick in 2019. Traded to the Angels on July 30, 2024, he debuted for them on August 25, then was sent to the Cubs on August 3, 2026.

Austin Gomber.blurb: Austin Gomber came to Colorado in the February 2021 trade that sent Nolan Arenado to St. Louis. In 2021 he went 9-9 with a 4.53 ERA in 23 starts before a back stress fracture ended his season.

Tim Murnane.blurb: Tim Murnane, likely born in Ireland, played first base and outfield in the majors, managed one season as a player-manager, then spent three decades as the leading baseball writer at The Boston Globe until his death in 1917.

Gene Richards.blurb: Gene Richards set a modern-day major-league rookie record with 56 stolen bases in 1977. That August he stood at first base as boyhood idol Lou Brock broke Ty Cobb's career steals record. Richards was born in Monticello, South Carolina, in 1953.

Orlando Cabrera.blurb: Orlando Cabrera arrived in Boston in the 2004 trade that sent Nomar Garciaparra to the Cubs, hitting .379 in that year's ALCS against the Yankees. A Colombian shortstop, he won two Gold Gloves, the first in 2001 with Montreal.

Ryan Madson.blurb: Ryan Madson is third all-time in postseason pitching appearances, behind only Mariano Rivera and Kenley Jansen. He won World Series titles with the Phillies in 2008 and the Royals in 2015, and his sinker and four-seamer averaged 95 mph.

Nelson Chittum.blurb: Nelson Chittum pitched only 40 major-league games, but in 1959 the Red Sox reliever went 3-0 after Boston called him up from Minneapolis, with a team-best 1.19 ERA in 21 August and September appearances.

Nate Pearson.blurb: Nate Pearson, the 28th overall pick of the 2017 draft by Toronto, debuted July 29, 2020 with five scoreless innings against Washington. On September 4, 2024, he pitched the eighth inning of a combined no-hitter with Shota Imanaga and Porter Hodge.

John Hiller.blurb: John Hiller won 17 games and lost 14 in 1974, all in relief, for a last-place Tigers team. A Toronto native, he missed all of 1971 after heart attacks yet returned, pitching for Detroit until retiring in 1980.

Ian Desmond.blurb: Ian Desmond won three straight NL shortstop Silver Sluggers from 2012 to 2014. In 2016 with Texas he hit .285 with 22 home runs and made the AL All-Star team.

Johnny Gooch.blurb: Johnny Gooch, a Tennessee catcher, played 805 games over 11 seasons between 1921 and 1933, batting .280 with just seven homers and 293 RBIs. He skipped organized ball in 1917 and 1918 to help on the family farm.

CJ Abrams.blurb: CJ Abrams was part of the 2022 package the Padres sent Washington for Juan Soto. The sixth overall pick of 2019, he was a 2026 All-Star with 33 homers and 106 RBIs, both Nationals records for a shortstop.

Henry Blanco.blurb: Catcher Henry Blanco led National League catchers with 39 baserunners caught stealing in 1999, then with a 58.2 percent rate in 2000, the highest since 1982. He later won the 2016 World Series with the Cubs as a coach.

Ryan Howard.blurb: Ryan Howard was a 6-foot-4, 250-pound first baseman who produced tape-measure homers and line drives, but struck out in nearly a third of his at-bats. A freak injury later sapped his power. Born in St. Louis in 1979, he had a twin brother, Corey.

Harry Ford.blurb: Atlanta-born catcher Harry Ford plays internationally for Great Britain because both parents were born there. Seattle drafted him 12th overall in 2021; he debuted in September 2025 and was traded to the Nationals that December.

Bob Bowman.blurb: Bob Bowman was acclaimed the majors' top pinch-hitter in 1958, hitting .406 (13-for-32) for the Phillies, including a pinch two-run homer off Sandy Koufax. He also pitched five games in 1959, the most of any position player that year.

Tyler Rogers.blurb: Tyler Rogers throws an extreme sidearm delivery, with a 1.33-foot release point, the lowest in MLB. A 10th-round Giants pick in 2013, he led the NL in games pitched in 2020 and 2021, and led MLB with 81 games in 2025.

Matt Thornton.blurb: Matt Thornton, born in Three Rivers, Michigan, ranks second all-time in American League history with 182 holds. The pitcher played for the Mariners, White Sox, Red Sox, Yankees, Nationals and Padres.

Tanner Roark.blurb: Drafted in the 25th round in 2008, Tanner Roark reached Washington in 2013. In 2016 he posted career bests of 16 wins, a 2.83 ERA, 172 strikeouts and 210 innings.

Doug Mirabelli.blurb: Doug Mirabelli became a two-time World Series champion by doing what few catchers can: catching a knuckleball. Boston preferred him as Tim Wakefield's batterymate, and arranged a police escort to Fenway after reacquiring him from the Padres.

Joe Charboneau.blurb: "Super Joe" won 1980 AL Rookie of the Year, hitting .289 with 23 homers and 87 RBIs for Cleveland. A back injury ended it fast: his 201 career games are the fewest for a position-player Rookie of the Year.

Juan Cruz.blurb: On Opening Day 2003, Juan Cruz struck out six consecutive batters for the Cubs. His best year came in 2004 with Atlanta, going 6–2 with a 2.75 ERA in 50 relief appearances, with opponents hitting .159 with runners in scoring position.

Wilson Ramos.blurb: Wilson Ramos, nicknamed "the Buffalo," had four hits in his 2010 MLB debut, the only catcher since 1900 to do so. In 2011 he made Baseball America's All-Rookie Team, then was kidnapped in Venezuela that November and rescued after about 50 hours.

Jim Greengrass.blurb: Outfielder Jim Greengrass started 153 of the Redlegs' 155 games in left field in 1953, hitting 20 home runs and driving in 100. Phlebitis began troubling him in 1955, and his major-league career ended in 1956.

Mark Grace.blurb: Mark Grace collected 1,754 hits in the 1990s, more than any other player that decade. The Cubs first baseman won three Gold Gloves between 1992 and 1995 and led the National League with 51 doubles in 1995.

Jonathan Lucroy.blurb: Jonathan Lucroy set the catcher record of 53 doubles in 2014 and made All-Star teams that year and in 2016. On July 31, 2016, he was traded from Milwaukee to Texas.

Norm Siebern.blurb: Norm Siebern, a glasses-wearing left-handed hitter, split time between first base and the outfield for six major-league teams. He went to Kansas City in the Yankees' package for Roger Maris and was an All-Star first baseman for the Athletics and Orioles.

Miguel Tejada.blurb: Born in extreme poverty in the Dominican Republic, Miguel Tejada won an MVP award and two Silver Sluggers, with six All-Star appearances over a 16-year career. He lied about his age for years, claiming 1976 instead of 1974.

Buddy Rosar.blurb: Buddy Rosar once left the Yankees without permission to take a police exam and be there for his son's expected birth. A five-time All-Star catcher, he caught 147 straight games without an error and hit for the cycle in 1940.

Ben McDonald.blurb: LSU's 6-foot-7 "Big Ben" McDonald was an Olympic gold medalist and, reportedly, an experienced alligator wrestler. Some scouts called him the best amateur pitcher they had ever seen, and his selection first overall was seen as inevitable.

Victor Martinez.blurb: Switch-hitting catcher Victor Martinez won back-to-back minor league batting titles in 2001 and 2002, then caught for Cleveland. After hitting .207 in mid-June 2005, he batted .380 after the All-Star break and finished at .305 with 20 homers and 80 RBIs.

Jake Bauers.blurb: Jake Bauers hit for the cycle against the Detroit Tigers on June 14, 2019, playing for Cleveland. A seventh-round Padres pick in 2013, he debuted with the Rays in June 2018 and hit a walk-off homer against the Yankees that month.

Jack Clements.blurb: Jack Clements was the lone position player to debut in 1884 and still be active in the final year of the nineteenth century. A left-handed-throwing catcher, he developed a chest protector he inflated before every game and wore a sweater everywhere.

Richie Hebner.blurb: Richie Hebner spent offseasons working at a cemetery run by his father and brother. The lefty-hitting third baseman won the 1971 World Series with Pittsburgh, homering off Jim Palmer in Game 2, and hit 203 home runs over 1968 to 1985.

Nathan Eovaldi.blurb: Nathan Eovaldi has won World Series titles with two clubs, the Red Sox in 2018 and the Rangers in 2023. He debuted in 2011, was an All-Star in 2021 and 2023, and has also pitched for the Dodgers, Marlins, Yankees and Rays.

Asdrubal Cabrera.blurb: Asdrubal Cabrera turned an unassisted triple play against Toronto on May 12, 2008. In 2011 he made the All-Star team and won the Silver Slugger, hitting 25 homers, a Cleveland record for a shortstop.

Stan Lopata.blurb: Stan Lopata was the first National League catcher to wear glasses. A two-time all-star, he caught for the Phillies and Milwaukee Braves across 13 seasons, hitting .254 with 116 home runs in 853 games.

Orlando Hudson.blurb: Orlando Hudson was a second baseman known for spectacular lunging catches and diving stabs at grounders. He won his first American League Gold Glove in 2005 with Toronto, and played in the majors from 2002 to 2012.

Morgan Ensberg.blurb: Morgan Ensberg, a ninth-round pick in 1998, starred in 2005: .283 with 36 home runs and a career-high 101 RBI for the World Series-bound Astros, plus a Silver Slugger at third base.

Jack Lynch.blurb: Jack Lynch threw the first pitch in the first professional game played in Manhattan, at the Polo Grounds on September 29, 1880. In 1884 he and Tim Keefe led the Metropolitans to the pennant, though injury kept him out of the first World Series.

Steve Olin.blurb: Steve Olin's low side-arm delivery earned him "Yellow Submarine" from the Cleveland Stadium organist. He saved 29 games for the Indians in 1992 with a 2.34 ERA, and died in a boating accident on March 22, 1993, aged 27.

Roy White.blurb: Roy White grew up in Compton, California, playing a stuffed-sock version of baseball he called sock ball. He became a quiet leader for the Yankees, evolving from speedy utility player into the team's cleanup hitter and one of its top sluggers.

William Bell.blurb: William Bell went 93-47 in a 12-year Negro League pitching career between 1923 and 1937, sometimes playing outfield when not pitching. He added a 25-17 mark in Cuba and was a finalist on a 2006 Hall of Fame ballot.

Eury Perez.blurb: Dominican righty Eury Perez signed with the Marlins in 2019 and reached the majors in May 2023, going 5-6 with a 3.15 ERA in 19 starts. Tommy John surgery then ended his 2024 season; he returned in June 2025.

Brad Lidge.blurb: Brad Lidge, nicknamed "Lights Out", went a perfect 41-for-41 in save opportunities for the 2008 Phillies. That year he won the NL Rolaids Relief Man Award and Comeback Player of the Year, after becoming Houston's closer in 2004.

Ethan Holliday.blurb: Ethan Holliday, younger brother of Jackson and son of Matt, went fourth overall to the Rockies in the 2025 draft. His $9 million bonus was a record for a high school player.

Damon Berryhill.blurb: Damon Berryhill, a switch-hitting catcher, hit the game-winning three-run homer for the Braves in Game 1 of the 1992 World Series against Toronto. Earlier he hit .259 in 95 games for the 1988 Cubs and made the Topps All-Star Rookie roster.

Rich Gedman.blurb: Worcester, Massachusetts native Rich Gedman fulfilled a childhood dream catching for the Red Sox, the team he grew up rooting for, in parts of 11 seasons (1980-1990). A two-time All-Star, he also played for Houston and St. Louis.

Roger Repoz.blurb: Roger Repoz went 347 straight games and 894 at-bats without grounding into a double play from 1967 to 1970, a record for nonpitchers. He later hit 122 home runs in Japan.

Tony Scott.blurb: Tony Scott signed with Montreal as a 71st-round pick in 1969 and played center field in the majors from 1973 to 1984 for the Expos, Cardinals and Astros. In 1979 he set career highs with 37 stolen bases and 68 RBIs.

Carlos Baerga.blurb: Carlos Baerga hit home runs from both sides of the plate in one inning on April 8, 1993, in a 15-5 win over the Yankees. The day after the boating accident that killed Steve Olin and Tim Crews, he volunteered to be the Indians' spokesman.

Edwin Jackson.blurb: Edwin Jackson played for 14 MLB teams, more than any other player when he reached the Blue Jays in 2019. He was a 2009 All-Star, threw a no-hitter on June 25, 2010, and won the 2011 World Series with the Cardinals.

Lenny Dykstra.blurb: Lenny Dykstra hit game-winning NLCS homers: in 1986 Game Three for the Mets, a ninth-inning shot off Dave Smith, and in 1993 Game Five for the Phillies, a 10th-inning shot off Mark Wohlers.

Jose Hernandez.blurb: Jose Hernandez hit 20 home runs in the 1997-98 Puerto Rican winter league, breaking Orlando Cepeda's record for a Puerto Rican, and won league MVP. In 2001 he set career highs with 25 homers and 78 RBIs.

Max Lanier.blurb: Max Lanier led the National League in ERA in 1943 and won the clinching game of the 1944 World Series against the Browns. He pitched 14 big-league seasons for the Cardinals, Giants and Browns; his son Hal became an infielder and manager.

Riley O'Brien.blurb: Riley O'Brien's grandfather Johnny played six major-league seasons. The Cardinals reliever, drafted in 2017 out of the College of Idaho, earned his first win August 4, 2025, and his first save two days later.

Cal McVey.blurb: Cal McVey joined the 1869 Cincinnati Red Stockings, the youngest professional player of his time, on their unbeaten tour. He hit .431 in 1871, finishing second in the league's first batting race, and managed Baltimore in 1873.

Oliver Marcell.blurb: Nicknamed "Ghost," Oliver Marcell was considered by most the greatest fielding third baseman in the Negro leagues throughout the 1920s. He hit .379 for the 1922 Bacharach Giants. Hall of Famer Judy Johnson admitted Marcell was the better defender.

Jack Leathersich.blurb: A fifth-round Mets pick in 2011, lefty Jack Leathersich struck out 126 as a college senior. He debuted in 2015, then needed Tommy John surgery and finished with a 2.70 MLB ERA.

Jay Johnstone.blurb: Jay Johnstone was one of baseball's premier flakes, a prankster who once trapped Tommy Lasorda in the manager's room at Dodgertown by tying his doorknob to a tree. He still played 15 full seasons from 1966 to 1985, hitting 102 home runs.

Salomon Torres.blurb: Dominican righty Salomon Torres debuted with the Giants on August 29, 1993. On April 20, 2003, a Torres fastball hit Sammy Sosa in the head and shattered his helmet. He saved 28 games for Milwaukee in 2008.

Mike Tiernan.blurb: Mike Tiernan, dubbed Silent Mike for speaking so little on the field, stayed clean-shaven when mustaches were nearly required of the Giants. He arrived in New York in 1887, declined to join the Players League, and remained a Giants stalwart for over a decade.

Moises Alou.blurb: Moisés Alou was the son of famed first baseman and manager Felipe Alou. Over 17 MLB seasons from 1990 to 2008, he was a six-time All-Star, a two-time Silver Slugger winner and a 1997 World Series champion.

Casey Candaele.blurb: Casey Candaele's mother and her sister played in the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League, and the page calls Casey and his mother the only mother/son pair to both play professionally. The switch-hitting utility man finished fourth in 1987 NL Rookie of the Year voting.

Aaron Boone.blurb: Aaron Boone hit the walk-off home run that won the 2003 American League Championship Series for the Yankees. After 13 playing seasons from 1997 to 2009 and several years at ESPN, he became Yankees manager in 2018.

Eric Orze.blurb: Eric Orze was diagnosed with testicular and skin cancer while at New Orleans. The Mets drafted him in 2020, he debuted in July 2024, and he posted a 3.02 ERA for Tampa Bay in 2025.

Shaun Marcum.blurb: Shaun Marcum, a third-round Blue Jays pick in 2003, went 12-6 in 2007 and was the 2010 Opening Day starter. With Milwaukee he went 13-7 with a 3.54 ERA in 2011 and hit a grand slam on July 4.

Bartolo Colon.blurb: Bartolo Colón went from a fastball near 100 mph to a roly-poly cult hero nicknamed "Big Sexy." Over 21 major-league seasons he went 247-188 with a 4.12 ERA, and ranks first in wins by a pitcher born in Latin America.

Jack Aker.blurb: In 1966 Jack Aker set a major league record with 32 saves, going 8-4 with a 1.99 ERA for the Athletics. The Sporting News named him AL Fireman of the Year.

Rocky Colavito.blurb: On May 12, 1961, Detroit left fielder Rocky Colavito, a Bronx native and boyhood Yankees fan, went over the rail at Yankee Stadium after seeing his father scuffling with a fan who had been annoying Colavito's wife Carmen.

Eddie Bressoud.blurb: Houston took Eddie Bressoud first in the 1961 expansion draft, then traded him to the Red Sox for Don Buddin before he played for Houston. In 1962 he hit .277 with 14 homers, 40 doubles and 68 RBIs.

Vince Coleman.blurb: On June 1, 1986, Reds pitcher Chris Welsh threw over to first base seventeen times, a major-league record, trying to hold Vince Coleman. Coleman stole second anyway, his 27th steal of that season, and added 80 more before the year ended.

Mike Easler.blurb: Mike Easler was nicknamed "The Hit Man" and "Line Drive" for his hitting. Over 14 seasons, 1973 to 1987, he hit .293 and topped .300 four times, made the 1981 NL All-Star team with Pittsburgh and played for the Red Sox in 1984 and 1985.

J.P. Howell.blurb: J.P. Howell's velocity and breaking pitches improved when Tampa Bay moved him to the bullpen in 2008. He went 6-1 with a 2.22 ERA in 64 games, and pitched in the World Series that fall.

Shelby Miller.blurb: Shelby Miller was a first-round pick of the Cardinals in 2009 and Baseball America's top Cardinals prospect from 2009 to 2011. In May 2013 he threw his first complete-game shutout, a one-hitter against the Rockies.

Dick Groat.blurb: Dick Groat was a two-time All-American at both Duke basketball and baseball, and skipped the minors. He won the 1960 NL MVP, then hit .319 with 201 hits and a league-best 43 doubles for the 1963 Cardinals.

Lorenzo Cain.blurb: Lorenzo Cain, a Royals center fielder known for defensive acrobatics, won four Wilson Defensive Player of the Year Awards and three Fielding Bible Awards. He won the 2014 ALCS MVP and finished third in 2015 MVP voting.

Kelly Johnson.blurb: Kelly Johnson was the first player to appear in a game for all five American League East teams; Steve Pearce became the second in 2018. Primarily a second baseman, he played every position except pitcher, catcher and center field.

Roberto H. Hernandez.blurb: Roberto Hernandez, a Puerto Rico-born reliever, saved 326 games and was an All-Star in 1996 and 1999. He pitched his 1000th game in 2007, the 11th pitcher to do so.

Curry Foley.blurb: Curry Foley, born in Ireland, hit for the first cycle in major-league history in 1882. He pitched and played the field for Boston and Buffalo from 1879 to 1883, then retired with rheumatism; under the reserve rule he couldn't take a job in organized baseball.

Pat Neshek.blurb: Pat Neshek's funky submarine-sidearm delivery survived his Butler coach's attempts to fix it. After debuting for his hometown Twins in July 2006, he went 4-2 with a 2.19 ERA, and finished a 13-year career with a 2.82 ERA.

Neck Stanley.blurb: Pitcher John "Neck" Stanley spent over twenty years in the Negro leagues, mostly with the New York Black Yankees. He threw a no-hitter for the New York Cubans against Newark in 1936 and shared another with Albert Stephens in 1948.

Tom Niedenfuer.blurb: Tom Niedenfuer went 8-3 with 11 saves and a 1.90 ERA in 66 games for the Dodgers in 1983. In the 1985 NLCS he gave up a Game 5 walk-off homer to Ozzie Smith and, two days later, a pennant-clinching three-run homer to Jack Clark.

Tim Wallach.blurb: Tim Wallach won three Gold Gloves (1985, 1988, 1990), the second most among NL third basemen from 1980 to 1990 behind only Mike Schmidt. A five-time All-Star with two Silver Sluggers, he played 17 years for Montreal, Los Angeles and California.

Rudy York.blurb: Rudy York hit two grand slams in one game for Boston on July 27, 1946, driving in 10 runs against the Browns. In 1943 he led the American League with 34 homers for Detroit.

Floyd Bannister.blurb: Floyd Bannister was the first overall pick in the 1976 draft, taken by Houston. A left-hander, he led the American League in strikeouts in 1982 with the Mariners, an All-Star year, and pitched in the majors from 1977 to 1992.

Kyle Schwarber.blurb: Kyle Schwarber, drafted in the first round in 2014 out of Indiana, debuted with the Cubs in 2015 and was on their 2016 World Series champions. He led the National League in home runs in 2022 with the Phillies.

Bobby Miller.blurb: Bobby Miller, the Dodgers' 29th overall pick in 2020, debuted May 23, 2023 and won it. He finished 11-4 with a 3.76 ERA in 22 starts, then struggled with shoulder trouble in 2024.

Joe Hesketh.blurb: Joe Hesketh's outstanding 1985 rookie season ended in August when he tripped over Mike Scioscia's leg at the plate and broke his own leg. The left-hander still won 29 games for Montreal and 31 for Boston over 11 seasons, 1984 to 1994.

Carson Benge.blurb: Carson Benge starred as a two-way player at Oklahoma State, then went 19th overall to the Mets in 2024 and chose the outfield. He homered in his March 26, 2026 debut and finished with 20 homers and 22 steals.

Antonio Bastardo.blurb: Antonio Bastardo went 9–0 with a 1.87 ERA at Low-A Lakewood in 2007 and debuted with the Phillies in 2009. In 2011 he earned his first save on April 24, served as interim closer, and finished 6–1 with a 2.64 ERA.

Kirk Gibson.blurb: Kirk Gibson hit two dramatic World Series homers, each against an eventual Hall of Fame reliever: a three-run shot off Goose Gossage clinching the 1984 title for Detroit, and a 1988 pinch-hit walk-off off Dennis Eckersley for the Dodgers. He was 1988 NL MVP.

Shane Reynolds.blurb: Shane Reynolds won a career-best 19 games for Houston in 1998 and made his lone All-Star team in 2000. In 1999 he led the league with 35 starts and won Game 1 of the NLDS against Atlanta.

Clay Carroll.blurb: Clay Carroll, nicknamed Hawk by teammates, saved a then-record 37 games in 1972 and was named Sporting News Fireman of the Year. The Big Red Machine reliever won Game Seven of the 1975 World Series.

Ken Boyer.blurb: Ken Boyer hit a grand slam off Al Downing in Game Four of the 1964 World Series, the year he won MVP. In 1961 he hit .329 with 24 homers and 95 RBIs.

Troy Tulowitzki.blurb: Troy Tulowitzki, nicknamed "Tulo", was the seventh overall pick of the 2005 draft by the Rockies. A five-time All-Star, two-time Gold Glove and two-time Silver Slugger winner, he played 13 MLB seasons, mostly for Colorado, before the Rockies traded him to Toronto in 2015.

TJ House.blurb: TJ House was a 16th-round pick by Cleveland in 2008 and debuted May 17, 2014. In March 2017 a spring training line drive struck his head and he left by ambulance; Toronto called him up that August.

Con Daily.blurb: Catcher Con Daily played from 1885 to 1896, including with the Brooklyn Grooms from 1891 to 1895. He hit .244 with two home runs and 262 RBI over his major league career.

Luis Perdomo.blurb: Luis Perdomo was a Rule 5 pick by Colorado in 2015 and landed with San Diego, where he started 29 games in 2017 and led the National League in ground ball rate. He later pitched in Japan, an NPB All-Star in 2023.

Bill Mueller.blurb: Switch-hitter Bill Mueller is the only major leaguer through 2019 to hit a grand slam from each side of the plate in one game, on July 29, 2003. He won that year's AL batting title at .326.

Andre Ethier.blurb: Andre Ethier, a second-round Athletics pick in 2003, spent his whole career with the Dodgers, 2006 through 2017. He earned All-Star selections in 2010 and 2011, a 2009 Silver Slugger, and a 2011 Gold Glove, mostly in right field.

Andy Seminick.blurb: Andy Seminick homered three times on June 2, 1949, as the Phillies tied a major-league record with five home runs in one inning against the Reds. In 1950, nicknamed "Grandpa Whiz," he hit .288 with 24 home runs in 130 games.

Alfredo Duno.blurb: Venezuelan catcher Alfredo Duno signed with the Reds as an international free agent in January 2023. Ranked the Reds' top prospect by both MLB Pipeline and Baseball America, he was named to the 2026 Futures Game on July 2.

Jeff Montgomery.blurb: Jeff Montgomery, born in Wellston, Ohio, debuted for the Reds on August 1, 1987, throwing two innings. He is a member of the Kansas City Royals Hall of Fame, inducted in 2003, and reached 300 saves with a single team.

Austin Jackson.blurb: Austin Jackson was a rookie center fielder for Detroit in 2010, hitting .293 with 10 triples and finishing second in AL Rookie of the Year voting behind Neftali Feliz. He won the 2011 Fielding Bible Award.

Jack Russell.blurb: Clearwater's Jack Russell Stadium, the Phillies' spring home from 1955 to 2003, was named for this right-hander, who never pitched for them. He worked 557 games over 15 seasons, going 85-141 lifetime, and shared the AL lead in losses in 1930 at 9-20.

Melky Cabrera.blurb: Melky Cabrera, nicknamed "the Melkman," won All-Star Game MVP in 2012 in his first appearance, with the Giants. The Dominican outfielder debuted with the Yankees in 2005 and had a strong year with the Royals in 2011.

Marcelino Guerra.blurb: Cuban outfielder Marcelino Guerra debuted in the Cuban League in 1909 with Club Fé. He began in the Negro leagues in 1916 and played seven seasons for the Cuban Stars (West).

Hubie Brooks.blurb: Hubie Brooks was drafted third overall by the Mets in 1978 and played 15 major league seasons, 1980 to 1994, for the Mets, Expos, Dodgers, Angels and Royals. He was a two-time All-Star, and pitcher Donnie Moore was his cousin.

Marshall Bridges.blurb: Nicknamed "Sheriff" and "Fox," Marshall Bridges led the 1962 world champion Yankees with 18 saves and an 8-4 record. In the World Series he gave up Chuck Hiller's grand slam, the first by an AL pitcher.

Jonathan Papelbon.blurb: Jonathan Papelbon won the 2007 World Series with the Boston Red Sox and was named the 2007 Delivery Man of the Year. He was an All-Star four straight years (2006–2009) before pitching for the Phillies from 2012 to 2015.
