Cla Meredith.blurb: Cla Meredith, "the Claw," went 28 straight appearances without allowing a run in 2006, covering 33⅔ innings, a Padres franchise record. That year he led the National League with a 1.07 ERA, minimum 50 innings.

Dave Tomlin.blurb: Lefty reliever Dave Tomlin pitched 13 seasons from 1972 to 1986, mostly for the Reds and Padres. Traded to Texas for Gaylord Perry after 1978, he was bought back by Cincinnati in 1979, then served as Boston's pitching coach from 1998 to 2006.

Nomar Garciaparra.blurb: Nomar Garciaparra's middle name is his father Ramon's spelled backwards. He won the 1997 AL Rookie of the Year, then batting titles in 1999 (.357) and 2000 (.372), and hit two grand slams on May 10, 1999.

Ron Hunt.blurb: Ron Hunt was hit by pitches 243 times in a 12-year career (1963-74), sixth all-time, including 50 in 1971, the highest single-season figure since 1900. The gritty second baseman was nicknamed "Scrap Iron" and "Pigpen."

Jesse Barfield.blurb: Jesse Barfield's throwing arm was so powerful that he gunned down 162 baserunners. The two-time Gold Glove right fielder hit an American League-leading 40 home runs in 1986, and played 12 seasons (1981-1992) with Toronto and the Yankees.

Elston Howard.blurb: Elston Howard became the Yankees' first Black player in 1955 and, in 1963, the first African-American AL MVP, hitting 28 home runs and winning a Gold Glove. He hit .348 in 1961.

Jeferson Quero.blurb: Venezuelan catcher Jeferson Quero signed with Milwaukee in 2019. A torn labrum and shoulder damage ended his 2024 after one Triple-A game; he reached the majors in March 2026, promoted when Andrew Vaughn went on the injured list.

Jay Bruce.blurb: Jay Bruce reached base in his first six plate appearances after debuting for the Reds on May 27, 2008. In 2017 he hit 29 homers for the Mets before a trade to Cleveland, finishing with 36 homers and 101 RBIs.

Toby Hall.blurb: Toby Hall did not sign when the Giants drafted him in 1995, but signed with Tampa Bay after the Devil Rays took him in 1997. The catcher set his career high with a .287 average in 2005, and now manages the Florence Y'alls.

Yu Darvish.blurb: Yu Darvish was considered by many the best pitcher in Japan before reaching MLB in 2012. He finished third in AL Rookie of the Year voting that year, then led MLB with 277 strikeouts in 2013 and placed second for the AL Cy Young.

Luke Hamlin.blurb: Luke Hamlin earned the nickname "Hot Potato" for juggling the ball before pitches. He won 20 games for Brooklyn in 1939, finishing tenth in NL MVP voting, then posted a 3.06 ERA in 1940.

Phil Masi.blurb: Phil Masi, pinch-running, was ruled safe at second by umpire Bill Stewart on Cleveland's pickoff attempt in Game One of the 1948 World Series, then scored the game's only run. A four-time All-Star catcher, he insisted for decades he was safe.

Dave Ferriss.blurb: Known as Boo, Dave Ferriss threw a five-hit 2-0 shutout in Philadelphia in his April 29, 1945 debut and opened with 22 1/3 scoreless innings. He went 21-10 as a rookie, then 25-6 in 1946.

Ezra Sutton.blurb: Ezra Sutton played in the first games of both the National Association and the National League. By 20 he was acknowledged as the country's finest third baseman, known for fearlessness and perhaps the strongest arm in the game.

Mike Matthews.blurb: Left-handed reliever Mike Matthews changed organizations twice in August 1999, first to the Red Sox, then to the Cardinals about three weeks later. He debuted for St. Louis May 31, 2000, and went 14-10 with a 4.54 ERA through 2005.

Brett Cecil.blurb: Lefty Brett Cecil is usually right-handed; pitching is the only thing he does left-handed. In 2013 he made the All-Star team, going 5-1 with a 2.82 ERA for Toronto.

Marcus Stroman.blurb: At 5 feet 7 inches, Marcus Stroman is one of only six pitchers under 5-10 to start an MLB game this century. A Duke product and 2012 first-round pick, he won a 2017 Gold Glove and was a 2019 All-Star.

Eddie Watt.blurb: When the Orioles won four pennants in six seasons (1966–1971), no Baltimore pitcher earned more saves or appeared in more games than Eddie Watt. He held right-handed hitters to a .200 average, usually with a wad of Red Man in his cheek.

Don August.blurb: Don August, drafted 17th overall by Houston in 1984, was called up by Milwaukee in 1988 and went 13-7 with a 3.09 ERA, finishing fourth in AL Rookie of the Year voting.

Larry Benton.blurb: Larry Benton pitched thirteen seasons between 1923 and 1935 for the Braves, Giants and Reds. He tied Burleigh Grimes for the National League lead in wins in 1928 with New York, finishing his career 128-128.

Tommy Bond.blurb: Irish-born Tommy Bond threw low sidearm with tremendous speed by the mid-1870s, pushing the underhand rules to their edge. By the time overhand pitching became legal, he had won 234 games and thrown over 3,600 innings.

William Contreras.blurb: Nicknamed "Wild Bill," Venezuelan catcher William Contreras signed with Atlanta in 2015, won a ring with the 2021 Braves, then won Silver Sluggers in 2023 and 2024 for Milwaukee and was MVP of the 2026 World Series.

Yordan Alvarez.blurb: Cuban slugger Yordan Alvarez was the unanimous 2019 AL Rookie of the Year, posting a .655 slugging percentage, the highest ever by a qualified rookie. He had defected from Cuba in 2016 and reached Houston by trade.

Jerry Browne.blurb: Nicknamed "The Guv'nor," Jerry Browne grew up in St. Croix, U.S. Virgin Islands. The Rangers called him up in September 1986 and he stayed nine years, moving from second base to become a handy utilityman.

Blake Treinen.blurb: Reliever Blake Treinen went from Baker and South Dakota State to an All-Star year with Oakland in 2018, then pitched for the Dodgers' World Series champions of 2020, 2024 and 2025.

Cecil Upshaw.blurb: At 6'6", Cecil Upshaw starred in basketball and baseball at Centenary College, where his 0.85 ERA in 1962 is still the school's single-season best. Showing off his basketball skills later cost him a season.

Adam Dunn.blurb: Nicknamed "Big Donkey," Adam Dunn hit 38 or more homers seven straight seasons, tying Babe Ruth's streak, including a 535-foot shot in 2004 that landed in another state. He also struck out 2,379 times.

Andrew McCutchen.blurb: Andrew McCutchen, the 11th pick in the 2005 draft, won the 2013 NL MVP with the Pirates. He also led the league in on-base percentage and OPS and helped Team USA win the 2017 World Baseball Classic.

Ryan Lavarnway.blurb: Catcher Ryan Lavarnway played for 27 teams in 16 pro seasons, was shuttled between the minors and majors 26 times, and played for eight big-league clubs. His one World Series ring came with the 2013 Red Sox.

Norm Cash.blurb: Norm Cash was born in Justiceburg, Texas, a railroad junction of about 25 people, and wore 25 for most of his career. The first baseman sang country songs in the clubhouse and drowned in a boating accident in 1986.

Dale Alexander.blurb: Nicknamed "Moose," the 6'3" Dale Alexander became Boston's first American League batting champion. The first baseman was born and died in Greeneville, Tennessee, on family land held since before 1796.

Art Nehf.blurb: Lefty Art Nehf was John McGraw's go-to clutch pitcher for the Giants, winning the deciding game of the 1921 and 1922 World Series against the Yankees. He won 184 games across a 15-year career, 1915 to 1929.

Terry Kennedy.blurb: Son of big-league man Bob Kennedy, Terry Kennedy learned hitting from Stan Musial and Ted Williams, then was named 1977 collegiate Player of the Year. The catcher later won a Silver Slugger and made four All-Star teams.

Phil Bradley.blurb: Phil Bradley was the starting quarterback at Missouri and Big Eight Offensive Player of the Year before baseball. The outfielder made the 1985 All-Star team for Seattle and played for four big-league clubs from 1983 to 1990.

Robby Thompson.blurb: Robby Thompson spent his entire career, 1986 to 1996, with the San Francisco Giants and was their starting second baseman for eleven straight years. A two-time All-Star, he was often overshadowed by Ryne Sandberg.

Maurice Archdeacon.blurb: On September 2, 1921, minor-leaguer Maurice Archdeacon circled the bases in 13.4 seconds, beating Hans Lobert's 1910 mark of 13.8, and was dubbed "the fastest man in baseball." He was a St. Louis native.

Prince Fielder.blurb: Prince Fielder is the youngest player in National League history to hit 50 home runs in a season. A six-time All-Star, he was the first Brewer to win the Home Run Derby (2009) and won it again in 2012.

Duke Brett.blurb: Duke Brett pitched for the Cubs in 1924 and 1925, going 1-1 with a 3.97 ERA. His only big-league win came August 5, 1925, over the Phillies; he then managed in the minors for years.

Roy Welmaker.blurb: Nicknamed "Snookie," Roy Welmaker pitched in the Negro leagues from 1932 to 1953. He won Games 1 and 5 of the 1944 Negro World Series against the Birmingham Black Barons.

Keith Hernandez.blurb: Keith Hernandez, one of the best-fielding first basemen ever, was traded from the Cardinals to the Mets in mid-1983 after a clash with manager Whitey Herzog. He had sat out his high school senior year over playing time.

Tom Gordon.blurb: Nicknamed "Flash," Tom Gordon won the 1998 Rolaids Relief Man award with Boston, leading the AL in saves. In 1998 and 1999 he converted 54 straight saves, then a major-league record.

Johnny Allen.blurb: Johnny Allen's temper was legendary. After one loss to the Red Sox he reportedly upended barstools, then sprayed a hotel hallway with a fire extinguisher. The fierce righty pitched thirteen seasons and died in 1959.

Damion Easley.blurb: Damion Easley once walked past a boy begging for his autograph at Tigers camp, then turned back, closed the clubhouse door and talked with the crying kid. He won a Silver Slugger and played 20 pro seasons.

Jack Kralick.blurb: On August 26, 1962, Jack Kralick pitched the Twins' first no-hitter. A walk to pinch-hitter George Alusik, who had homered off him earlier that month, was all that kept it from a perfect game.

Julio Franco.blurb: Hailed as the next Robin Yount, Julio Franco went from the Phillies to Cleveland in the trade for Von Hayes. It began one of the longest careers in baseball history, and he returned to the game in 2015.

Neal Cotts.blurb: Lefty reliever Neal Cotts was part of the 2005 champion White Sox. He later went back to college to keep a promise to his mother and returned to the majors after nearly four seasons away.

Hal Lanier.blurb: Hal Lanier was a brainy, defense-first infielder for the Giants and Yankees, and the son of pitcher Max Lanier. As a rookie manager in 1986 he led the Astros to a division title and Manager of the Year.

Kent Mercker.blurb: Kent Mercker threw six hitless innings in a combined no-hitter on September 11, 1991, then tossed his own no-hitter against the Dodgers on April 8, 1994. He later reinvented himself as a crafty setup man over 18 seasons.

Starling Marte.blurb: Dominican outfielder Starling Marte debuted with the Pirates in 2012. A two-time Gold Glove winner and two-time All-Star, he led the majors with 47 stolen bases in 2021.

Max Flack.blurb: Max Flack, born Conrad Flach, stood 5'7" and 150 pounds. His 12-year big-league career was long remembered mostly for one thing: playing for two major-league teams on the same day.

Bill Force.blurb: Lefty Buddie Force pitched in the Negro leagues for Detroit, Baltimore and Brooklyn, going 60-52 with a 4.21 ERA. He threw a no-hitter against St. Louis on June 27, 1922.

Bruno Block.blurb: Catcher Bruno Block, born James John Blochowicz and known as Jimmy Block, reported to the Senators the very day Walter Johnson debuted. He later caught Ed Walsh's no-hitter on August 27, 1911.

Irvin Brooks.blurb: Irvin Brooks spent his entire career, 1918 to 1933, with the Brooklyn Royal Giants, playing pitcher, infield and outfield. Books wrongly list him as Bahamian-born "Chester"; he was born in Key West. Cumberland Posey ranked him an all-time Negro league all-star.

Mike Garcia.blurb: Nicknamed "The Big Bear," Mike Garcia anchored Cleveland's early-1950s rotation beside Feller, Lemon and Wynn. At 13 he weighed under 100 pounds and dreamed of being a jockey, until a horse threw him in his only race.

Art Ditmar.blurb: Art Ditmar was Casey Stengel's choice to start Game One of the 1960 World Series, a decision critics have condemned ever since. The Winthrop, Massachusetts native was a rookie with the Kansas City Athletics in 1955.

Jimmy Sheckard.blurb: Jimmy Sheckard led the National League at various times in triples, homers, slugging, runs, on-base percentage, walks and stolen bases. Named left fielder on a 1962 all-time Cubs team, he was also a top defensive outfielder.

Esteban Montalvo.blurb: Cuban outfielder Esteban Montalvo, nicknamed "Mayarí," debuted in the Negro leagues in 1923 with the Cuban Stars (West) and played four seasons for them. He also played in the Cuban League and died young, in 1930.

Ceddanne Rafaela.blurb: Curaçao-born Ceddanne Rafaela signed with Boston in 2017 and debuted in 2023. In June 2025 he hit a walk-off homer at Fenway that was the shortest of its kind since Statcast tracking began in 2015.

Dansby Swanson.blurb: Nicknamed "Three-point Swanson" for his basketball touch at Marietta High, Dansby Swanson was the 2014 College World Series Most Outstanding Player for Vanderbilt. Arizona then took him first overall in the 2015 draft.

Johnny Estrada.blurb: Johnny Estrada came to Atlanta in December 2002 in a salary-driven deal for Kevin Millwood. After Javy Lopez left, he became the Braves' starting catcher in 2004 and hit .314 with nine homers and 76 RBI.

Don Baylor.blurb: Don Baylor crowded the plate and was hit by 267 pitches, the most of any 20th-century player, leading the AL eight times. He hit 338 homers in 19 seasons and later won Manager of the Year honors.

Nick Swisher.blurb: Switch-hitter Nick Swisher, son of former catcher Steve Swisher, hit at least 20 home runs in nine straight seasons from 2005 to 2013. He won the 2009 World Series with the Yankees.

Charlie Hough.blurb: Charlie Hough pitched at the big-league level for a quarter century on a knuckleball he learned in the minors to revive a stalled career. Born in Honolulu, his father had been a POW in World War II.

Ping Bodie.blurb: Born Francesco Pezzolo, Ping Bodie got his name from the sound of the ball off his 52-ounce bat and from Bodie, a California ghost town where he once lived. He was one of the first Italian ballplayers in the majors.

Tug McGraw.blurb: Reliever Tug McGraw coined "Ya Gotta Believe" for the 1973 Mets. In 1980 he struck out Willie Wilson to end the World Series, giving the Phillies their first championship.

Mark McGwire.blurb: Nicknamed "Big Mac," Mark McGwire hit 49 homers as a rookie in 1987 and 70 in 1998, both records at the time. His 583 career homers came at a major-league-best rate of one per 10.6 at-bats.

Ken Singleton.blurb: Switch-hitting Ken Singleton paired patience with power, making three All-Star teams as an Orioles right fielder and serving as DH for Baltimore's 1983 champions. He later became a popular Yankees broadcaster.

Mike Myers.blurb: Left-handed submariner Mike Myers was the premier LOOGY of the late 1990s and early 2000s. Over 13 years with nine teams, he helped change how bullpens were used.

Cy Williams.blurb: Cy Williams was the National League's career home run leader, with 251, until Rogers Hornsby passed him in 1929. The 6'2" center fielder is best remembered for his 1920s slugging with the Phillies.

Barry Latman.blurb: Barry Latman, a 6'3" Jewish pitcher from Los Angeles, would not pitch on the High Holidays. In 1959 he helped the White Sox win the pennant after 40 lean years.

Wilbert Robinson.blurb: "Uncle Robbie" Wilbert Robinson caught for the 1890s Baltimore Orioles, then managed Brooklyn from 1914 to 1931 to two pennants and a record of 1,399-1,398. He was one of baseball's most beloved characters.

Charlie Hollocher.blurb: After hitting .316 for the 1918 pennant-winning Cubs, shortstop Charlie Hollocher was hailed as the next Honus Wagner. Six years later, mysterious stomach ailments forced him to retire.

Craig Lefferts.blurb: Craig Lefferts was born in Munich, West Germany, to an Air Force officer, and fought childhood asthma. He lasted a decade in the majors and became famous for sprinting from the bullpen to the mound.

Kris Bryant.blurb: Kris Bryant won the 2013 Golden Spikes Award at San Diego and went second overall to the Cubs. He took the 2015 NL Rookie of the Year Award and won the 2016 World Series.

Pat Borders.blurb: Catcher Pat Borders was the first American to win both a World Series ring and an Olympic gold medal. He was the MVP of the 1992 World Series and played 17 seasons for nine teams.

Clay Bryant.blurb: In 1938 Clay Bryant won 19 games and led the National League in strikeouts. He threw seven straight complete games in September's first 25 days to help the Cubs erase a nine-game deficit and win the pennant.

Cristian Javier.blurb: Dominican righty Cristian Javier started two combined no-hitters for the 2022 champion Astros, including Game 4 of the World Series, the first pitcher in MLB history to do so.

Curt Davis.blurb: Curt Davis did not reach the majors until age 30, held back four years when the Seals refused to sell him. His 158 wins are the most by any pitcher who debuted after turning 30.

Sonny Siebert.blurb: Before a start on June 10, 1966, Sonny Siebert told his wife that if she stopped nagging he would throw a no-hitter. That night he did, against the Senators, half in jest.

Gary Peters.blurb: Gary Peters needed five call-ups before sticking with the White Sox in 1963. He won 124 games and was a strong hitter, with 19 career homers that made him a frequent pinch-hitter.

Joe Start.blurb: Joe Start began playing in 1859 at age 16 and stayed a superior player for over 25 years, through the game's rules, equipment and professional changes.

Ossie Orwoll.blurb: In 1927 Ossie Orwoll led the American Association in winning percentage (.739) while hitting .370, second best, which got Connie Mack to buy him. Arm trouble and Mack's anger ended his run by August 1929.

Jake Stahl.blurb: Jake Stahl was a 6'2" slugger who played on Boston's 1903 title team and managed the 1912 "Speed Boys" to a 105-47 pennant season, making him part of two Red Sox championships.

Socks Seybold.blurb: Ralph "Socks" Seybold was the last man Connie Mack signed for the 1901 Athletics, at about age 30. Maligned for his round figure and big appetite, he proved deceptively quick and became a top AL slugger.

Sandy Alomar Jr..blurb: Sandy Alomar Jr. homered in five straight games in April 1997 and had 11 homers by the All-Star break, hosted at Cleveland. He said pitches looked like beach balls.

Jerry Augustine.blurb: Jerry Augustine, born in Green Bay, played high school, college and pro ball in Wisconsin, pitching for the Brewers for a decade. He became left-handed when a half-brother handed him a lefty's glove.

Ice Box Chamberlain.blurb: Elton "Ice Box" Chamberlain, called Ed by friends, earned his nickname for his austere calm in the face of hostility. He was born in Warsaw, New York, in 1867 and loved barrooms and night life.

Greasy Neale.blurb: Earle "Greasy" Neale was an outfielder on a World Series winner who then coached in the Rose Bowl and led back-to-back NFL champions. He is in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Slim Sallee.blurb: Catcher Roger Bresnahan said Slim Sallee had the best control of any southpaw ever. The lefty fought alcohol and training-rule fines yet was one of the NL's best pitchers for what may have been the Dead Ball era's worst team.

Lance Blankenship.blurb: Utility man Lance Blankenship played his entire career with Oakland, 1988 to 1993, including the 1989 World Series sweep of the Giants. A rotator cuff injury ended his career with a .222 average.

Brad Radke.blurb: Brad Radke pitched 12 years for the Twins, praised by teammates for toughness and heart. As a kid he hit a home run in a tournament in Mexico that killed a chicken.

Kevin Gausman.blurb: Kevin Gausman was an All-American at LSU and the fourth pick of the 2012 draft by Baltimore. He made All-Star teams in 2021 and 2023 and led the American League in strikeouts in 2023.

Willie Gisentaner.blurb: Southpaw Willie "Three Finger" Gisentaner, born in Ozark, Alabama, in 1899, had a truncated index finger, making him the Negro Leagues' answer to Mordecai "Three Finger" Brown. He moved between teams for two decades and was a smart pitcher and good hitter.

Mike Hegan.blurb: At 12, Mike Hegan was the Indians' batboy at Yankee Stadium in 1954 and got interviewed by Red Barber. The son of Indians catcher Jim Hegan, he made his own major-league debut in the same stadium ten years later.

Jesse Chavez.blurb: Jesse Chavez is the most traded player in MLB history, dealt eleven times. A 42nd-round pick out of Riverside Community College in 2002, he pitched for nine big-league clubs and won a ring with the 2021 Braves.

Reggie Sanders.blurb: Reggie Sanders played for eight clubs. His best year came with the 2001 Diamondbacks: a career-high 33 home runs and 14 hits in 16 postseason games as Arizona won its first World Series.

Wally Backman.blurb: Wally Backman was perhaps the first major-league manager fired before his team played a game. A 16th overall pick in 1977 from Aloha High, Oregon, he also had three short jail stints and a bankruptcy.

Todd Benzinger.blurb: Reds first baseman Todd Benzinger took the final out of the 1990 World Series. With Cincinnati up 2-1 in Game Four, Carney Lansford's foul pop finished the sweep of the Athletics.

Johnny Hayes.blurb: Johnny Hayes, born in Independence, Missouri, played for seven Negro league teams from 1934 to 1951, with time out for Army service in World War II. He appeared in the 1947 and 1951 East-West All-Star games.

Chuck Stobbs.blurb: One of baseball's original bonus babies, Chuck Stobbs signed with the Red Sox at 17. The lefty went 107-130 over 15 seasons, mostly for losing teams; his father had played pro football for the 1921 Detroit Tigers.

Ernie Koob.blurb: Lefty Ernie Koob jumped from college to the St. Louis Browns in mid-1915, then tossed the first no-hitter by a Brownie at Sportsman's Park, in 1917. He went 23-31 in parts of four seasons.

Trevor Rosenthal.blurb: Trevor Rosenthal was a shortstop at Cowley Community College before the Cardinals took him in the 21st round of 2009. He became a bullpen power arm whose fastball reached 100 miles per hour or more.

Don Blasingame.blurb: Nicknamed "The Blazer," Don Blasingame played 12 big-league seasons, with an All-Star Game and a World Series. He married a Miss America finalist, a famous ballplayer's daughter, and later spent 16 years playing, coaching or managing in a far-off land.

Lee Mazzilli.blurb: Brooklyn-born Lee Mazzilli could hit and throw both left- and right-handed and was a seven-time national youth speedskating champion. After 14 playing years he became an actor, businessman, manager and broadcaster.

Aleck Smith.blurb: Researchers still cannot say which side of the plate Aleck Smith batted from. He threw right-handed, spent nine seasons in the majors from 1897 to 1906, and was on the 1903 Boston Americans.

Tommy Byrne.blurb: Tommy Byrne had three successful careers: hard-throwing lefty for thirteen major-league seasons, businessman, and two-term mayor of his adopted hometown. The Baltimore native grew up idolizing Babe Ruth.

Vinegar Bend Mizell.blurb: Wilmer Mizell was born in Leakesville, Mississippi, but took the nickname "Vinegar Bend" from the tiny Alabama town where he got his mail. The pitcher later became a U.S. Congressman.

Dave Rozema.blurb: Called "The Rose," Dave Rozema was Detroit's rookie phenom of 1977, a year after Mark Fidrych. At 6'4" with a fastball seldom above 85 mph, he leaned on a devastating changeup and excellent control.

Spud Chandler.blurb: Spud Chandler pitched with the intensity of a man facing a mortal enemy. The Georgia righty won an AL MVP award, set a modern record for career winning percentage, and was on six World Series champions.

Fritz Maisel.blurb: Nicknamed "The Catonsville Flash," Fritz Maisel stole 74 bases for the Yankees, a team single-season record until Rickey Henderson broke it in 1985, 71 years later. He spent 57 years in Baltimore baseball.

Jim Thorpe.blurb: Jim Thorpe, an Olympic champion in the pentathlon and decathlon, played six big-league seasons. His baseball was disappointing: .252 with seven homers in 289 National League games, and he admitted he couldn't hit curves.

Kazuhiro Sasaki.blurb: Closer Kazuhiro Sasaki saved 252 games in Japan and 129 in the majors. In 2000 he won AL Rookie of the Year for Seattle with 37 saves, a Mariners record and a rookie record.

Bill Pulsipher.blurb: Lefty Bill Pulsipher was once a top prospect in the Mets' heralded "Generation K." Injuries, including Tommy John surgery, plus depression and anxiety, derailed a career that ran from 1995 to 2005.

Steve Rogers.blurb: Many remember Steve Rogers for the 1981 NLCS homer he allowed to Rick Monday. He was also a five-time All-Star, an ERA leader and the ace of the Expos in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

George Britt.blurb: George Britt pitched in the Negro leagues from before World War I until nearly his 50th birthday in World War II. He played for the 1931 Homestead Grays, which some researchers rank the best club ever.

Roy Sievers.blurb: Roy Sievers won the first AL Rookie of the Year Award in 1949, then fought through shoulder injuries to become the 18th player with 300 homers. Called Mr. Clutch, he hit nine walk-off homers.

Jeff Blauser.blurb: Jeff Blauser pitched two Little League no-hitters in three weeks at age 12. A first-round pick in 1984, he became an offense-first shortstop with the Braves, a two-time All-Star on four World Series teams.

Josh Naylor.blurb: Canadian first baseman Josh Naylor was the 12th pick in 2015 and debuted with the Padres in 2019. He was an All-Star with Cleveland in 2024 and has played for Canada in three World Baseball Classics.

Danny Graves.blurb: Danny Graves, born to a Vietnamese mother and an American serviceman, is the only Vietnam-born player in major-league history. He became the Reds' all-time saves leader and won the 2002 Lou Gehrig Memorial Award.

Ed Figueroa.blurb: Ed Figueroa won more games than Catfish Hunter or Ron Guidry for the Yankees' 1976-78 pennant teams. A sinkerballer from Puerto Rico, he had a 20-win season before elbow trouble ended his run.

Otto Schomberg.blurb: Milwaukee-born Otto Schomberg was a hitting wonder in his one full big-league year, 1887. Poor fielding and health problems ended it, and he went on to a career as a lumberman.

Jesse Williams.blurb: Jesse "Bill" Williams was a premier defensive shortstop in the Negro leagues. He is also known as the Kansas City Monarchs player who switched positions to make room for Jackie Robinson.

Ron Guidry.blurb: In 1978 Ron Guidry went 25-3 with a 1.74 ERA, nine shutouts and 248 strikeouts for the Yankees. He set a team record with 13 straight wins early on and won the Cy Young.

Seth Morehead.blurb: In 1957 Birdie Tebbetts called Seth Morehead the best young left-hander in the National League, with 25-game-winner potential. He won just five games in 132 appearances, out of the majors by 26.

Ron Hassey.blurb: Ron Hassey is the only catcher to be behind the plate for two perfect games. His 14-year career, with six franchises, included only five seasons of 100 or more games.

Spike Owen.blurb: Spike Owen got his first name from his mother's maiden name, Spikes. The Cleburne, Texas native was a switch-hitting shortstop for 13 seasons with the Mariners, Red Sox, Expos, Yankees and Angels.

Dante Bichette.blurb: In 1995 Dante Bichette led the National League in homers, slugging and total bases, and the majors in hits and RBI, finishing second for MVP. In 1996 he joined the 30-30 club.

Johnny Cueto.blurb: Johnny Cueto emerged as the Reds' ace by 2011. In 2014 he won 20 games with a 2.25 ERA, tied for the NL lead with 242 strikeouts, and finished second in the Cy Young voting.

Logan Forsythe.blurb: Logan Forsythe, an Arkansas product, played mostly second base for six big-league clubs. He appeared in at least one game at every position except center field and catcher.

Red Dooin.blurb: Just 5'6" and never over 145 pounds, Red Dooin was a spike-fearless catcher who blocked the plate against the heaviest runners. His 1,124 games behind it were a Phillies record until Mike Lieberthal topped it in 2006.

Rube Walberg.blurb: Rube Walberg was "discovered" at 25, hurling chunks of coal at fence posts in his brother's Seattle coal yard. Fewer than two years later he was in the majors. He was born on a Minnesota farm in 1896.

Henry Rodriguez.blurb: Montreal fans threw Oh Henry! bars onto the field after Henry Rodriguez homered. In 1996 he made the All-Star team and hit a then-Expos-record 36 home runs. He later cleaned up behind Sammy Sosa for the 1998 Cubs.

Xander Bogaerts.blurb: Aruban shortstop Xander Bogaerts debuted in 2013 and helped Boston win that year's World Series and another in 2018. A five-time Silver Slugger, he set the Red Sox record for games at shortstop in 2022.

Doggie Miller.blurb: Doggie Miller, also nicknamed "Foghorn" and "Calliope," shunned catcher's protective gear, so his teams played him all over the field. He became the first major leaguer with 20 or more games at all eight non-pitching positions.

Harry Coveleski.blurb: As a Phillies rookie in 1908, Harry Coveleski became the "Giant Killer," beating New York three times in five days and costing John McGraw's club the pennant. His endurance came from working in Pennsylvania coal mines.

Joe Torre.blurb: Joe Torre waited a record 4,272 major-league games, as player and manager, before his first World Series game, in 1996. It took two trades and three firings to get there.

Davey Lopes.blurb: Davey Lopes made four straight All-Star Games for the Dodgers and set a major-league record for consecutive stolen bases without being caught. The Cape Verdean-Irish second baseman also won a Gold Glove and two stolen base titles.

Coot Veal.blurb: Coot Veal is remembered more for his nickname than his play, yet the "good field, no hit" shortstop's .976 fielding percentage beat Luis Aparicio's by four points. He hit .231 over 247 games in parts of six seasons.

Howie Pollet.blurb: Lefty Howie Pollet was a New Orleans pitching prodigy whose arm injuries stunted his career. His family pronounced the name "pol-LET," and his next-door neighbor was future Red Sox lefty Mel Parnell.

Dee Strange-Gordon.blurb: In 2015, his first year with Miami, Dee Strange-Gordon led the NL with a .333 average, 205 hits and 58 steals. He was the first to lead the league in average and steals since Jackie Robinson in 1949.

Lou Whitaker.blurb: From the late 1970s to the mid-1990s, Tiger Stadium crowds greeted "Sweet Lou" Whitaker with a drawn-out "ooooo" so familiar that outsiders mistook it for booing.

Tim Foli.blurb: Nicknamed "Crazy Horse," Tim Foli was a talented but hot-tempered infielder who played 16 years for six teams. He earned his World Series ring with the 1979 Pirates.

Herb Thormahlen.blurb: Jersey City lefty Herb Thormahlen won 29 big-league games and 159 in the minors between 1916 and 1933. Databases list him as Hank, but no news story researched ever called him that.

Frank Lary.blurb: Known as the "Yankee Killer," Tigers righty Frank Lary went 28-13 lifetime against New York. In his peak 1961 season he was 23-9, and he was an All-Star in 1960 and 1961.

George Weidman.blurb: Stump Weidman led the National League with a 1.80 ERA in 1881 and won 45 games in 1882 and 1883. He threw more innings for the Detroit Wolverines, 1,654, than any other pitcher in club history.

Roy McMillan.blurb: Roy McMillan, Cincinnati's "Mr. Shortstop," was so good with the glove that he made the September 9, 1957 Sports Illustrated cover, despite a best batting average of just .272.

Joel Hanrahan.blurb: Closer Joel Hanrahan saved 76 games for the Pirates in 2011 and 2012, the best two-year total in club history. From spring 2011 to the 2012 All-Star Game he allowed 23 earned runs in 102 2/3 innings.

Turk Wendell.blurb: Reliever Turk Wendell pitched for four National League clubs between 1993 and 2004. A switch-hitter, he had just three career hits, all from the left side.

Bill Hallahan.blurb: "Wild Bill" Hallahan lived up to his name, leading the NL in walks and wild pitches three times each. He also led in strikeouts twice, threw two World Series shutouts and started the 1933 All-Star Game.

Roy Oswalt.blurb: Roy Oswalt went 14-3 as a 2001 rookie and won 20 games in both 2004 and 2005. He was MVP of the 2005 NLCS that sent Houston to its first World Series.

Jerry Don Gleaton.blurb: Lefty Jerry Don Gleaton was an All-American at Texas, the 18th pick of the 1979 draft and a big-leaguer that July. He pitched mainly in relief for six clubs through 1992.

Matt Olson.blurb: Matt Olson led the majors in home runs and RBI in 2023. A first-round pick by Oakland, he was traded to Atlanta before 2022 and signed an eight-year extension; he has won four Gold Gloves.

Clyde Sukeforth.blurb: Backup catcher Clyde Sukeforth hit .264 with two homers, yet shaped baseball history as a scout and coach. He had a hand in discovering Jackie Robinson, signing Roberto Clemente, and sending Ralph Branca in to face Bobby Thomson.

Lenny Harris.blurb: Utility infielder Lenny Harris is best known for the major-league career record for pinch hits, 212. The 5'10", 195-pound infielder batted left-handed and threw right-handed, and played in the majors for years.

Antonio Alfonseca.blurb: Dominican reliever Antonio Alfonseca is known for having an extra digit on each hand and foot. He closed for the Florida Marlins from 1997 to 2001, then pitched for the Cubs, Braves, Rangers and Phillies.

Jim Konstanty.blurb: Reliever Jim Konstanty won the 1950 National League MVP award as a reliever. He pitched for the Phillies from 1948 to 1954, then the Yankees and Cardinals.

Jim Maloney.blurb: Jim Maloney was among the hardest throwers of the 1960s. The Reds righty threw two no-hitters, won ten or more games each year from 1963 to 1969, and struck out over 200 batters four straight seasons.

John Axford.blurb: Canadian closer John Axford, nicknamed "Ax Man," debuted with the Brewers in 2009. In 2011 he led the National League in saves and won the Rolaids Relief Man Award.

Munetaka Murakami.blurb: Fans in Japan called Munetaka Murakami "Murakami-sama," a kami-sama or god, for his feats at the plate. The nickname was Japan's word of the year for 2022, before he joined the White Sox.

Johnny Romano.blurb: Catcher Johnny Romano was a four-time All-Star and considered one of the American League's top catchers in the early 1960s, until injuries cut his career short. He played for the White Sox, Indians and Cardinals.

George Pinkney.blurb: Third baseman George Pinkney was the first player to appear in 500 consecutive major-league games. He played in the National League and American Association from 1884 to 1893.

Tom Morgan.blurb: Right-hander Tom Morgan was nicknamed "Plowboy" because he farmed in his native California. A Yankees signee in 1949, he later pitched for the Athletics, Tigers, Senators and Angels.

Scott Garrelts.blurb: Scott Garrelts spent 1982 to 1991 with the Giants. In 1989 he went 14-5 with a 2.28 ERA, leading San Francisco to a World Series against its Bay Area rivals, the Athletics.

Freddy Leach.blurb: Outfielder Freddy Leach hit .300 or better six times, topping out at .329 in 1926. Across ten seasons with the Phillies, Giants and Braves, he batted .307 in 991 games.

John Leary.blurb: John Leary played first base and catcher for the St. Louis Browns in 1914 and 1915. He then coached football at Waltham High School from 1920 to 1947, and its Leary Field bears his name.

Oneil Cruz.blurb: Dominican center fielder and shortstop Oneil Cruz debuted with the Pirates in 2021 and led the National League in stolen bases in 2025. He won a bronze medal with the Dominican Republic at the 2026 World Baseball Classic.

Riley Greene.blurb: Riley Greene went fifth overall to the Tigers in 2019, debuted in 2022 and won a Silver Slugger Award in 2025. The outfielder has been selected to three All-Star teams.

Camilo Doval.blurb: Camilo Doval signed with the Giants out of the Dominican Republic in 2015 and debuted in 2021. His fastball has hit 104.5 miles per hour, and he has also pitched for the Yankees and Pirates.

Anthony Bender.blurb: Anthony Bender went from Santa Rosa Junior College to the 613th pick of the 2016 draft, in the 20th round by the Royals. He reached the majors in 2021 and now pitches for Miami.

Claude Johnson.blurb: Youngstown native Claude "Hooks" Johnson played second base in the Negro leagues from 1916 to 1930. He spent three seasons each with the Cleveland Tate Stars and Detroit Stars and finished with Birmingham.

Jhonny Level.blurb: Venezuelan shortstop who signed with the Giants in 2024 for $997,500. Hit ten home runs in 48 games in his first pro summer, then batted .325 at San Jose in 2026 to earn a promotion to High-A Eugene.

David Davalillo.blurb: Signed by the Mets in 2021 and released a year later without ever pitching for them. The Rangers picked him up, and in 2025 he posted a 2.44 ERA with 126 strikeouts in 107 innings to earn protection from the Rule 5 draft.

Dave Roberts.blurb: An asthmatic child who came through elbow surgery, shoulder bursitis and two minor-league waivers, then remade himself as a control pitcher. Lost 17 games for the last-place 1971 Padres, five by shutout, and won 103 in all, plus a 1979 ring with Pittsburgh.

Evan Phillips.blurb: Earned his first career save in his Rays debut in August 2021 and was designated for assignment the very next day. The Dodgers claimed him off waivers, and three days later he won his first game for them.

Frank Blake.blurb: Negro leagues pitcher nicknamed "Powerhouse". Played for the Baltimore Black Sox in 1932, the New York Black Yankees in 1934 and the New York Cubans in 1935; his date of death is unknown.

Hayden Wesneski.blurb: Traded twice for big names: the Yankees sent him to the Cubs for Scott Effross in 2022, and the Cubs sent him to Houston in the Kyle Tucker deal in 2024. Threw five scoreless innings with eight strikeouts in his debut.

Robert Stephenson.blurb: Gatorade California Player of the Year in high school, with a 1.19 ERA and 142 strikeouts in 76 2/3 innings. The Reds took him 27th overall in 2011; he reached the majors in 2016 and has pitched for five clubs.

Jake McCarthy.blurb: On July 3, 2026, became the first player ever with a leadoff home run, a grand slam and a stolen base in one game, in a 15-3 Rockies win over the Giants. Stole 36 bases in 38 tries at Virginia.

Sandy Leon.blurb: Sprained his ankle in a home-plate collision in the fourth inning of his 2012 debut. Hit .310 for Boston in 2016, won the 2018 World Series with the Red Sox, and got a second ring from the 2023 Rangers.

Jose Vizcaino.blurb: One of three players to suit up for all four past and present New York teams: Yankees, Mets, Dodgers and Giants. His 12th-inning single won Game 1 of the 2000 World Series, then the longest Series game ever played.

Brian Dozier.blurb: In 2016 became the first American League second baseman to hit 40 home runs, finishing with 42. Homered in his first All-Star at-bat in 2015 and won a Gold Glove in 2017. Minnesota drafted him in the eighth round.

Jhoan Duran.blurb: Came to Minnesota from Arizona in the 2018 Eduardo Escobar trade and posted a 1.86 ERA as a rookie in 2022. Traded to the Phillies in July 2025, he saved 32 games that year and made his first All-Star team in 2026.

Alex Wilson.blurb: Went from Boston to Detroit in the 2014 Rick Porcello trade, alongside Yoenis Cespedes. Had a 2.19 ERA for the Tigers in 2015 and went 4-0 in 2016. Collegiate Baseball's national Freshman Pitcher of the Year in 2006.

Brian Wolfe.blurb: His 2007 debut was the game in which Alex Rodriguez may have shouted to distract Toronto's third baseman from catching a pop fly. Had a 2.98 ERA in 38 games that year, then pitched for three clubs in Japan.

Cole Sands.blurb: Turned down the Astros as a 22nd-round pick in 2015 to pitch at Florida State. Earned his first career save with four innings of relief, and one season went 9-1 in 62 relief appearances for the Twins.

Samuel Deduno.blurb: Pioneer League Pitcher of the Year in 2004 and the Texas League strikeout leader in 2007. Went 8-8 with a 3.83 ERA in 18 starts for the 2013 Twins, though a high walk rate followed him throughout his career.

Ryan Schimpf.blurb: Reached the majors in June 2016 and the next month set a Padres rookie record with nine home runs in July, earning National League Rookie of the Month. Won the 2009 College World Series with LSU.

Storm Davis.blurb: Won 19 games for the 1989 A's with an ERA worse than league average, a season Bill James cites as proof that win-loss records mislead. Won Game Four of the 1983 World Series for Baltimore; a two-time champion.

Norm Charlton.blurb: One of the Reds' "Nasty Boys" with Rob Dibble and Randy Myers on the 1990 champions. Teammates called him "The Genius" for his triple major at Rice; Mariners broadcaster Dave Niehaus later nicknamed him "The Sheriff". Threw one career shutout.

David Dahl.blurb: Opened his career in 2016 with a 17-game hitting streak, tying a record set in 1941. Earlier he had his spleen removed after an injury so he could return to the field sooner. An All-Star for Colorado in 2019.

Brad Boxberger.blurb: The first major-league pitcher known to throw an immaculate inning with the bases loaded: nine pitches, three strikeouts, for Tampa Bay. A first-round pick by the Reds in 2009, he was traded for Mat Latos and debuted with San Diego in 2012.

Ed Vande Berg.blurb: Pitched in 78 games as a rookie for the 1982 Mariners, a major-league rookie record until 1986, going 9-4 with a 2.37 ERA as Bill Caudill's setup man. Traded to the Dodgers for Steve Yeager in 1985.

Jeimer Candelario.blurb: Got a 2016 World Series ring with the Cubs after playing only five games for them. Traded to Detroit in 2017, he hit .297 in 2020 and homered in both games of a doubleheader that September.

Brad Clontz.blurb: From Stuart, Virginia, population 1,400. Struck out the first big-league batter he faced in 1995 and pitched in that year's World Series for Atlanta. Later traded to the Mets with Hideo Nomo for Greg McMichael, whose closer job he had briefly taken.

Jovani Moran.blurb: Drafted by the Twins in 2015 out of the Carlos Beltran Baseball Academy in Puerto Rico. Had a 2.21 ERA with 54 strikeouts in 40 2/3 innings in 2022, missed 2024 after Tommy John surgery, and was traded to Boston.

Ken Griffey.blurb: His own father never played catch with him. He became a regular on the Big Red Machine, the 1980 All-Star Game MVP, and in 1990 hit back-to-back home runs with his son, Ken Griffey Jr., as Seattle teammates.

Darltie Cooper.blurb: Nicknamed "Dolly", an Arkadelphia, Arkansas native who pitched in the Negro leagues from 1923, with the Indianapolis ABCs, to 1940, with the Newark Eagles. His brother Anthony also played. Died in Schenectady, New York, at 41.

James Loney.blurb: Scouts wanted him mostly as a pitcher after a 12-1 senior year with a 1.52 ERA, but the Dodgers drafted him 19th overall in 2002 as a hitter. As a 2006 rookie he drove in nine runs in one game, tying Gil Hodges' franchise record.

Darren O'Day.blurb: A rare submarine pitcher whose family name was originally Odachowski. Claimed by Texas in 2009, he pitched minutes after arriving from the airport, wearing Kason Gabbard's jersey. Undrafted out of Florida; an All-Star in 2015.

Rhett Lowder.blurb: Went 15-0 at Wake Forest in 2023, leading Division I in wins with a school-record 143 strikeouts, and was twice ACC Pitcher of the Year. The Reds drafted him seventh overall that summer and called him up in August 2024.

JR Ritchie.blurb: Gatorade Washington Player of the Year as a high school junior, when he had a 0.38 ERA and also batted .531. Finished his senior year 7-0 with 74 strikeouts and four walks. Reached the Braves in April 2026.

Chuck Churn.blurb: Nicknamed "Slim", he pitched only 25 big-league games but won twice and saved another in September 1959 as the Dodgers chased the pennant. One of those wins handed Elroy Face his only loss in an 18-1 season.

Randal Grichuk.blurb: Drafted 24th overall by the Angels in 2009, one pick ahead of Mike Trout. Played in the Little League World Series in 2003 and 2004, won a minor-league Gold Glove in 2013, and has since played for eight major-league clubs.

Brian Tallet.blurb: A 6-foot-6 pitcher who won a national championship at LSU in 2000. In 2009 he gave up Matt Tuiasosopo's first career home run, which Mike Blowers had correctly predicted in detail. Spent most of his career with Toronto.

Bryce Eldridge.blurb: A two-way player until 2024, when he gave up pitching to play first base. MVP of the 2022 U-18 Baseball World Cup, drafted 16th overall by the Giants in 2023, and in the majors by September 2025.

Mark Loretta.blurb: Hit .335 with 208 hits for the 2004 Padres, joining Tony Gwynn as the only San Diego players with a 200-hit season. An infielder who once pitched for the Brewers, he coached Israel's national team in a 2012 qualifier.

Masataka Yoshida.blurb: Nicknamed "Macho Man" and called "Masa" by teammates. A first-round pick of the Orix Buffaloes in 2015, he set a World Baseball Classic record with 13 RBIs for Japan in 2023, then joined the Red Sox.

Ken Dayley.blurb: The third overall pick in 1980 and a stellar postseason reliever for the Cardinals, with one exception: his first pitch to Kent Hrbek, bases loaded in Game 6 of the 1987 World Series, went over the center field fence for a grand slam.

Jose Alvarado.blurb: Threw an immaculate inning against Milwaukee in August 2017, his debut season with Tampa Bay. Traded to the Phillies in 2020; in Game 4 of the 2022 World Series he entered with the bases loaded and hit Yordan Alvarez with his first pitch.

Luis Medina.blurb: Went from the Yankees to Oakland in the 2022 trade for Frankie Montas and Lou Trivino, along with JP Sears and Ken Waldichuk. Played in the 2021 All-Star Futures Game and debuted in 2023, going 3-10 as a rookie.

Alcides Escobar.blurb: Hit an inside-the-park home run on Matt Harvey's first pitch in Game 1 of the 2015 World Series, the first in a Series game since 1929. MVP of that year's ALCS, batting .478, and a Gold Glove shortstop.

John Grim.blurb: A catcher whose 11 big-league seasons ran from 1888 to 1899. Became Louisville's starter in 1892 and had his best year in 1894, batting .299 with 71 RBI, then spent five seasons in Brooklyn. Also pitched one game and umpired three. Died at 93.

Vicente Padilla.blurb: Came to the Phillies in the 2000 trade for Curt Schilling and was an All-Star two years later, going 14-11. In July 2009 he tested positive for swine flu, believed to be the first major U.S. athlete to catch it.

Collin McHugh.blurb: Went 0-4 with the 2012 Mets and 0-3 with the 2013 Rockies, then led the 2014 Astros with a 2.73 ERA. Won 19 games in 2015; he and Dallas Keuchel were the first Astros pair with 19 wins each since 1999.

Tom Daly.blurb: A second baseman and catcher whose big-league career ran from 1884 to 1903, with stops including Brooklyn and both Chicago clubs. Hit .278 with 385 stolen bases and 103 triples; his brother Joe also played professionally.

Ed Olwine.blurb: Shares the major-league record for most games pitched without a win: 80, all for the Braves from 1986 to 1988. Was the winning pitcher in the Cape Cod League's 1979 all-star game at Fenway Park.

Vic Power.blurb: Stole home twice in one game on August 14, 1958, the first to do it since 1927 and still the last, in a year he stole only three bases. Born Victor Pellot in Arecibo, Puerto Rico, he turned pro at 15 for $100 a week.

Sal Stewart.blurb: The 2026 National League Rookie of the Year and the first Reds rookie with 30 home runs and 100 RBI. That August he became the third rookie ever to reach 100 RBI before anyone else in the majors.

Atlee Hammaker.blurb: Gave up the only grand slam in All-Star Game history, to Fred Lynn in 1983, the same year he led the National League with a 2.25 ERA. With the Giants he was part of the devout group of pitchers known as the "God Squad".

Peter Lambert.blurb: Struck out nine over seven innings at Wrigley Field in his 2019 debut for the Rockies. Had Tommy John surgery in 2020, and in April 2025 tied a Japanese league record with three wild pitches in one inning for the Yakult Swallows.

Jake Odorizzi.blurb: Twice dealt in blockbusters before he was established: from Milwaukee to Kansas City for Zack Greinke in 2010, then to Tampa Bay for James Shields and Wade Davis in 2012. Taken 32nd overall by the Brewers in 2008.

Bob Klinger.blurb: Lost his mother in a fire in 1909 and never knew his father. Joined the Red Sox in May 1946, led the league with nine saves, and was Joe Cronin's choice to face Enos Slaughter in the eighth inning of World Series Game Seven.

Nate Robertson.blurb: Threw five shutout innings to win Game 1 of the 2006 ALCS, starting Detroit's sweep of Oakland and its first pennant since 1984. Came to the Tigers from Florida in a trade for Mark Redman.

Andrew Alvarez.blurb: Won his major-league debut in 2025 with five innings of one-hit ball in a 2-0 Nationals victory, on the same day his catcher also debuted. Washington's Minor League Pitcher of the Year in 2023.

Ted Easterly.blurb: Sent to the Whittier State Reform School as a teenager, where he found baseball. His first big-league start came on his 24th birthday in 1909, catching Cy Young; he was said to swing the heaviest bat in the majors. Hit .300 for his career.

Chad Cordero.blurb: Saved 15 games in June 2005, tying the major-league record for one month, on his way to a majors-best 47 for the Washington Nationals. An All-Star that summer, he struck out the only batter he faced, Ivan Rodriguez.

Jack Smith.blurb: A left-handed outfielder from Chicago who played for the Cardinals from 1915 to 1926 before finishing with the Boston Braves. Hit .287 with 228 stolen bases and 783 runs in 1,406 games.

Trevor Megill.blurb: Got the final six outs of the last game of the 2026 World Series against Tampa Bay, sealing the Brewers' first championship. A seventh-round pick in 2015, he became Milwaukee's closer in 2024 and an All-Star in 2025.

Larry Corcoran.blurb: Called "Little Corcoran" at 5-foot-3 and 127 pounds. He signaled his curves to catcher Silver Flint by shifting a mammoth chew of tobacco in his mouth. The first pitcher to throw three no-hitters; died of Bright's disease at 32.

Justin Crawford.blurb: Singled on the first pitch he saw in the majors, off Nathan Eovaldi, in 2026. The son of 15-year major leaguer Carl Crawford, he was the Phillies' first-round pick in 2022 and a Florida State League MVP.

Grant Anderson.blurb: Struck out the first four batters he faced in his major-league debut for Texas on May 30, 2023. Had a 13.80 ERA as a college freshman, then went 8-0 as a sophomore. Traded to Milwaukee in January 2025.

Brock Burke.blurb: Named Texas Rangers Rookie of the Year by the DFW-area baseball writers in 2022 after a 1.97 ERA with 90 strikeouts in 82 1/3 innings. Went 7-1 in 69 appearances for the Angels in 2025.

Tsung-Che Cheng.blurb: Known as "Z" because all three characters of his name start with that letter in pinyin. The Taiwanese infielder hit for the first cycle in Worcester Red Sox history and led the 2026 World Baseball Classic with four steals.

Henry Bolte.blurb: Tied a Pacific Coast League record in May 2026 with hits in 12 consecutive at-bats for Las Vegas, and was called up by the Athletics days later. Singled in his first two big-league at-bats.

Corey Knebel.blurb: In 2017 he struck out at least one batter in 45 straight relief appearances, breaking Aroldis Chapman's record. The draft slot Detroit used on him in 2013 was the first traded pick in major-league history.

Bill Robinson.blurb: Known around his hometown of Elizabeth, Pennsylvania, as "Weaser", a nickname he could not explain. Called himself baseball's No. 1 utility man in 1977, then hit .304 with 26 homers and 104 RBIs that year while starting at four positions.

Miguel Sano.blurb: Runner-up to Aaron Judge in the 2017 Home Run Derby, the year he was an All-Star. His $3.15 million bonus from the Twins in 2009 was then the second highest ever for a Dominican amateur. Hit a career-high 34 home runs in 2019.

Greg McMichael.blurb: Told at 13 that a rare cartilage disease in his knees had ended his sports career. Released by Cleveland, he made the 1993 Braves as their only rookie, then won his 1995 World Series ring against the Indians, the team that drafted him.

Daniel Norris.blurb: Lived in a van and on $800 a month despite a $2 million signing bonus. In 2014 he became the first pitcher in Buffalo Bisons history with back-to-back starts of ten or more strikeouts; traded to Detroit in the 2015 David Price deal.

Joe Niekro.blurb: Caught on the mound in 1987 with an emery board and sandpaper flying out of his pocket, he said he had been filing his nails and was suspended ten games. In 1979 he and brother Phil tied for the major-league lead in wins.

David Bell.blurb: When he debuted for Cleveland in 1995, the Bells became the second family, after the Boones, with three generations of major leaguers. On April 15, 1998, he hit the first inside-the-park home run ever at Jacobs Field.

Brian Fisher.blurb: Figured in two notable trades: Atlanta sent him to the Yankees for Rick Cerone in 1984, and New York sent him with Doug Drabek to Pittsburgh after 1986. Pitched seven major-league seasons for four clubs.

Vic Harris.blurb: The fiery heart and soul of the Homestead Grays, feared on the bases: Buck Leonard said he would cut the uniform right off an infielder's back. Became the Grays' manager in 1935 and was picked for seven East-West All-Star Games.

Barney Brown.blurb: Negro leagues pitcher and outfielder who played from 1931 to 1949. His teams included the Cuban House of David, also known as Pollock's Cuban Stars, the Philadelphia Stars and the New York Black Yankees.

Jonathan Broxton.blurb: His first big-league strikeout victim was Albert Pujols. An All-Star closer for the Dodgers who saved the 2010 All-Star Game, he tied a dubious record in 2012 by ending and losing a game on consecutive hit batters.

Chase Silseth.blurb: The first player from the 2021 draft to reach the majors, debuting in May 2022 even though he was an 11th-round pick. Had a 0.56 ERA as a high school junior in Farmington, New Mexico.

Geraldo Perdomo.blurb: His first career home run, in June 2022, was a grand slam. An All-Star shortstop in 2023, when he helped the Diamondbacks win their first National League pennant since 2001. Debuted in 2021.

Cade Cavalli.blurb: Went 1,076 days between his first and second major-league appearances, returning in August 2025. The 22nd pick of the 2020 draft, he once led the minor leagues with 175 strikeouts and also hit .319 as a college sophomore.

Danny Coulombe.blurb: Felt a pop in his shoulder in the first inning of his first college start at USC. Reached the Dodgers in 2014, did not make an Opening Day roster until 2022, and later posted a 1.16 ERA in 40 games for the Twins.

Tommy Hanson.blurb: The first pitcher named MVP of the Arizona Fall League. With Atlanta in 2009 he became the first National League rookie to win consecutive starts against the Yankees and Red Sox, and finished third in Rookie of the Year voting. Died at 29.

Roberto Hernandez.blurb: Had a vein from his leg transplanted into his pitching arm, and a doctor told him he would never pitch again. He was back on a mound that July, made two All-Star teams as a closer, and recorded his 300th save in 2002.

Chris Bassitt.blurb: Starred in both basketball and baseball in high school and at Akron, where he pitched in only one game as a sophomore to focus on academics. Traded with Marcus Semien to Oakland in 2014; AL Pitcher of the Month in September 2020.

Danny Green.blurb: Took over center field for the Chicago Orphans in 1898 when Bill Lange retired to get married, then jumped to the White Sox in 1902. Hit .293 with 192 steals; died three days after his 38th birthday.

Myril Hoag.blurb: Missed part of 1936 with a blood clot on the brain after an outfield collision with teammate Joe DiMaggio. Had six hits in one game in 1934, a feat no Yankee matched until 1996, and won three World Series.

Jim O'Toole.blurb: A Chicago policeman's son and Golden Gloves boxer. After his lone 1958 start, a 2-1 loss to the Braves, Parade magazine flew him to The Ed Sullivan Show to advise the Yankees on pitching to Milwaukee. Went 19-9 for the 1961 pennant-winning Reds.

Terry Forster.blurb: David Letterman mocked his weight on national television in 1985; he answered by eating a sandwich on Letterman's set and recording a novelty song, "Fat Is In". Led the American League with 24 saves in 1974 and won a ring with the 1981 Dodgers.

Armando Cabanas.blurb: Nicknamed "Chino", a Cuban second baseman and outfielder who played from 1899 to 1916 for clubs including Almendares, Habana and the Cuban Stars. Elected to the Cuban Baseball Hall of Fame in 1959, the year he died.

Earl Wilson.blurb: In 1962 he became the first African American to throw a no-hitter in the American League, a 2-0 Red Sox win. That year he also became one of the first pro athletes with an agent, starting Bob Woolf's career. Won 121 games.

Robbie Ray.blurb: Grew up near Nashville playing travel ball alongside Mookie Betts, and threw three no-hitters, one of them a perfect game, as a high school senior. Won the 2021 American League Cy Young Award with Toronto while leading the majors in strikeouts.

Jake Bennett.blurb: Traded from the Nationals to the Red Sox in December 2025 for another pitching prospect, Luis Perales. Opened 2026 with a 0.86 ERA over five outings at Worcester and was in the majors by May 1.

Mike Armstrong.blurb: A first-round pick by the Reds in 1974 out of the University of Miami. Kansas City traded him to the Yankees after 1983 for Steve Balboni, who hit over 100 home runs for the Royals while Armstrong arrived with a sore arm.

Tanner Scott.blurb: Became the Marlins' closer in 2023 and was National League Reliever of the Month that September, finishing with a 2.31 ERA and 104 strikeouts in 78 innings. Debuted with Baltimore in 2017; later an All-Star and a Dodger.

Keider Montero.blurb: Threw a shutout against Colorado as a rookie while facing the minimum 27 batters: all three hits he allowed were erased on double plays. Went 10-9 with a 3.48 ERA for the 2026 Tigers.

Kevin Youkilis.blurb: Homered in his first major-league game and came back to a silent dugout, a prank organized by Pedro Martinez. Went from July 2006 through all of 2007 without an error at first base. Now brews beer, including the Greek God of Hops.

Keibert Ruiz.blurb: Homered in his first major-league at-bat, off Julio Teheran in 2020. Went to Washington in the 2021 trade for Trea Turner and Max Scherzer. In 2025 he suffered a concussion when a foul ball hit him in the dugout.

Josh Collmenter.blurb: Built his extreme overhand delivery as a boy throwing tomahawks at trees and snakes with his brothers, and learned pitch grips from Sports Illustrated. Led his Michigan high school to a 38-0 season with a 0.13 ERA and 13 shutouts.

Kutter Crawford.blurb: Led the league with 33 starts for Boston in 2024, and with 16 losses, while striking out a career-high 175. A 16th-round pick who had Tommy John surgery in 2019; his older brother Jonathon was a first-round pick in 2013.

Orion Kerkering.blurb: Shares the first name Richard with his father and grandfather, though all three go by their different middle names. Climbed four minor-league levels in 2023 with a 1.51 ERA and reached the Phillies that September.

Yennier Cano.blurb: Retired the first 24 batters he faced in 2023 without a baserunner, tying an Orioles record, and made the All-Star team that summer. Came from Minnesota in the 2022 trade for Jorge Lopez.

Clyde Vollmer.blurb: Reached the ballpark in 1942 with a doubleheader already under way and told manager McKechnie he didn't know the take sign. Told to swing at the first pitch, he homered on it in his first at-bat. Teammates called him Big 'Un.

Matt Harrison.blurb: One of five players Atlanta sent to Texas for Mark Teixeira in 2007, along with Elvis Andrus and Neftali Feliz. Won the game that clinched the 2011 division title, then went 18-11 as an All-Star in 2012.

Yoenis Cespedes.blurb: Nicknamed "La Potencia", The Power. Hit 169 home runs in eight seasons for Granma in Cuba before defecting; back then his first name was usually spelled Yoennis. Won the Home Run Derby in 2013 and 2014.

MacKenzie Gore.blurb: Threw a no-hitter with 18 strikeouts in high school, where he won three state titles and was MVP of each final. Went to Washington in the 2022 Juan Soto trade, then struck out the first six Padres he faced in a 2023 start.

Dylan Beavers.blurb: Hit his first major-league home run in his first plate appearance at Camden Yards in August 2025, only the third Oriole to do that. An International League MVP and twice first-team All-Pac-12 at California.

Juan Eichelberger.blurb: Nearly threw the Padres' first no-hitter in June 1982: the only Cubs hit was a ground ball the scorer chose not to call an error. Twice led the Pacific Coast League in walks; known for an unusual set position.

Jeremy Jeffress.blurb: Sent with Alcides Escobar, Lorenzo Cain and Jake Odorizzi to Kansas City for Zack Greinke in 2010. Kept returning to Milwaukee, where he saved 27 games in 2016 and was an All-Star in 2018.

Zach Agnos.blurb: A two-way player at East Carolina, taken by the Rockies in the 10th round in 2022. Did not allow a run in his first six big-league outings in 2025, capping the streak with saves on back-to-back days.

Dustin May.blurb: Won the World Series with the Dodgers in 2020 and with the Brewers in 2026. A third-round pick in 2016; in his first start back from injury in August 2022 he struck out nine over five one-hit innings.

David Peralta.blurb: Signed by the Cardinals in 2004 as a pitcher, was released, and remade himself as an outfielder in independent leagues. Reached Arizona in 2014, then won a Silver Slugger in 2018 and a Gold Glove in 2019.

Chris Bosio.blurb: Walked the first two Red Sox he faced on April 22, 1993, then retired 27 in a row for the second no-hitter in Mariners history. Won 16 games for Milwaukee in 1992; later a big-league pitching coach.

Alexis Diaz.blurb: Earned his first save in 2022 on the same day his brother Edwin earned one, making them the third pair of brothers to save games on the same day. An All-Star closer for the Reds in 2023 with 37 saves.

Bill Joyce.blurb: Nicknamed "Scrappy" as a young rolling-mill worker in St. Louis. Hit four triples in one game in 1897, held out the entire 1893 season over salary, and in 1896 was called the most conspicuous character in baseball. Career on-base percentage: .435.

Seranthony Dominguez.blurb: Says he isn't sure where his unusual first name comes from. In 2018 he became the first pitcher in recorded history to allow no run, hit or walk in his first six appearances. Has twice won Game 1 of a World Series.

Andrew Walters.blurb: A consensus first-team All-American closer at Miami in 2023, with a 1.21 ERA and 72 strikeouts in 44 2/3 innings. Earlier led the ACC with 14 saves, and reached the Guardians in September 2024.

Don Schwall.blurb: A 6-foot-6 former Oklahoma basketball center who once outscored Wilt Chamberlain. American League Rookie of the Year for Boston in 1961, when he struck out Stan Musial in an All-Star Game and gave up Mickey Mantle's 54th and last home run of the season.

Charlie Leibrandt.blurb: Went 17-9 with a 2.69 ERA for the 1985 champion Royals, but is best known for October hard luck, above all the walk-off home run Kirby Puckett hit off him in Game 6 of the 1991 World Series.

Heathcliff Slocumb.blurb: Showed up to his first baseball tryout, as a high school junior in Queens, without a glove. An All-Star in 1995, but best remembered for the 1997 trade that sent him to Seattle for Derek Lowe and Jason Varitek.

Martin Perez.blurb: Took a perfect game into the seventh inning against Houston in May 2022, his All-Star season, when he had a 2.89 ERA for Texas. Won the 2023 World Series with the Rangers and has pitched for seven clubs.

Akil Baddoo.blurb: Homered on the first pitch he saw in the majors in April 2021, hit a grand slam the next day, and had a walk-off hit the day after. No player since at least 1900 had done all that in his first three games.

Trevor Rogers.blurb: National League Rookie of the Month in both April and May 2021, an All-Star that July, and runner-up to Jonathan India for Rookie of the Year with a 2.64 ERA. The 13th pick of the 2017 draft; traded to Baltimore in 2024.

Eddie Moore.blurb: Hit the last "bounce" home run in the majors in 1930, when a ball bouncing into the stands counted as a homer. Pittsburgh sold him in 1926 after a dugout shouting match that began when his nervous smile after an error was taken for indifference.

J.J. Hardy.blurb: Won three straight Gold Gloves at shortstop for Baltimore from 2012 to 2014, passing Cal Ripken Jr. for second most by an Orioles shortstop, plus a Silver Slugger in 2013. An All-Star with Milwaukee in 2007.

Yuki Matsui.blurb: Struck out 22 in one high school game, and five clubs picked him in Japan's 2013 draft. Pitched ten seasons for the Rakuten Golden Eagles before signing a five-year, $28 million deal with San Diego. Stands 5-foot-8.

Evan Sisk.blurb: Traded three times: from St. Louis to Minnesota in 2021, to Kansas City in 2023, and to Pittsburgh in 2025 for Bailey Falter. Had a 1.57 ERA with 15 saves at Omaha in 2024 and debuted in April 2025.

Dennis Martinez.blurb: The first Nicaraguan in the majors, in 1976. Ken Singleton nicknamed him "El Presidente" in 1979. Overcame an alcohol problem to win more than half of his 245 games afterward, and threw a perfect game on July 28, 1991.

Victor Mesa Jr..blurb: Hit his first big-league home run on his 24th birthday in 2025. Traded to Tampa Bay, he hit a go-ahead two-run homer off Max Fried in the deciding game of the 2026 Division Series against the Yankees.

Tim Mayza.blurb: Gave up Aaron Judge's 61st home run in September 2022, the one that tied the American League record. A 12th-round pick from Millersville, he went 8-1 with a 3.14 ERA for Toronto that same season.

Desmond Jennings.blurb: Led all junior college wide receivers with 54 catches before the Rays drafted him in 2006. His first walk-off home run, in September 2011, gave Tampa Bay the 1,000th win in franchise history.

Nathan Flewelling.blurb: Canadian catcher from Red Deer, Alberta, who played summer ball for the Sylvan Lake Gulls before Tampa Bay drafted him in the third round in 2024. Began his pro career in 2025 with Charleston and Bowling Green.

Luis Arraez.blurb: Nicknamed "La Regadera", The Sprinkler. From 2022 to 2024 he became the first player to win three straight batting titles with three different teams, spoiling Triple Crown bids by Aaron Judge and Shohei Ohtani along the way.

Adrian Morejon.blurb: Debuted with San Diego in 2019, the year he pitched in the All-Star Futures Game. Went 5-1 in a career-high 26 appearances in 2022 and became an All-Star in 2025, replacing Zack Wheeler on the roster.

Ryan Mountcastle.blurb: His 33 home runs in 2021 were the most ever by an Orioles rookie and led all rookies in the majors. Hit three in one game that June, and in April 2023 tied a club record with nine RBI against Oakland.

Hector Rondon.blurb: Came back from Tommy John surgery in 2010 and a fractured elbow in 2011 to be taken by the Cubs in the 2012 Rule 5 Draft. Became their closer in 2014 and was on the 2016 team that ended a 108-year drought.

Elmer Dessens.blurb: A newspaper boy at age ten in Hermosillo, Mexico. Released by Pittsburgh in 1999, he pitched a season for the Yomiuri Giants in Japan, then returned with Cincinnati in 2000 and went on to pitch for eight major-league clubs.

Edward Cabrera.blurb: Tied a Marlins record for strikeouts by a reliever in one game with eight against the Dodgers. Signed in 2015, he went 8-7 with a 3.53 ERA in 2025 before being traded to the Cubs for three players.
